title: Precision gene editing in infant neuroblastoma: a review of nanoparticle: enabled CRISPR/Cas9 therapies.
abstract: Infant neuroblastoma (NB), defined by diagnosis during the first year of life, represents a clinically heterogeneous disease spectrum ranging from localized tumours with favourable outcomes and a capacity for spontaneous regression, to high-risk metastatic disease requiring intensive multimodal therapy. In infants, treatment intensity is determined by disease stage, tumor biology, MYCN status, risk classification, symptoms, response to therapy, and metastatic involvement, particularly relevant to high-risk disease, consequently the potential toxicity of intensive treatment is specific to high-risk disease, as compared to favorable risk tumors which can be managed with surgery, reduced frequency techniques, or observations. Important determinations of neuroblastoma biology and prognosis are genetic alterations involving MYCN and ALK, but the predominately investigated field with therapeutic feasibility of targeting these changes with CRISPR/Cas9 is in preclinical neuroblastoma models rather than in infants. An investigational hypothesis is accordingly considered by their potential relevance to infant neuroblastoma rather than an established clinical application. The safe and efficient in vivo delivery of CRISPR/Cas9 components remains a major challenge, owing to cargo size, immunogenicity, and degradation, particularly within the delicate physiological environment of infants. This review emphasises the need for advanced delivery systems, focusing on the potential of nanoparticle-mediated approaches. Emerging preclinical findings support the feasibility of nanoparticle-mediated CRISPR/Cas9 delivery, although direct evidence in infant neuroblastoma remains limited. Importantly, the evidence for nanoparticle-mediated CRISPR/Cas9 therapy remains largely preclinical. Studies performed in general neuroblastoma models, non-cancer models, or adult cancers should not be interpreted as direct evidence of efficacy in infant neuroblastoma.

title: Modeling Moyamoya disease using patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells and organoids.
abstract: The underlying mechanisms of Moyamoya disease (MMD), a rare, progressive cerebrovascular disorder marked by distal internal carotid artery stenosis or occlusion and the formation of fragile collaterals, remain poorly understood, in part because conventional models fail to capture the genetic, vascular, and neurovascular complexity of human MMD. Driven by recent advances in disease modeling, MMD research has moved beyond early endothelial progenitor cell studies toward patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-based platforms. Here, we summarize the generation and validation of MMD-specific iPSCs and their differentiation into endothelial cells (ECs), vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), and related vascular lineages, and we discuss how two-dimensional (2D) iPSC-based models have provided insights into impaired angiogenesis, endothelial dysfunction, abnormal VSMC behavior, and disrupted vascular cell interactions. We then highlight the emerging use of three-dimensional vascular and neurovascular organoids, which reproduce cellular heterogeneity, vessel-like organization, and neurovascular unit interactions more closely than conventional 2D cultures. These models may provide a more integrated platform for investigating the complex vascular pathophysiology of MMD. Finally, we discuss future directions for MMD modeling, including the integration of multi-omics profiling and CRISPR-mediated genome editing with patient-derived iPSC and organoid platforms. These approaches may help clarify genotype-phenotype relationships, RNF213-dependent and RNF213-independent mechanisms, and disease-relevant molecular pathways. With further standardization and validation, iPSC- and organoid-based models could support mechanistic studies, therapeutic screening, and personalized disease modeling. Our review underscores the emerging role of patient-derived stem cell and organoid technologies in advancing MMD research and in informing future translational efforts.

title: Why does siRNA delivery still fail in neurodegenerative diseases? Biological barriers, nanocarrier engineering, and future translational directions.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases remain largely untreatable at the disease-modifying level, with currently approved therapies providing primarily symptomatic benefits. Small interfering RNA (siRNA) has emerged as a promising therapeutic modality because of its ability to selectively silence disease-associated genes. However, a major obstacle to clinical translation is not the gene-silencing mechanism itself, but the efficient delivery of therapeutic siRNAs to target cells within the central nervous system.This review examines the barriers that limit siRNA-based therapies for neurodegenerative diseases. We adopt a barrier-oriented framework that follows the sequential challenges encountered during siRNA delivery, including extracellular instability, unfavorable pharmacokinetics, immune recognition, limited transport across the blood-brain barrier, inefficient cellular internalization, and endosomal entrapment. Rather than cataloguing available delivery systems, we evaluate how nanocarrier engineering strategies have been developed to address these barriers and assess their impact on delivery. Evidence from Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and Huntington's disease is synthesized to distinguish shared limitations from disease-specific challenges and to evaluate the translational performance of lipid-based nanoparticles, polymeric nanocarriers, engineered exosomes, and hybrid platforms.Available evidence indicates that delivery platforms can improve specific aspects of siRNA transport but have not consistently overcome the sequential biological barriers required for therapy. Although nanocarrier engineering has enhanced siRNA stability, brain targeting, intracellular trafficking, and gene-silencing efficiency in preclinical models, manufacturing scalability, biological heterogeneity, long-term safety, reproducibility, and regulatory feasibility remain important barriers to clinical translation. Future progress will likely depend on delivery systems that integrate effective brain transport, endosomal escape, controlled intracellular release, and scalable manufacturing within clinical platforms.

title: Fluorogenic RNA aptamers in cancer: emerging platforms for molecular imaging, biosensing, and precision oncology.
abstract: Fluorogenic RNA aptamers have emerged as powerful molecular tools for cancer imaging, biosensing, and biomarker detection due to their high specificity, low background fluorescence, and genetic encodability. These short RNA molecules activate fluorescence upon binding specific fluorogens, enabling real-time visualization of intracellular targets and dynamic molecular processes in living systems. Recent advances in RNA structural engineering, fluorophore optimization, and biosensor integration have significantly expanded the translational applications of fluorogenic aptamers in oncology. This mini-review summarizes the structural principles, fluorescence activation mechanisms, and cancer-related applications of fluorogenic RNA aptamers and related nucleic acid biosensors. Foundational studies describing the architecture of fluorogenic aptamer families, including Spinach, Broccoli, Mango, Pepper, Squash, and Beetroot, are discussed with emphasis on G-quadruplex-mediated fluorogen stabilization and fluorescence enhancement. Furthermore, recent developments in CRISPR/Cas-assisted fluorogenic biosensors, dual-color RNA imaging systems, fluorogenic DNAzymes, and amplification-driven aptamer platforms are highlighted. Direct applications across multiple malignancies, including brain, breast, colorectal, liver, lung, prostate, and skin cancers, demonstrate the growing utility of these technologies for tumor-associated RNA detection, epigenetic biomarker analysis, molecular imaging, and therapeutic monitoring. In addition, advances in fluorescence brightness, structural stability, and multiplex imaging strategies have improved the sensitivity and adaptability of fluorogenic RNA systems for complex biological environments. Despite current limitations related to RNA stability, intracellular delivery, and tissue penetration, fluorogenic RNA aptamers represent highly promising tools for next-generation precision oncology. Continued integration with nanotechnology, live-cell imaging, artificial intelligence, and molecular diagnostics is expected to enhance further their clinical and translational potential in cancer research and personalized medicine.

title: CRISPR genome editing in food and feed crops: intellectual property challenges, global accessibility, and the Indian perspective.
abstract: The ever-increasing global demand for food and feed, coupled with population growth and climate change, necessitates the development of high-yielding and stress-resilient crops. CRISPR (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) technology has emerged as a transformative genome-editing tool due to its efficiency, precision, and ability to generate targeted genetic modifications. This review highlights recent advances in CRISPR genome editing, including base editing, prime editing, and novel Cas variants, together with emerging approaches such as epigenome editing, mitochondrial genome editing, and hypercompact Cas systems, and their applications in improving crop productivity, stress tolerance, and nutritional quality. In food and feed crops, these applications also include crop-specific priorities such as grain and nutritional quality in food crops and digestibility, forage quality, and mineral bioavailability in feed and forage crops. Particular emphasis is placed on the complex intellectual property (IP) landscape surrounding CRISPR technologies, including patents on editing systems, delivery platforms, and proprietary vectors. These intellectual property barriers can restrict research access, technology transfer, and commercialization, particularly in developing countries. The review further discusses patent limitations, licensing frameworks, and strategies to enhance equitable global access through collaborative approaches such as non-exclusive licensing, humanitarian licensing, indigenous technology development, and international partnerships. Overall, the review underscores the need to balance innovation, intellectual property protection, and global accessibility to ensure that CRISPR-based technologies contribute effectively to worldwide food and feed security and sustainable agriculture.

title: Generation of DFNA5-deficient chickens reveals a species-specific role of pyroptosis in avian antiviral immunity.
abstract: The global burden of viral diseases in both humans and agricultural animals is exacerbated by dysregulated inflammatory cell death and cytokine storms. Pyroptosis, executed by gasdermin family proteins, is a key driver of this pathology, yet its functional conservation and therapeutic targeting in avian species remain critically unexplored. Here, we establish the first germline-edited heterozygous DFNA5-mutant chicken model using primordial germ cell mediated genome editing. We demonstrate that genetic disruption of DFNA5 markedly attenuates Raptinal-induced pyroptosis and reduces IL-1β and IL-18 secretion. Using an optimized adenoviral dual-sgRNA delivery system, we successfully generated chimeric chickens with stable germline transmission of a frameshift deletion in DFNA5. Notably, DFNA5 deficiency is associated with reduced expression of the viral gp85 gene following avian leukosis virus subgroup J (ALV-J) infection. Mechanistically, transcriptome analysis reveals that downregulated genes in ALV-J-infected DFNA5-mutant cells are enriched in apoptosis and NOD-like receptor signaling pathways, while upregulated genes are associated with cell adhesion, extracellular matrix organization, and homeostatic pathways, suggesting a possible shift from pyroptotic inflammation toward cellular integrity and repair. This work provides genetic evidence that a possible association between DFNA5-mediated pyroptotic responses and establishes a genetic strategy for poultry disease resistance research and for understanding host-virus evolution and viral-induced inflammatory pathologies across vertebrates.

title: Bacterial extracellular vesicles as emerging biostimulants in plant microbe signaling and stress tolerance.
abstract: Bacterial extracellular vesicles (BEVs) are nanosized membrane-bound nanoparticles naturally secreted by Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria. These vesicles mediate intercellular communication through delivery of diverse bioactive cargo, including proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, metabolites, and signaling molecules. Initially recognized as virulence determinants in pathogenic bacteria, BEVs are increasingly recognized as multifunctional platforms with potential applications in sustainable agriculture. This review examines BEV biogenesis, cargo composition, plant uptake, and emerging roles in plant growth promotion, stress adaptation, and disease resistance. Emphasis is placed on BEV-mediated modulation of plant immunity through pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), pattern-triggered immunity (PTI), and induced systemic resistance (ISR). Potential roles of vesicle-associated phytohormones, ACC deaminase, siderophores, extracellular enzymes, and regulatory RNAs in nutrient acquisition, phytohormone homeostasis, and stress responses are critically evaluated. Emerging evidence linking BEVs to drought, salinity, heat, heavy metal, and nutrient-deficiency responses is examined, with emphasis on antioxidant defense, osmotic adjustment, ion homeostasis, and stress-responsive signaling. The review also discusses engineered BEVs as potential biostimulants, nano-biofertilizers, biocontrol agents, and precision delivery systems, including CRISPR-based engineering, synthetic vesicles, AI-guided cargo optimization, and smart nanoformulations. Major challenges include scalable production, standardization, biosafety, regulation, and field validation. However, critical knowledge gaps remain regarding BEV perception, cellular uptake, cargo delivery, and the causal basis of plant responses, together with uncertainties surrounding biosafety, reproducibility, and performance under field conditions. Collectively, BEVs represent promising biological nanocarriers for climate-resilient and sustainable agriculture, but further mechanistic, methodological, and field-based research is required to establish their reliability and practical agricultural potential.

title: Optimization of lipid nanoparticles reduces hepatic accumulation and enhances local delivery of mRNA.
abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have emerged as the most widely used non-viral gene delivery system, particularly for mRNA therapeutics. However, predominant hepatic accumulation and poor local delivery remain major barriers to their broader application. To address this challenge, we employed a design of experiments (DOE) strategy to systematically refine LNP composition and identified an optimized formulation, SM102M. Compared with the parental SM102 formulation, SM102M markedly reduced liver-associated signal after both intramuscular and intravenous administration, while preserving or enhancing local expression after local delivery. Across multiple local administration routes, including intramuscular, intracerebroventricular, and intravitreal injection, SM102M supported localized gene delivery and gene editing with minimal liver-associated signal. Mechanistically, the altered biodistribution of SM102M was associated with reduced apolipoprotein E (ApoE) binding, lower systemic exposure, and diminished lysosomal escape in hepatocytes. SM102M also showed favorable tolerability and maintained local delivery performance under repeated administration. Together, these findings establish DOE as a practical framework for rational LNP engineering and identify a formulation with reduced hepatic reporter expression and improved local delivery performance.

title: Current understanding and new promises of umbilical cord blood in emerging clinical applications.
abstract: Umbilical cord blood (UCB) has become an important resource for regenerative medicine owing to its unique cellular composition, immune immaturity, and abundance of bioactive factors. Although UCB was initially applied in hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, accumulating evidence indicates that its diverse cellular and paracrine components possess broad regenerative potential. Beyond conventional hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, substantial progress has expanded the therapeutic scope of UCB to immune cell-based therapies, the treatment of genetic and metabolic disorders, and tissue repair. In this review, we focus on the biological characteristics of the key cellular and noncellular components of UCB and analyze how these properties support tissue repair, immunomodulation, and regeneration across multiple organ systems. We further summarize recent technological advances, including cell engineering, gene modification, and manufacturing technologies, that have enhanced the scalability and therapeutic potential of UCB-derived products. In addition, we highlight current challenges that limit their widespread clinical application. This review aims to provide a framework for optimizing UCB-based therapies and accelerating their clinical translation. Optimizing UCB collection, processing, and application strategies may further unlock its therapeutic potential, thereby improving clinical efficacy and expanding its applicability to a broader range of diseases.

title: Targeting Apolipoprotein C-III in Hypertriglyceridemia: Implications for Pancreatitis and Cardiovascular risk.
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Apolipoprotein C-III (apoC-III) has emerged as a validated target for lowering triglycerides, triglyceride-rich lipoproteins, and remnant cholesterol. This review summarizes the biology of apoC-III, the genetic and clinical trial evidence supporting its inhibition, and remaining questions.
RECENT FINDINGS: Loss-of-function variants in APOC3 are associated with lower levels of triglycerides and reduced cardiovascular risk. Pharmacologic inhibition of apoC-III with RNA-based agents has led to substantial reductions in apoC-III and triglycerides across familial chylomicronemia syndrome (FCS), severe hypertriglyceridemia (sHTG), and moderate hypertriglyceridemia (mHTG). In FCS, agents volanesorsen, olezarsen, and plozasiran have demonstrated reductions in triglycerides and acute pancreatitis. In sHTG, olezarsen has extended this benefit to a larger, multifactorial population. In mHTG, olezarsen and plozasiran lower triglycerides, remnant cholesterol, non-HDL-cholesterol, and apolipoprotein B, but an imaging study with olezarsen demonstrated neutral findings on coronary plaque composition, and cardiovascular event reduction has not been demonstrated. ApoC-III inhibition provides a potent strategy for lowering triglycerides and triglyceride-rich lipoproteins. Its most immediate clinical role is in FCS and sHTG, where prevention of acute pancreatitis is the main objective. Its future as a cardiovascular therapy will depend on whether reductions in remnant cholesterol and apolipoprotein B translate into fewer atherosclerotic events in a dedicated cardiovascular outcomes trial.

title: RNA-Based Therapies for Lipoprotein(a) Reduction: Antisense Oligonucleotides, Small Interfering RNAs, and Emerging Platforms.
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is an independent, genetically determined, and causal risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) and calcific aortic valve stenosis. Elevated Lp(a) affects approximately 20% of the global population and is not meaningfully modified by lifestyle intervention or existing lipid-lowering pharmacotherapy. This review summarizes the biology of Lp(a) as a therapeutic target, evaluates the efficacy of currently available lipid-lowering agents against this target, and describes the mechanistic principles, clinical evidence, and unresolved questions associated with RNA-based and emerging small-molecule and gene-editing approaches to Lp(a) reduction.
RECENT FINDINGS: Four RNA-directed agents targeting hepatic apolipoprotein(a) [apo(a)] synthesis have entered phase 2/3 development. This includes pelacarsen, an antisense oligonucleotide (ASO), and olpasiran, zerlasiran, and lepodisiran, which are N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc)-conjugated small interfering RNAs (siRNAs). Phase 2 data demonstrate Lp(a) reductions ranging from 79% to approximately 97% on a placebo-adjusted basis, approaching the practical limit of apo(a) suppression, with favorable short-term safety profiles. A fifth, structurally distinct siRNA conjugated with GalNAc at both strand termini has recently completed first-in-human testing, sustaining reductions up to 97% through 48 weeks after a single dose without injection-site reactions. Recently, the topline results of phase 3 Lp(a) HORIZON (pelacarsen) were released and demonstrate a substantial Lp(a) reduction without meeting the trial's primary composite cardiovascular endpoint. Two further outcomes trials, OCEAN(a)-Outcomes (olpasiran) and ACCLAIM-Lp(a) (lepodisiran), remain ongoing. An oral small molecule, muvalaplin, achieved comparable reductions in phase 2 testing. Lastly, early non-human primate data, together with a completed phase 1 trial of an analogous CRISPR-Cas9 construct targeting a related hepatic lipid gene, support the feasibility of a CRISPR-Cas9-based gene-editing approach capable of durable apo(a) suppression from a single administration. The pharmacology of Lp(a) suppression is now well characterized across three distinct therapeutic modalities. Whether the magnitude of biochemical reduction observed translates into a meaningful and safe reduction in cardiovascular events across different populations remains undetermined and will be addressed by the ongoing outcomes trials.

title: Revisiting Ehrlich carcinoma in the era of precision oncology: bridging classical models with modern systems biology.
abstract: Ehrlich carcinoma (EC) and its ascitic form, Ehrlich ascites carcinoma (EAC), are among the oldest and most widely used experimental tumor models in cancer research. Although they have traditionally been used for anticancer drug screening, their potential to address broader aspects of aggressive tumor biology has received comparatively less attention. EC/EAC exhibits several characteristics associated with advanced malignancy, including rapid tumor growth, angiogenesis, immune dysregulation, metabolic changes, therapeutic resistance, and complex interactions between the tumor and host. These features make EC/EAC a useful complementary model for studying different aspects of tumor progression. However, research using these models has largely focused on transcriptional changes and individual signalling pathways, while post-transcriptional regulatory mechanisms remain less explored. In particular, the role of the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC), a major component of microRNA-mediated gene regulation, is still poorly understood in EC/EAC. In this review, we discuss the major limitations of current EC/EAC research, including the limited use of multi-omics approaches, single-cell and spatial analyses, functional genomics, immune checkpoint profiling, and integrated systems-level studies. We further discuss how incorporating RISC-centered regulatory networks with emerging approaches such as CRISPR-based studies, spatial transcriptomics, and metabolic profiling could provide deeper mechanistic insights and improve the translational value of these models. Bringing together the strengths of this established tumor model with contemporary approaches in cancer biology could help reposition EC/EAC as a relevant and versatile platform for studying tumor progression and therapeutic responses.

title: Advances in Extracellular Vesicle-Based Innovative Drugs Targeting Alzheimer's Disease.
abstract: The scarcity of effective therapies for Alzheimer's disease (AD) underscores the urgent need for innovative strategies. This review focuses on the targeted delivery of engineered small extracellular vesicles (sEVs, 30-150 nm). By capitalizing on their intrinsic properties as natural nanocarriers-including low immunogenicity and excellent biocompatibility-these EVs can be engineered to co-deliver therapeutic cargoes such as specific miRNAs, neurotrophic factors (e.g., BDNF), and nucleic acid modalities (e.g., siRNA/ASO targeting BACE1). While a single construct simultaneously delivering all these agents with proven in vivo synergy remains a conceptual framework rather than a validated reality, independent studies have demonstrated that EV-mediated delivery of each cargo type exerts beneficial effects on AD pathology, including Aβ clearance, Tau pathology alleviation, and neuroinflammation suppression. The intranasal administration offers a significant brain-targeting advantage by enabling direct nose-to-brain delivery, bypassing the blood-brain barrier and minimizing peripheral biodistribution. Recently, a phase I/II trial (Ruijin Hospital) demonstrated that intranasal MSC-EVs are safe and produce durable cognitive improvements (ADAS-Cog ↓ 2.33 points at week 12, sustained to - 3.98 points at week 36) in the medium-dose cohort, exceeding the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) of ≥ 2 points for AD. Based on these demonstrated clinical and preclinical evidence, we propose that rationally engineered EVs, following rigorous systematic pharmacology and safety assessments, hold transformative potential to pioneer a safe, efficacious, and non-invasive breakthrough therapy for AD, while acknowledging that critical challenges in GMP manufacturing, biodistribution, and regulatory approval remain to be resolved.

title: Mycoplasma pneumoniae infections in the Post-COVID era: recent advances from pathogenesis to clinical management.
abstract: M.pneumoniae is a major cause of human respiratory infection whose pathogenicity relies on adhesion proteins, secreted virulence factors, and immune evasion mechanisms. This review contextualizes these strategies within the broader phylogeny of clinically relevant Mycoplasma species while addressing the diverse extrapulmonary manifestations of M. pneumoniae. Current challenges in managing M. pneumoniae infections are multifaceted. The post-pandemic resurgence reflects a population-level immune debt resulting from prolonged non-pharmaceutical interventions, with test positivity rising sharply after restrictions were lifted and driving pneumonia outbreaks across age groups. Macrolide resistance remains persistently high in East Asia and is emerging at variable rates in other regions; routine diagnostics cannot detect resistance in real time, complicating first-line empirical therapy. Vaccine development continues to face obstacles including antigenic variation mediated by recombination between repetitive genomic sequences, the IL-17 A paradox wherein protective Th17 responses also drive vaccine-enhanced disease, and the inability of systemic vaccines to induce mucosal secretory IgA and tissue-resident memory T cells. In response, we evaluate emerging diagnostics-including metagenomic sequencing, CRISPR-Cas platforms, and host biomarkers-and discuss resistance-guided therapies involving doxycycline, quinolones, and novel agents like lefamulin and omadacycline. We further analyze vaccine development hurdles alongside the potential of mRNA-LNP platforms targeting conserved adhesin epitopes. Our findings indicate that the lag between mechanistic insight and clinical implementation remains the most pressing challenge. Future research must shift from simple mechanistic elucidation to addressing real-world clinical dilemmas, including distinguishing colonization from infection through integrated pathogen-host evaluation, exploring synergistic use of antibiotics and immunomodulators targeting the IL-17 A pathway, advancing vaccine design that circumvents IL-17 A-mediated immunopathology via conserved epitope selection and mucosal delivery, and establishing real-time surveillance networks integrating genomics and clinical phenotypes. Collectively, this work provides a practical roadmap spanning molecular pathology to clinical practice for the precise management of M. pneumoniae infections.

title: Emerging nanostructured platforms for improved oral delivery of antidiabetic agents: overcoming physiological barriers and enhancing therapeutic efficacy.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Diabetes mellitus, a chronic metabolic disorder affecting over 537 million individuals worldwide, represents one of the most burdensome global health challenges of the 21st century. Despite the availability of numerous oral antidiabetic agents, their therapeutic effectiveness is significantly compromised by poor aqueous solubility, chemical instability in the gastrointestinal (GI) environment, extensive hepatic first-pass metabolism, low membrane permeability, and inadequate systemic bioavailability. Nanotechnology-based drug delivery systems have emerged as transformative platforms capable of circumventing these multifaceted physiological and biopharmaceutical limitations.
OBJECTIVE: This comprehensive review critically evaluates the landscape of nanostructured platforms designed to enhance oral bioavailability and therapeutic outcomes of antidiabetic agents, with particular emphasis on mechanistic insights into nanoparticle-epithelial interactions, surface functionalization strategies using targeting ligands (lectins, transferrin, folic acid, bile acid conjugates), and stimuli-responsive release mechanisms.
METHODS: A structured literature search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect for articles published between January 2010 and 2026, with emphasis on publications from 2022 to 2026. We systematically analyzed and compared eleven distinct nanocarrier platforms, including polymeric nanoparticles, solid lipid nanoparticles (SLNs), nanostructured lipid carriers (NLCs), self-emulsifying drug delivery systems (SEDDS), liposomes, nanoemulsions, dendrimers, cyclodextrin inclusion complexes, mesoporous silica nanoparticles, metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), and hybrid nanocomposites, evaluating how each platform addresses specific absorption barriers including GI enzymatic degradation, mucus layer penetration, enterocyte uptake, and efflux pump activity.
RESULTS: Rational formulation design, in vitro-in vivo correlations, and pharmacokinetic enhancement data indicate that nanoformulated antidiabetic drugs consistently outperform conventional formulations in bioavailability and absorption across multiple drug classes and delivery platforms. Emerging paradigms including exosome-inspired nanocarriers, CRISPR-integrated systems, and artificial intelligence-guided formulation optimization further extend the mechanistic and translational scope of oral nanomedicine for diabetes management.
CONCLUSION: Nanostructured platforms offer a mechanistically diverse and increasingly translatable strategy for overcoming the physiological and biopharmaceutical barriers that limit oral antidiabetic therapy. Realizing their full clinical potential will require continued progress in addressing translational challenges, harmonizing regulatory frameworks, and advancing scalable manufacturing toward clinically viable oral nanomedicines for diabetes management.

title: Correspondence on: "Targeting the HERV-K102 envelope elicits pyroptosis and represents a novel therapeutic strategy for acute myeloid leukemia".
abstract: Zong et al. reported that CRISPR-Cas9-mediated deletion of the HERV-K102 envelope (K-Env) induces apoptosis and pyroptosis in acute myeloid leukemia cells via S100A9/NLRP3 inflammasome activation. We examine four methodological concerns: the absence of evidence using a pathway-specific inhibitor to distinguish pyroptosis from secondary necrosis; the lack of a mechanistic rescue experiment confirming S100A9 as the proximal driver; the non-specificity of primers at the mRNA level; and the inability of the immunocompromised xenograft model to capture immune evasion by K-Env. The prognostic and therapeutic implications of the study require qualification.

title: Development and Evaluation of an RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a Molecular Assay for Rapid Diagnosis of Theileria annulata Infection in Bovines.
abstract: Tropical theileriosis, caused by Theileria annulata, continues to be the most significant tick-borne disease affecting cattle, particularly in endemic regions where it leads to significant production losses. Prompt and reliable diagnosis is critically important for timely treatment and disease control; however, conventional diagnostic methods have important limitations. Microscopic examination lacks sensitivity, particularly in carrier animals, while PCR requires specialized laboratory infrastructure. To overcome these limitations, a fluorescence-based RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a assay targeting the multicopy mitochondrial cytb gene was developed for rapid detection of T. annulata. Five RPA primer pairs were designed and evaluated, and primer set-5, generating a 324-bp amplicon, exhibited the best amplification performance. A CRISPR RNA (crRNA) was designed within the selected amplicon to enable specific Cas12a-mediated target recognition. The assay was completed within 50 min and demonstrated no cross-reactivity with DNA from Theileria orientalis, Babesia bigemina, Babesia bovis, Anaplasma marginale, and bovine host DNA, confirming excellent analytical specificity. Sensitivity analysis using recombinant plasmid DNA demonstrated a detection limit of approximately ten copies per reaction. The field evaluation of the assay was done by testing 206 bovine field samples. showed that the developed assay identified 163 positive samples, exceeding the detection rates obtained by PCR (151 positives) and microscopy (116 positives). On comparison with PCR, the assay achieved 100% diagnostic sensitivity, 78.18% specificity, 92.64% positive predictive value, 100% negative predictive value, with an overall agreement of 94.17%. These findings indicate that the RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a platform is a rapid, sensitive, and accurate molecular diagnostic approach with strong potential for field application and point-of-care diagnosis of bovine tropical theileriosis, particularly in resource-constrained settings.

title: Pelacarsen and Lp(a)HORIZON: Interpreting the Disconnect Between Lipoprotein(a) Lowering and Cardiovascular Outcomes.
abstract: Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a genetically determined causal risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and calcific aortic valve stenosis. Pelacarsen, a hepatocyte-directed antisense oligonucleotide targeting apolipoprotein(a), was evaluated in Lp(a)HORIZON, the first large phase 3 cardiovascular outcomes trial specifically designed to test whether pharmacological Lp(a) lowering reduces cardiovascular events. Topline results announced in September 2026 indicated that pelacarsen lowered Lp(a) but did not reduce the primary composite cardiovascular endpoint in patients with established cardiovascular disease. Full trial data are awaited, and the mechanisms underlying this neutral result remain uncertain. We discuss potential explanations, including treatment after prolonged cumulative Lp(a) exposure, advanced vascular disease, intensive background prevention, the magnitude and duration of Lp(a) suppression, patient selection, baseline cardiovascular risk, and biological heterogeneity. We also examine implications for emerging therapies, including olpasiran, zerlasiran, lepodisiran, and muvalaplin, and for the design of ongoing cardiovascular outcome trials.

title: Pushing the Boundaries of Knowledge in Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency.
abstract: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (AATD) is a rare inherited disorder caused by mutations in the SERPINA1 gene. AATD is one of the leading causes of emphysema in young adults and of liver cirrhosis in children and adults. Despite significant underdiagnosis and high clinical variability, recent research is rapidly transforming the field. Advances in molecular biology and translational medicine have identified new biomarkers and therapeutic targets, although reliable predictors of disease progression remain limited. While augmentation therapy is the only approved pharmacological option for pulmonary involvement and no specific treatment exists for liver disease, innovative strategies are remodeling the therapeutic landscape. Gene therapy, RNA interference, gene editing, and epigenetic modulation are showing promising preclinical and early clinical results, aiming to correct the underlying defect rather than manage symptoms. This review focuses on these emerging advances, highlighting cutting-edge preclinical and translational developments with potential to redefine AATD management and move toward curative approaches.

title: USP36-mediated stabilization of NAT10 promotes osteosarcoma progression via ac4C-dependent KIF23 mRNA stabilization.
abstract: Osteosarcoma is an aggressive bone malignancy with a propensity for pulmonary metastasis, yet the molecular mechanisms linking protein homeostasis to epitranscriptomic regulation remain incompletely understood. Here, integrated transcriptomic, survival, protein-interaction, and CRISPR dependency analyses identified the deubiquitinase USP36 as a driver of osteosarcoma progression. USP36 was elevated in osteosarcoma datasets, and higher expression was associated with poorer survival in univariable analysis. Functional studies showed that USP36 depletion suppressed osteosarcoma-cell proliferation and invasion, whereas USP36 overexpression enhanced these phenotypes. Re-expression of wild-type USP36, but not the catalytically inactive C131A mutant, restored clonogenic growth and invasive capacity in USP36-deficient cells, indicating that its tumor-promoting effects depend on catalytic activity. Mechanistically, USP36 interacted with NAT10, prolonged NAT10 protein stability, and reduced K48-linked NAT10 polyubiquitination in cells. USP36 depletion decreased ac4C enrichment on KIF23 mRNA, accelerated KIF23 transcript decay, reduced KIF23 and β-catenin abundance, and impaired Wnt/β-catenin transcriptional activity. Importantly, wild-type NAT10, but not the catalytically inactive NAT10-G641E mutant, restored KIF23 ac4C enrichment, KIF23 expression, Wnt reporter activity, and clonogenic growth after USP36 depletion. TCF3 bound the USP36 promoter and positively regulated endogenous USP36 expression, whereas Wnt inhibition reduced USP36 transcription, supporting a reinforcing TCF3-USP36-NAT10-KIF23-Wnt regulatory relationship. In vivo, USP36 depletion reduced orthotopic tumor burden and experimental pulmonary metastatic colonization. Collectively, these findings identify USP36 as an upstream regulator of NAT10 stability and establish a mechanistic link between ubiquitin-dependent protein turnover and ac4C-mediated KIF23 mRNA stabilization in osteosarcoma. The USP36-NAT10-KIF23 axis may therefore represent a molecular vulnerability warranting further biochemical and clinical investigation.

title: The expression window as a safety parameter for mRNA medicines.
abstract: Messenger RNA therapeutics are engineered, with few exceptions, for stability and output. For an expanding class of payloads that objective is wrong. Once a nuclease has finished editing, a cytokine has initiated a response, or an in vivo generated receptor has cleared its target, continued expression adds no benefit while the liability accumulates. The goal is then predictable disappearance, and the quantity to engineer is the expression window: the time course of active protein. This review formulates it as the convolution of three layers. Formulation and route supply the input function, dominate the rise and peak, and can dominate the apparent decay; once release is complete, RNA and protein turnover set the tail, which declines at the slower of the two rates. Levers at these layers are not substitutes. In a protein-limited window, RNA destabilisation leaves the terminal decay rate unchanged and reduces exposure almost entirely by lowering the peak. In the worked example, each unit of peak surrendered buys about a sixth of the tail reduction available at the protein layer, and the ranking reverses when the RNA is limiting. Choosing a lever therefore requires knowing which layer is limiting, which a paired RNA-and-protein time course decides once release is separated from decay. Three reportable metrics - rise, peak and offset time - replace the single stated duration, and cumulative exposure, not peak, matches an accumulating liability. The asymmetry is structural: of the established RNA-layer levers reviewed here, every one extends the window or restricts it in space.

title: Osteoporosis treatment via programmed delivery of IRF5 siRNA to macrophages in bone tissue combined with ROS scavenging.
abstract: Postmenopausal osteoporosis (PO) is not merely a consequence of increased osteoclast activity. Estrogen deficiency induces oxidative stress and pro-inflammatory M1 macrophage polarization in bone tissue, thereby sustaining osteoclastogenic stimuli and pathological bone resorption. Interferon regulatory factor 5 (IRF5) is a key regulator of M1 polarization, and silencing its gene by small interfering RNA (siIRF5) may attenuate the pathogenesis of PO. However, selective delivery of siIRF5 to M1 macrophages within the osteoporotic bone microenvironment is challenging. Herein, we develop a nanomedicine, termed siP@WM, for programmed sequential targeting of bone tissue and macrophages. The siP@WM integrates a platinum nanozyme core with mesoporous silica shell loading siIRF5. The shell with enlarged pores (10-15 nm) provides effective siRNA encapsulation and programmable surface grafting of two kinds of poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) derivatives. The longer poly(aspartic acid)-terminated PEG chain promotes bone enrichment. ROS-triggered thioketal cleavage shortens this chain, reduces bone-matrix adhesion, and exposes the shorter folic acid-functionalized PEG chain to enhance M1 macrophage uptake. In vitro, siP@WM scavenges ROS, facilitates endosomal escape, achieves approximately 60% IRF5 knockdown, and promotes M2 polarization. In ovariectomized mice, systemic administration of siP@WM ameliorates bone loss, restores trabecular microarchitecture and mechanical strength, and shows no overt short-term toxicity in major organs. Transcriptomic and histological analyses support attenuated AP-1-associated inflammatory signaling, suppressed osteoclast differentiation, and modulated extracellular matrix remodeling. Together, programmed siIRF5 delivery to macrophages in bone tissue combined with ROS scavenging restores bone homeostasis and provides an adaptive biomaterial strategy for PO treatment.

title: Chemically tailored lipids mediate solid-phase RNA programming of mineralized microenvironments.
abstract: The localized delivery of RNA therapeutics to mineralized tissue interfaces is limited by poor retention and rapid clearance at the target site. We report the development of a solid-phase transfection platform that functionalizes mineralized surfaces into bioactive nucleic acid reservoirs. Through the rational design and screening of a library of 21 piperazine-linked bisphosphonate ionizable lipids, we identified a lead formulation of bisphosphonate lipid nanoparticle (BP-LNP) that maximizes hydroxyapatite affinity without compromising transfection potency. Upon adsorption onto mineral substrates, these BP-LNPs resisted fluid removal and maintained surface-mediated, sustained delivery of encapsulated RNA cargo to adjacent cells. We demonstrated the versatility of this Mineralized Tissue-Targeting Expression System (MiTEX) composed of BP-LNPs in two therapeutic contexts: Cre recombinase mRNA-functionalized allogeneic bone grafts to genetically label de novo bone formation in vivo, and STAT3 siRNA delivery to reduce inflammation in human gingival explants. This platform provides a universal strategy for transforming inert calcium phosphate materials and tissues into locally bioactive RNA delivery systems for regenerative and immunomodulatory applications.

title: Unipoint-anchored cascade amplification strategy integrating FUSE probe-activated CRISPR-Cas12a for dual mode osteopontin detection toward osteosarcoma assessment and therapeutic response evaluation.
abstract: Reliable assessment of disease status and therapeutic response in osteosarcoma remains an unmet clinical need. Integrative bioinformatics analysis and protein-level verification in paired clinical specimens prioritized secreted phosphoprotein 1 (SPP1, osteopontin) as a liquid biopsy target associated with osteosarcoma progression and patient survival. On this basis, CRUMP, a CRISPR-Cas12a and FUSE Probe-based dual-mode biosensing platform, was developed for SPP1 quantification. A bifunctional NH2-ZIF-8 probe co-immobilizes the components required for target recognition and Cas12a activation, while MoS2@AuNPs interfaces transduce the resulting signals. Signal amplification is achieved through a unipoint-anchored multisite cascade based on a DNA tetrahedron-HCR architecture, enabling one-to-multiple parallel amplification while balancing stability and sensitivity. A single Cas12a cleavage event simultaneously decreases the electrochemical (EC) signal and increases the fluorescence (FL) signal. These reciprocal changes allow the two readouts to provide an internal consistency check for each measurement. Each channel covers more than five orders of magnitude, with detection limits of 167.7 fg/mL for EC and 331.6 fg/mL for FL. The broad measurement ranges allow most serum samples to be analyzed directly, without the per-sample dilution optimization that ELISA requires, and the complete analysis takes only approximately 85 min. Validation across osteosarcoma cell lines, clinical specimens, and tumor-bearing mouse models provided preliminary evidence for the feasibility of CRUMP in SPP1 quantification and endpoint assessment of chemotherapeutic response. By combining biomarker prioritization, biosensor engineering, and preliminary application testing, this work presents CRUMP as a candidate platform for SPP1-based assessment of osteosarcoma and its therapeutic response.

title: From base transitions to expanded editing tools: development and applications of plant base editors.
abstract: Plant base editing enables targeted nucleotide substitutions and provides a powerful approach for functional genomics and crop improvement. The toolkit has expanded from canonical cytosine and adenine editors to dual-base, transversion, Cas12-based, and organelle-targeted systems, broadening the range of accessible mutations and genomic targets. These advances create new opportunities for generating useful alleles, modifying gene function, and enabling directed evolution. However, expanded base-editing capabilities do not necessarily ensure predictable outcomes or successful breeding applications. This review summarizes the development of plant base editors, computational tools for target design, and their applications in crop research. We examine editor architectures and compare editing efficiency, product purity, and specificity, with particular attention to transversion editing. We also highlight the intrinsic technical limitations of base editors and the bottlenecks encountered when moving from laboratory research to field applications. By connecting base editor development with practical constraints, this review provides guidance for editor selection and identifies priorities for applying base editing to crop improvement.

title: From off-target to on-demand: Precision engineering and translational evaluation of next-generation base editors.
abstract: Due to the increasing demand for clinical gene therapy and the limitations of current treatment methods, there is an urgent need to develop gene-editing tools that are safer, more precise, and more clinically implementable. Deaminase-based base editors have emerged as gene-editing platforms with significant therapeutic potential because they can achieve precise single-base substitutions without inducing DNA double-strand breaks. However, the challenges of applying base editing in clinical practice extend beyond whether the intended edit can be achieved. The critical question is whether the editing system can reliably provide predictable, controllable, and verifiable outcomes across complex sequence contexts, diverse cell environments, and actual delivery conditions. This review focuses on the engineering optimization and clinical translation of base editors. We first systematically analyze the major factors affecting the clinical translation of base editors across four dimensions: editing efficiency, editing precision, safety, and delivery, together with the corresponding optimization strategies. We then summarize the applications of artificial intelligence and computational approaches in base editor design, screening, and risk assessment. We further discuss the ex vivo and in vivo pathways for clinical translation, including their respective requirements for product quality and safety evaluation. Finally, based on representative clinical programs, we discuss how editing performance, safety, and delivery factors influence development decisions for candidate base-editing systems across different therapeutic contexts, and propose minimum reporting recommendations to improve the consistency of key data and cross-study comparability.

title: Uncovering the importance of lipofection for aptamer-mediated therapeutic oligonucleotide delivery in a HER2+ SKBR3 breast cancer cell line.
abstract: The human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) plays an important role as a transmembrane receptor, contributing to signaling activities implicated in cellular proliferation, differentiation, and survival. Across select tumor types, HER2 is pro-oncogenic, facilitating cancer initiation, progression and metastatic spread, leading towards treatment resistance. Further, cell surface presentation and signaling activity of HER2 has led to the development of precision oncology therapeutic approaches. In this study, a HER2-targeting DNA aptamer was modified into a novel chimeric sequence with an RNA sense strand that was hybridized with a complementary antisense RNA or DNA sequence for aptamer-mediated HER2 cellular uptake in a representative HER2 positive (+) SKBR3 breast cancer cell line. The incorporation of antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) and short interfering (si) RNA within the chimeric HER2-aptamer elicited favorable hybrid duplex secondary structures and thermal stability profiles for biological activity. Enzymatic (Ribonuclease H, RNase H) digestion of the RNA sense strand made the chimeric HER2-aptamer:ASO hybrid applicable for antisense and with siRNA for RNA interference (RNAi) gene silencing activities against the stress-inducible oncoprotein, Glucose Regulated Protein 78, GRP78, as a key regulator of cancer cell survival and apoptosis. The chimeric ASO and siRNA conjugated aptamer demonstrated cellular binding and uptake activities directly in the HER2 presenting SKBR3 cell line and downstream GRP78 silencing (siRNA) activity that was dependent on a Lipofectamine-based formulation, underscoring the importance of the transfection agent for cellular delivery of genetic therapies.

title: Long-term real-world outcomes of nusinersen treatment in patients with spinal muscular atrophy types I-III.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is an autosomal recessive neuromuscular disorder caused by mutations or deletions in the survival motor neuron 1 (SMN) gene, with disease severity influenced by SMN2 copy number. Nusinersen, an antisense oligonucleotide therapy, has emerged as an effective treatment option. This study aimed to evaluate the long-term clinical outcomes of nusinersen treatment in SMA patients.
METHODS: Patients with SMA types I-III who received nusinersen between 2017 and 2024 were retrospectively analyzed. SMA type I patients were evaluated using the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia Infant Test of Neuromuscular Disorders (CHOP-INTEND), while types II and III were followed with the Hammersmith Functional Motor Scale-Expanded (HFMSE).
RESULTS: In SMA Type II (n = 11; mean age 17.8 ± 5.7 years), mean HFMSE scores improved from 11.3 ± 16.3 to 14.1 ± 17.4 after fourth dose. In SMA Type III patients (n = 9; mean age 20.2 ± 6.4 years), scores improved from 38.8 ± 22.1 to 43.0 ± 21.8. Linear mixed-effects analysis demonstrated a significant association between cumulative nusinersen dose and improved motor function (p < 0.001). Clinically meaningful improvement was maintained in 75% of patients with SMA types II and III at the final follow-up, whereas outcomes in SMA type I were heterogeneous and could not be interpreted conclusively because of the small sample size, late treatment initiation, and advanced disease severity.
CONCLUSION: Nusinersen was associated with early motor improvement and long-term stabilization, a clinically meaningful outcome given the progressive nature of SMA.

title: Genome-wide CRISPR screen identifies PKMYT1 inhibition as a synthetic lethal vulnerability in IDH1-mutant glioma.
abstract: Mutations in isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) are frequently observed in several aggressive malignancies, including gliomas, chondrosarcomas, and acute myeloid leukemia. Mutant IDH enzymes exhibit neomorphic activity that produces the oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate (D-2-HG), leading to widespread DNA and histone hypermethylation. This aberrant epigenetic state remodels chromatin accessibility, thereby compromising both DNA repair and replication. However, the mechanisms underlying IDH mutation-induced DNA replication stress and the therapeutic potential of this vulnerability remain elusive. Through a whole-genome CRISPR screen, we defined differential genetic dependencies between IDH1 wild-type and mutant cells. We identified the G2/M checkpoint kinase PKMYT1 as a selective survival factor for IDH1-mutated cells. Pharmacologic or genetic inhibition of PKMYT1 profoundly suppresses the growth of IDH1-mutated tumor cells in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistically, IDH1-mutated cancer cells exhibit profound replication stress, characterized by reduced nucleotide incorporation, slowed replication fork progression, and delayed S-phase entry. D-2-HG elevates H3K9 trimethylation by inhibiting KDM4A, thereby impeding DNA replication initiation and fork progression. PKMYT1 blockade alters cell cycle timing, forcing unscheduled mitotic entry with incompletely replicated genomes, resulting in elevated DNA damage and mitotic catastrophe. Collectively, our findings demonstrate a mechanistic link between IDH1-driven epigenetic dysregulation, replication stress, and heightened reliance on the G2/M checkpoint. Our findings propose PKMYT1 inhibition as a therapeutic strategy that exploits the intrinsic replication deficiency of IDH1-mutant glioma.

title: CRISPR-based interrogation of alternative lengthening of telomeres: mapping dependencies, stress-buffering pathways, and therapeutic vulnerabilities.
abstract: Alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) is a telomerase-independent telomere maintenance mechanism that supports the growth of approximately 5-10% of human tumors and represents an attractive but insufficiently explored therapeutic target. CRISPR-based functional genomics has emerged as a powerful approach to systematically interrogate ALT biology and identify genetic dependencies associated with the ALT state. In this Review, we discuss the CRISPR-based strategies applied to ALT, including hypothesis-driven targeted loss-of-function screens, phenotype-driven optical screens, in silico mining of large-scale dependency datasets, and genome-wide screens in ALT-adjacent states. Across these approaches, recurrent dependencies converge on pathways mediating replication stress buffering, DNA repair, and telomere maintenance, including FANCM, SMARCAL1, and SUB1. Collectively, these findings support a model in which ALT-positive cells rely not on a unique ALT-specific factor, but rather on stress-buffering mechanisms that prevent chronic telomeric dysfunction from triggering replication catastrophe and cell death, highlighting these pathways as promising candidates for further therapeutic investigation.

title: Targeting the H3K4me3-HNRNPC-CD24 Axis Overcomes Stemness and Immunosuppression in Hepatocellular Carcinoma.
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is driven by cancer stemness and an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, which collectively contribute to therapeutic resistance. While the RNA-binding protein HNRNPC has been implicated in tumor progression, it has primarily been characterized as a downstream effector, and its autonomous regulatory functions, particularly in governing cancer stemness, remain entirely unexplored. Through multi-omics analyses of HCC cohorts, we identified HNRNPC as a pivotal driver of a high-risk molecular subtype. Mechanistically, HNRNPC expression was transcriptionally activated via WDR5/KMT2A complex-mediated deposition of H3K4me3 at its promoter. Functionally, HNRNPC was essential for maintaining cancer stemness, promoting tumor growth and metastasis, and conferring oxaliplatin resistance. Notably, depletion of HNRNPC reprogrammed the immunosuppressive microenvironment by enhancing CD8+ T cell infiltration, reducing T cell exhaustion, and polarizing macrophages toward an M1-like anti-tumor phenotype. At the molecular level, HNRNPC bound to the m6A-modified 3'UTR of CD24 mRNA in an RNP2 motif-dependent manner, thereby enhancing its stability and elevating CD24 protein expression. Therapeutically, we developed a novel lipid nanoparticle (LNP) encapsulating siRNA against HNRNPC. Systemically administered AP-EG-si potently suppressed tumor growth, attenuated stemness, and synergized with anti-PD-L1 therapy to enhance anti-tumor immunity. Our findings thus unveil the H3K4me3-HNRNPC-CD24 axis as a central epigenetic and post-transcriptional regulatory pathway that coordinately drives HCC stemness and immune evasion, nominating HNRNPC-targeted nanotherapy as a promising strategy for advanced HCC.

title: 2-Hydroxyisobutyrylation of SRSF9 Regulates CD44 Alternative Splicing to Promote Colorectal Cancer Liver Metastasis.
abstract: Colorectal cancer liver metastasis (CRLM) remains a major cause of cancer mortality, yet the metabolic mechanisms that remodel metastatic RNA-splicing programs are poorly defined. Here, integrated quantitative proteomics and lysine 2-hydroxyisobutyrylation (Khib) proteomics of patient-matched normal mucosa, primary CRCs, and liver metastases revealed a progressive increase in global Khib, with enrichment on RNA-splicing proteins. Serine/arginine-rich splicing factor 9 (SRSF9) emerged as a Khib-modified splicing factor whose expression and K155 Khib levels increased from normal tissue to primary tumors and liver metastases. Gain and loss of function studies in CRC cell lines, patient-derived organoids, subcutaneous xenografts, and splenic injection liver metastasis models showed that SRSF9 promotes proliferation, invasion, tumor growth, and liver colonization. Mechanistically, K155 Khib stabilized SRSF9 protein; the K155R mutation accelerated degradation and abolished SRSF9-driven malignant phenotypes. KAT7 and SIRT6 act as regulators of Khib modification, which positively and negatively modulate the K155 Khib modification of SRSF9, respectively. SRSF9 bound CD44 pre-mRNA through its RRM1 domain and promoted alternative splicing toward the oncogenic CD44V8-10 isoform, which was elevated in patient tumors and metastases and rescued the impaired proliferation and metastatic capacity caused by SRSF9 loss. Finally, a CD44V8-10-targeting antisense oligonucleotide suppressed CRC growth and liver metastasis in preclinical models. These findings define a KAT7/SIRT6-regulated Khib-SRSF9-CD44V8-10 axis that couples metabolic acylation to metastatic splicing and nominate CD44V8-10 as a therapeutic vulnerability in CRC liver metastasis.

title: Advances in molecular techniques for detecting Mycobacterium leprae: A narrative review of Progress, challenges, and future directions.
abstract: Leprosy remains a neglected infectious disease where delayed diagnosis leads to disability and ongoing transmission, particularly in paucibacillary and pure neural forms. This narrative review summarizes molecular diagnostic approaches for Mycobacterium leprae, including polymerase chain reaction (PCR), isothermal nucleic acid amplification tests, clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-Cas-based diagnostic systems, next-generation sequencing (NGS), microarrays, and biosensors. PCR remains the most established method, now expanded to multiplex, quantitative, and droplet digital formats for improved detection and antimicrobial resistance surveillance. Isothermal methods such as loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP), recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA), and multiple cross displacement amplification (MCDA) offer rapid, field-deployable options but require further validation. Emerging platforms, including CRISPR-Cas diagnostics, targeted sequencing, and biosensors, show promise but remain limited by cost and infrastructure needs. Overall, molecular approaches have substantially expanded the diagnostic and surveillance capacity for leprosy, particularly in paucibacillary, pure neural, and clinically ambiguous presentations where conventional methods lack sensitivity. Future advances should integrate optimized biomarkers, improved sample processing, and simplified platforms to further enable early diagnosis, treatment monitoring, and antimicrobial resistance surveillance, thereby supporting global leprosy control and elimination.

title: A high-confidence plant mitochondrial proteome via protein correlation profiling.
abstract: Plant mitochondria share many features with animal mitochondria but also possess unique traits, including presence of both circular and linear mitochondrial DNA, RNA editing, a branched electron transport chain, and metabolic pathways supporting photosynthesis. An accurate mitochondrial proteome is crucial for studying these conserved and lineage-specific functions. Here, we introduce a novel approach to defining plant mitoproteomes that combines serial mitochondrial enrichment, mass spectrometry, and protein correlation profiling. This approach allows us to experimentally define a mitochondrial protein inventory of 1,462 proteins with high sensitivity and specificity. Integration of our experimental inventory with literature and microscopy validation yields the Arabidopsisthaliana MitoCarta (AtMitoCarta) atlas of 1,609 mitochondrial proteins, including 236 newly defined proteins and 147 proteins of unknown functions. A comparative analysis across eukaryotic organisms reveals that 15% of mitochondrial protein families are plant specific, including expanded pentatricopeptide repeat proteins. The AtMitoCarta inventory and the experimental workflow applicable to wild-type plants will enable comparative studies of plant mitochondria.

title: In vivo genome-editing therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy: Preclinical studies and first-in-human trial.
abstract: We report the preclinical and early clinical evaluation of in vivo genome editing for Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), delivered via a single AAV9 vector. In humanized DMD mice, systemic administration achieved targeted genome editing, partial dystrophin restoration, and improved muscle function. In non-human primates, efficient on-target editing was achieved with no dose-limiting toxicity identified under the conditions tested. In an open-label, dose-escalation, first-in-human clinical trial (NCT06594094), post-treatment muscle biopsies provided early molecular evidence of hfCas12Max-mediated genome editing and detectable dystrophin expression in participants with DMD. However, at the higher dose level (1.0 × 1014 vg/kg), one participant experienced a treatment-related fatal serious adverse event, characterized by marked complement activation and systemic cytokine response shortly after dosing. This work provides initial human proof-of-concept for muscle genome editing while crucially highlighting the critical role of immunologic risks and the narrow therapeutic window of systemic adeno-associated virus (AAV)-CRISPR therapies, underscoring the need to develop safer dosing and immunomodulation strategies.

title: Epidermal growth factor receptor activation is associated with NSCLC cells resistance to ferroptosis and correlates with ROS-NRF2-GCLC/GCLM pathway activation.
abstract: Mutations of epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) closely correlate with differential ferroptosis sensitivity in select cell lines, but the underlying mechanism is poorly understood. In this study, we identified the epidermal growth factor (EGF)-activated EGFR as a correlate of ferroptosis suppression in non-small cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC) cells, an effect linked to increased mitochondrial mass and functional capacity. EGF treatment attenuated ferroptosis induced by ML210, RSL3, or Erastin, whereas CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of EGFR (EGFRKO) downregulated GCLC/GCLM expression and glutathione (GSH) levels, thereby sensitizing cells to ferroptosis. Across the cell lines tested, sensitivity to ferroptosis inducers varied and could not be attributed solely to EGFR mutation status. In tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI)-resistant cells and in post-TKI tumor tissues from NSCLC patients harboring EGFR mutations, we observed downregulation of xCT/SLC7A11 and GCLC/GCLM. Notably, while TKI-resistant cells acquired resistance to the system xc- inhibitor Erastin, they remained sensitive to the GPX4 inhibitor RSL3, suggesting that alternative antioxidant pathways, such as the FSP1/CoQ10 system, may compensate for impaired cystine uptake in the resistant setting. Collectively, our results reveal a correlative link between EGFR signaling, mitochondrial metabolism, and the ROS-NRF2-GCLC/GCLM pathway in modulating ferroptosis in NSCLC cells in a GSH-dependent manner. Furthermore, the sustained vulnerability of TKI-resistant cells to GPX4 inhibition suggests that targeting GPX4 represents a promising therapeutic strategy to overcome TKI resistance, though our findings are hypothesis-generating and require further mechanistic validation.

title: Heterogeneous contributions of APOBEC3 deaminases to substitution and indel mutagenesis in lung adenocarcinoma.
abstract: APOBEC3 cytosine deaminases are major sources of cancer mutations. In lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), APOBEC3 activity drives tumor evolution and therapy resistance, nominating these enzymes as therapeutic targets. Although APOBEC3A drives most APOBEC3-associated mutational signature burden across cancers, the relative contributions of individual paralogs in LUAD remain unclear. Here, we define the roles of endogenously misregulated APOBEC3 deaminases using CRISPR-Cas9 knockouts and whole-genome sequencing of 197 long-term propagated single-cell clones. APOBEC3 mutagenesis falls into three patterns, driven predominantly by APOBEC3A, by both APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B, or minimal despite detectable enzyme expression. Commonly used surrogate measures, including mRNA and protein levels and in vitro deaminase activity, do not predict these contributions. We also provide the first causal evidence that endogenous APOBEC3A generates the indel signature InD9a, linking it to uracil excision following cytosine deamination. These heterogeneous contributions highlight the need for biomarkers that resolve individual APOBEC3 activities to guide therapeutic targeting.

title: A phage-encoded small RNA that mimics chimeric guide to inhibit CRISPR-Cas9.
abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 relies on a dual CRISPR RNA (crRNA)-trans-activating crRNA (tracrRNA) guide, yet whether RNA-based anti-CRISPRs exist for this system has remained unknown. Here, we identify a phage-encoded small non-coding RNA, rAcrIIA1, that adopts an unexpected chimeric crRNA-tracrRNA architecture, faithfully recapitulating the entire single-guide RNA (sgRNA) of Cas9. Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of the Cas9-rAcrIIA1 binary complex and the Cas9-rAcrIIA1-DNA ternary complex reveal that rAcrIIA1 engages Cas9 nearly identically to the native sgRNA, competitively blocking crRNA and tracrRNA loading and thereby abolishing DNA interference. Strikingly, beyond its natural inhibitory function, rAcrIIA1 is fully reprogrammable: with variable guide sequences, it directs Cas9 for sequence-specific DNA cleavage with efficiency comparable to the canonical sgRNA, and it activates trans-cleavage more potently. Thus, rAcrIIA1 provides an experimentally validated, mechanistically resolved RNA-based inhibitor of CRISPR-Cas9, reveals a distinct anti-CRISPR mechanism through complete sgRNA mimicry, and serves as a versatile bifunctional scaffold for genome editing and diagnostics.

title: Advances in genetically engineered and humanized mouse models for dissecting sepsis mechanisms and therapeutic response.
abstract: Sepsis remains a major cause of global mortality, yet translation from preclinical studies to effective targeted therapies has been limited. A key barrier is that conventional animal models incompletely capture human immune circuitry and patient heterogeneity. Recent progress in mouse genetics, CRISPR/Cas-based genome editing, conditional alleles (Cre-loxP), and next-generation humanized platforms has expanded the toolkit for functional interrogation of host pathways that shape sepsis outcomes. Germline and cell-type-restricted perturbations have helped map roles for pattern-recognition signaling, inflammasome modules, cell-death effectors, and immune checkpoints, while also showing that the same pathway can produce different phenotypes depending on cellular context. Cross-species differences in innate immune gene networks and caspase biology motivate validation in humanized systems and integration with human genetic evidence. Emerging "wildling" and genetically diverse panels provide complementary approaches to model environmental exposure and host variation. Coupling these platforms with single-cell multi-omics and endotype stratification can link genotype-to-phenotype mechanisms with biomarker-informed therapeutic testing.

title: Single-strand break repair pathway disruption impacts radiosensitivity to both low- and high-LET radiation.
abstract: Differences in individual radiosensitivity are not currently reflected in radiotherapy treatment planning, and identifying genetic drivers of this variation is a key step in personalising future treatments. While the role of DNA double-strand break (DSB) repair in radiosensitivity is well-studied, the impacts of single-strand break (SSB) repair defects are relatively unexplored. Through targeted SSB repair gene knockout, we show that disrupted SSB repair increases radiosensitivity, with stronger effects for high Linear Energy Transfer (LET) radiation. Mechanistic studies identified both an increase in DSB production at low LETs, due to delayed SSB repair, and higher levels of unrepaired complex damage at high LETs. This altered sensitivity is also reflected by differences in disease-specific survival for patients with SSB repair gene alterations in a retrospective pan-cancer clinical analysis. SSB repair pathway disruption may therefore be clinically relevant and important to consider for radiotherapy personalisation, particularly for high-LET radiation treatments.

title: Triphenyl phosphate promotes PXR-associated, MEN1-dependent exposure-conditioned enzalutamide tolerance in prostate cancer.
abstract: Androgen receptor pathway inhibitors (ARPIs) prolong survival in prostate cancer, yet durable control is frequently lost through transcriptional adaptation and lineage plasticity. Whether environmental endocrine-disrupting chemicals can actively bias this trajectory and create tractable resistance dependencies remains unclear. Here we show that chronic low-dose exposure to triphenyl phosphate (TPP) induces exposure-conditioned, partially persistent and reversible enzalutamide tolerance in AR-positive prostate cancer cells, accompanied by increased colony formation. Tolerance persists initially after exposure withdrawal but declines during washout, and TPP rechallenge increases GR50 again. A pooled CRISPR screen across two genetic backgrounds converged on MEN1 as the most robust concordant hit, and genetic perturbation and rescue identified a MEN1 dependency that was most apparent in the TPP-conditioned tolerant state. Mechanistically, TPP induced NR1I2 and MEN1 mRNA, endogenous target genes, and PXR-associated reporter activity; antagonist-sensitive transcriptional responses, SPA70-mediated reversal of tolerance, and MEN1-locus regulatory-region visualization were consistent with engagement of a PXR/NR1I2-associated receptor program. Targeted chromatin profiling identified MEN1-dependent changes in H3K4me3, H3K27ac and accessibility at selected AR and plasticity-associated loci. TPP_long reduced H3K4me3 and accessibility at AR loci, while MEN1 CRISPRi opposed the major transcriptional and chromatin changes. In LNCaP-luc xenografts, TPP exposure attenuated enzalutamide-mediated tumor suppression, and MEN1 CRISPRi reduced tumor burden in the TPP + enzalutamide background. This reduction in enzalutamide control was not reproduced in the exploratory VCaP model under androgen deprivation. Together, these data support an exposure-conditioned receptor-to-chromatin model in which MEN1 supports an AR-low/plasticity-high adaptive state.

title: Deletion of a rheumatoid arthritis risk enhancer in mouse disrupts Bim expression and immune homeostasis.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to characterise the in vivo function of a murine regulatory region syntenic to the human rheumatoid arthritis (RA)-associated enhancer at the ACOXL locus and its role in immunity.
METHODS: Using CRISPR-Cas9, we generated the Bim-eΔ mouse model by excising a 15 kb genomic region syntenic to the human RA-associated locus tagged by rs13401811 from C57BL/6J zygotes. Bim expression was assessed by quantitative polymerase chain reaction. Thymocytes and splenocytes were profiled by flow cytometry, and whole-spleen RNA-seq was used to define transcriptional changes. Immune responses were tested using a Trichuris muris infection model and an antigen-induced arthritis (AIA) protocol.
RESULTS: Bim-eΔ mice show reduced Bim expression vs wild-type counterparts. This indicates that Bim is a transcriptional target of this region. Enhancer loss was correlated with differences in T cell proportions across age- and sex-stratified cohorts consistent with altered thymic selection. Splenic T and B cells were altered, and the transcriptome skewed toward inflammation. Bim-eΔ and wild-type mice mounted comparable responses to T. muris, whereas Bim-eΔ mice developed a severe adverse response during the sensitisation phase of the AIA protocol.
CONCLUSIONS: A murine noncoding regulatory region modulates Bim expression and immunity in vivo. Enhancer deletion altered the splenic transcriptional profile and lymphocyte composition while revealing a context-dependent phenotype upon inflammatory in vivo challenge. These findings support a role for RA-associated regulatory architecture in shaping immunity and point to BIM regulation as a potential therapeutic lever for restoring immune balance.

title: MINOS1-Mediated Mitochondrial Remodeling: A Critical Regulator of Apoptosis in Hypoxic Intestinal Epithelium.
abstract: Intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) are highly vulnerable to mitochondrial dysfunction and lethal apoptosis under severe hypoxic stress. However, the upstream genetic determinants governing mucosal redox resilience remain poorly defined. To investigate the mechanisms of intestinal epithelial cell apoptosis under cobalt chloride ()-induced hypoxic conditions, we established a -induced lethal hypoxia model in IPEC-J2 cells and performed a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screen. This screen identified MINOS1 as an essential gene for tolerance to -induced hypoxic cell death. Systematic cell phenotyping and transcriptomic analyses revealed that exposure triggers robust intrinsic apoptosis and oxidative stress, whereas MINOS1 ablation remodels the basal transcriptomic landscape to establish an adaptive pro-survival state. Ultrastructural observation via transmission electron microscopy and subcellular functional assays demonstrated that MINOS1 deficiency eliminates canonical crista junctions (CJs) and induces distinctive concentric, "onion-like" remodeling of the inner mitochondrial membrane. Under severe hypoxia, MINOS1-knockout (KO) enterocytes retained stable mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), suppressed pathological mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) opening, sustained antioxidant enzyme (SOD and CAT) activities, and abrogated intracellular ROS accumulation and lipid peroxidation. Pharmacological intervention with the mitochondria-targeted antioxidant Mitoquinone mesylate precisely phenocopied the cytoprotective phenotype of MINOS1 ablation, confirming a mitochondria-dependent redox regulatory mechanism. Crucially, subcellular fractionation assays verified that remodeled concentric mitochondrial membranes form a unique topological barrier that physically sequesters cytochrome c within mitochondria, blocking its cytosolic release and subsequent activation of caspase-9 and caspase-3. Accordingly, MINOS1-deficient enterocytes tolerate extreme hypoxic stress by structurally uncoupling mitochondrial oxidative stress from downstream apoptotic execution. Collectively, these findings establish MINOS1-dependent cristae topology as a fundamental biophysical gatekeeper of intestinal mucosal redox homeostasis, providing a novel structure-targeted therapeutic strategy for hypoxia-associated intestinal disorders.

title: Gene Therapy for Inherited Platelet Disorders: From Proof of Concept to Clinical Translation.
abstract: Inherited platelet disorders (IPDs) comprise a heterogeneous group of rare genetic diseases affecting platelet production and/or function, with clinical manifestations ranging from mild mucocutaneous bleeding to severe hemorrhage, multisystem disease, and predisposition to hematologic malignancy. Treatment remains predominantly supportive, and curative options are limited. Future translation will require disease-specific selection of gene addition, allele-specific approaches, or precise genome editing, together with safer conditioning, efficient lineage-restricted correction, and rigorous long-term assessment of genotoxicity and clonal evolution. A shared hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells platform combined with disease-specific genetic engineering may ultimately enable curative treatment of selected severe IPDs.
