title: Self-Catalyzed Transesterification Transforms Ionizable Amphiphilic Janus Dendrimers into Multicomponent Vectors and Generates Complex Design Strategies for mRNA Delivery.
abstract: Genetic nanomedicine delivers nucleic acids by viral and synthetic vectors to produce drugs directly in the body's own cells. Each approach presents relative advantages, but synthetic vectors are distinguished by their effectively unlimited synthetic capabilities. The leading synthetic vectors are the four-component lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) used in the Pfizer and Moderna Covid-19 vaccines, which deliver mRNA to the liver. Inspired by this concept, our laboratories developed a one-component, multifunctional, sequence-defined ionizable amphiphilic Janus dendrimer (IAJD) that delivers mRNA predominantly to the more desirable spleen, as well as to other organs. Benzoyl, benzyl, and aliphatic biodegradable esters connect the hydrophobic and hydrophilic domains of IAJDs. IAJDs have already been used in preclinical studies of therapeutics and vaccines, and several are commercially available. Here we report that, unexpectedly, the least stable benzyl-ester-based IAJDs, which contain the 1-(2-hydroxyethyl)piperazine ionizable amine (IA), undergo an extraordinarily slow, self-catalyzed transesterification at room temperature that transforms the one-component system into a multicomponent one. This reaction progressively extends the hydrophilic ionizable-amine domain from monomer to dimer, trimer, tetramer, and pentamer, generating a mixture of the original IAJD, its oligomers, and the released benzyl alcohol. Remarkably, at up to 50% transesterification, the in vivo activity of this multicomponent system remains similar to that of the parent one-component IAJD. Beyond providing a simple in situ method to convert one-component IAJDs into an unprecedented multicomponent IAJDs system, these results establish a new design strategy to construct the hydrophilic domain of one-component IAJDs through a complex, "vertical", sequence-defined arrangement of IAs.

title: Patient-derived teratomas as a humanized platform for dystrophin restoration by ex vivo cell therapy and in vivo base editing.
abstract: Cell and gene therapies hold great promise for treating monogenic disorders, yet their preclinical evaluation remains limited by the lack of scalable, human-specific models. Here we establish a patient-derived teratoma xenograft platform as a proof-of-concept system to evaluate ex vivo and in vivo therapeutic strategies for Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD). Teratomas generated from DMD patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells contained mesodermal derivatives, including skeletal muscle-like tissue, enabling assessment of dystrophin restoration after therapeutic intervention. For ex vivo cell therapy, myogenic progenitors derived from adenine base editor-corrected induced pluripotent stem cells were transplanted into DMD teratomas, resulting in partial restoration of shorter dystrophin isoforms but not reproducible recovery of full-length Dp427m. For in vivo gene editing, local delivery of adenine base editor mRNA encapsulated in lipid nanoparticles induced dose-dependent editing and restoration of shorter dystrophin isoforms, including Dp71. Full-length, muscle-specific Dp427m was detected only in a subset of sequentially matured secondary teratomas with enriched muscle differentiation, indicating that myogenic maturation is a critical determinant of this therapeutic readout. Together, these findings support patient-derived DMD teratomas as an exploratory humanized platform for evaluating patient-specific gene correction and dystrophin isoform restoration, while highlighting the need for further optimization to reproducibly model full-length Dp427m recovery.

title: Cancer cell-specific FOXP3 licenses MMP19-dependent matrix remodeling and metastatic dissemination in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is characterized by a dense desmoplastic stroma and early metastatic dissemination, both of which contribute to its poor prognosis. While forkhead box protein 3 (FOXP3) is best known as a lineage-defining transcription factor in regulatory T cells (Tregs), its aberrant expression in cancer cell-specific FOXP3 (c-FOXP3) may also support tumor-cell-intrinsic progression. Our findings suggest that high c-FOXP3 expression is closely linked to aggressive disease behavior and metastatic progression in PDAC. c-FOXP3 enhanced migration, invasion within three-dimensional collagen-rich matrices, and dissemination in orthotopic models. Integrated transcriptomic analysis, chromatin immunoprecipitation, and wild-type versus binding-site-mutant promoter assays identified matrix metalloproteinase 19 (MMP19) as a direct transcriptional target of c-FOXP3. MMP19 silencing significantly attenuated c-FOXP3-driven migration, matrix invasion, and metastasis. Single-cell sequencing further showed that MMP19 is abundant in cancer-associated fibroblasts but also defines a distinct epithelial pool that is reduced after epithelial Foxp3 deletion. Pharmacological profiling did not identify a validated MMP19-selective inhibitor, whereas the FOXP3-targeting antisense oligonucleotide AZD8701 reduced FOXP3 together with MMP19 mRNA and was accompanied by lower PDAC-cell migration and invasion in vitro. Together, these findings extend the known functions of FOXP3 beyond its classical role in immune tolerance and define a tumor-cell-intrinsic c-FOXP3-MMP19 program that supports matrix-invasive behavior in PDAC and provide preliminary evidence that c-FOXP3 is pharmacologically accessible.

title: Bioengineering strategies for improving the immunogenicity of mRNA vaccines.
abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines have reshaped modern vaccinology by enabling rapid antigen design, scalable manufacturing, and coordinated induction of humoral and cellular immunity. Their clinical success has established mRNA as a versatile platform for infectious diseases, cancer immunotherapy, and emerging therapeutic applications. However, expansion into cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, autoimmune, and metabolic disorders imposes indication-specific requirements that cannot be addressed by uniform design strategies. Vaccine performance depends not only on antigen output, but also on how RNA architecture and delivery systems regulate innate sensing, intracellular trafficking, tissue distribution, and adaptive immune programming. In this review, we summarize bioengineering strategies for improving mRNA vaccine immunogenicity by coordinating antigen-expression efficiency with innate immune regulation. We compare non-replicating mRNA, self-amplifying RNA, and circular RNA in terms of expression kinetics, translational logic, safety considerations, and innate immune activation. We then discuss molecular engineering approaches that enhance stability, translation, and immune control, including optimization of cap structures, untranslated regions, poly(A) tails, nucleotide modifications, codon usage, and platform-specific designs for saRNA and circRNA. We further examine delivery systems, including lipid nanoparticles, exosomes, polymer-based carriers, virus-like particles, and hybrid platforms, emphasizing their dual roles in cargo transport and immune modulation. Finally, we discuss indication-specific design principles, manufacturing constraints, and translational challenges. We propose that next-generation mRNA vaccines will require disease-matched co-design of RNA molecules and delivery platforms to enhance antigen expression, tune immune activation, and strengthen clinical translation.

title: α7 integrin co-regulates chromatin accessibility and gene expression in HPV-negative head and neck cancer.
abstract: Epigenetic regulation and gene transcription are dynamically modulated by extracellular signals, including focal adhesions; however, the role of integrins in these processes remains poorly understood. In this study in HPV-negative head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, (HNSCC), we combined investigations in physiological three-dimensional, matrix-embedded cell models and patient-derived organoids with multi-omics analyses, bioinformatics and artificial intelligence, to unmask the integrin effector signaling network that reshapes chromatin to drive cancer. Among the 12 α/β1 integrin receptors, α7 integrin (ITGA7) emerged as the most potent modulator of histone post-translational modifications, associated with significant changes in gene transcription and chromatin accessibility. Depletion of ITGA7, achieved independently by CRISPR/Cas9 knockout and RNA interference, reduced chromatin accessibility at the AURKA locus and downregulated an AURKA-centered transcriptional program. Mechanistically, phosphoproteomics revealed significant inhibition of MAPK- and PI3K/AKT-dependent signaling with concomitant functional impairment of cell cycling and cell survival upon ITGA7 depletion. Across all analyses, machine-learning-based feature selection consistently nominated AURKA as the dominant downstream node, and tumor ITGA7 expression stratified patient overall survival in a non-linear manner. In summary, these findings establish α7 integrin as a key co-regulator of chromatin accessibility and gene transcription in HPV-negative HNSCC, acting through an AURKA-centered axis that couples adhesion signaling to cell cycle control and patient survival, and nominate AURKA, potentially targetable with clinical Aurora-A inhibitors such as alisertib, as an actionable therapeutic node downstream of the currently non-druggable ITGA7.

title: Arrhythmic events and genetic variants as drivers for Takotsubo Syndrome: a patient-specific atrial stem-cell model.
abstract: Takotsubo Syndrome (TTS) is an acute, potentially life-threatening condition often complicated by ventricular dysfunction and arrhythmias. Atrial fibrillation (AF) is common in TTS patients and associated with increased mortality. However, the arrhythmic mechanisms, genetic variability underlying TTS, and personalised therapy remain unclear. We generated induced pluripotent stem cell-derived atrial and ventricular cardiomyocytes (iPSC-CMs) from TTS patients and provoked TTS-like events by isoprenaline (Iso) stimulation. Compared with controls, atrial TTS iPSC-CMs exhibited enhanced diastolic sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) Ca²⁺ leak and increased arrhythmogenic potential following Iso exposure. Iso-induced stress further increased systolic Ca²⁺ transient amplitude and reduced phosphodiesterase 4 (PDE4) activity in TTS iPSC-CMs. Under baseline conditions, atrial TTS iPSC-CMs demonstrated unchanged Ca2+ transient amplitude, reduced diastolic Ca2+, elevated SERCA2 activity with faster Ca²⁺ decay compared to controls, which could be explained by increased phosphorylation of PKA-specific phospholamban S16. In contrast, ventricular TTS-iPSC-CM showed increased L-Type Ca2+ current density, but reduced Ca2+ transient amplitude with increased resting Ca2+ leak and reduced PDE4 activity post-Iso-exposure. In atrial TTS iPSC-CMs, the PDE4 activator MR-L2 restored PDE4 activity, normalised several defects in Ca²⁺ handling and prevented arrhythmias more efficiently than the β-blocker metoprolol. Genetic analyses identified variants in the Ca²⁺ handling genes AHNAK and CASQ2 in TTS. Using CRISPR/Cas9, we generated isogenic rescue and mutation-insertion lines, confirming a causal role of p.P5390T in catecholamine-induced arrhythmogenic phenotypes in atrial TTS iPSC-CMs. Our findings support a mechanistic link between genetic predisposition to an excessive catecholaminergic stress response, dysregulated PDE/cAMP signalling, and atrial arrhythmogenesis in TTS-CMs, identifying PDE4 as a potential therapeutic target in this critical condition.

title: FDX1-short proteoform induces caspase-independent cell death in tumor cells.
abstract: Cell death is a crucial process for the maintenance of physiological functions in organisms. In recent years, cuproptosis, a novel form of cell death induced by copper overload in mitochondria, has emerged as a critical regulatory mechanism. Ferredoxin 1 (FDX1), a key electron transfer protein in this pathway, is essential for copper metabolism and the regulation of cuproptosis. In this study, we characterized a natural short proteoform of FDX1, FDX1-Short Proteoform (FDX1-SP). Lacking the canonical N-terminal mitochondrial targeting sequence, FDX1-SP is widely distributed throughout the cell, with a pronounced propensity for nuclear accumulation. The accumulation of FDX1-SP protein triggers cleavage and degradation of tumor cell DNA. This disrupts nuclear membrane integrity and induces cell death in a caspase-independent manner. FDX1-SP preferentially damages highly accessible chromatin regions in tumor cells, thereby inducing tumor cell death. Based on these findings, we developed an FDX1-SP mRNA therapeutic, which exhibited significant DNA damage and anti-tumor effects in patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models. Our research uncovers the mechanism of death mediated by FDX1-SP, providing new directions for tumor therapy.

title: CRISPRa screen unveils noncanonical NF-κB to boost the antitumor activity of TCR-based CAR-T cells.
abstract: Engineering autologous T cells for adoptive therapies has revolutionized cancer treatment, yet limited persistence remains a major barrier to robust clinical responses and durable disease control. Although costimulation with 4-1BB markedly improves CAR-T-cell persistence, no comparably effective approach has been identified to enhance persistence in T-cell therapies that rely on native TCR signaling, including conventional TCR-T cells and synthetic T-cell receptor and antigen receptor (STAR) T cells. To identify intrinsic persistence regulators in a TCR-based context, we performed an in vivo CRISPR activation screen in STAR-T cells and identified the noncanonical NF-κB axis, with RELB as the top hit. Direct RELB overexpression, however, exhibited dose-dependent cytotoxicity, motivating a translational alternative: overexpression of p52, the ncNF-κB transcription partner of RELB. Under prolonged antigen exposure, p52 overexpression sustained proliferation, preserved effector functions, and increased the intratumoral trafficking potential, particularly in CD8⁺ T cells, thereby yielding superior tumor control. Mechanistically, transcriptomic profiling revealed coordinated upregulation of cell cycle programs and chemokine receptors, along with downregulation of apoptosis and exhaustion-associated modules. Moreover, p52 overexpression restored RELB nuclear translocation in the context of PD-1/PD-L1 engagement, indicating partial resistance to checkpoint-mediated suppression and sustained ncNF-κB activity in PD-L1hi immunosuppressive environments. Collectively, our findings identify p52 as an antigen-dependent enhancer of ncNF-κB, conferring durable persistence and checkpoint resilience on TCR-based T cells and providing a feasible strategy to improve therapeutic effects in solid tumors.

title: Discovery of direct-acting small-molecule RIG-I agonists through creation of a selective CARD activation platform.
abstract: Retinoic acid-inducible gene-I (RIG-I) plays a pivotal role in recognizing and combating RNA viruses in humans, and it has become a drug target of significant interest. RIG-I agonists composed of dsRNA represent antiviral and antitumor therapies, however the development of small-molecule RIG-I agonists, with their potential for improved pharmacokinetics, remains an unmet need. Here, we report small-molecule RIG-I agonists that directly activate the RIG-I receptor protein. These agonists stimulate the first step in RIG-I signaling by triggering release of the signaling domains (CARDs) from an autorepressed form of the protein. This was achieved by developing a sensitive high-throughput screening (HTS) assay that directly monitors CARD expulsion through optical methods. The resulting screen hits were refined and optimized, leading to a specific RIG-I agonist that induces a robust interferon response. This study establishes a pharmacophore and assay for development of small molecules that precisely modulate RIG-I signaling.

title: Multimodal precision diagnostics in clinical xenotransplantation.
abstract: Recent breakthroughs in pig-to-human xenotransplantation have successfully prevented hyperacute rejection of kidney, heart, liver and lung xenografts, marking a milestone long considered a critical barrier. However, these major advances also brought new challenges into focus, as immune-mediated graft injuries including antibody-mediated rejection, T cell-mediated rejection and innate immune activation have been observed in most xenotransplantation procedures to date. Detection and management of these injuries remain a critical bottleneck, as conventional histopathology and standard clinical monitoring lack the sensitivity required to identify subclinical injury early enough to guide timely intervention. This diagnostic gap underscores an urgent need for the development of advanced, multimodal precision diagnostic frameworks to enhance immune surveillance, which will be essential for standardizing clinical protocols and enabling pathogenesis-driven therapeutic intervention. This approach will inform both immunosuppressive regimens and future gene editing strategies aimed at engineering rejection-resistant porcine organs, ultimately prolonging graft survival. Broad adoption of such an integrative strategy will be essential to transition xenotransplantation from an experimental intervention into a safe, scalable and patient-centred clinical therapy. In this Review, we synthesize recent progress in xenotransplantation and position multimodal precision diagnostics as a pivotal strategy to address the remaining immunological and clinical barriers to widespread clinical implementation.

title: Engineered human Argonaute 2 for targeted C-to-U RNA base editing.
abstract: Tools for manipulating RNA that rely on nonhuman proteins, such as ISC-based and Cas-based scaffolds, can lead to unintended and little-understood effects on human cells and present challenges in therapeutic translation. Replacing them with human proteins engineered for expanded, programmable functions could bypass the limitations of these foreign proteins. Here we demonstrate that human Argonaute 2 (AGO2) can be repurposed as a modular RNA targeting domain. AGO2 fused to a C-to-U deaminase enables AGO-led targeted editing of RNA (ALTER). Using guide RNAs that remodel target RNA structure for selective editing and reduced nuclease activity, we show that ALTER achieves, on average, 1.9-fold higher C-to-U editing on mRNA targets in HEK293T cells compared with Cas13 editors CURE and RESCUE. Transcriptome-wide RNA-seq revealed similar or lower levels of off-target editing compared to the same Cas13-based editors. Machine learning models predict that far fewer immunogenic peptides will result from ALTER and we show that ALTER is amenable to a validated workflow for artificial intelligence-directed deimmunization.

title: Lineage identity governs oncogene dependence in mouse NSCLC models of KRAS inhibitor resistance.
abstract: Primary and acquired resistance to targeted therapy represent significant challenges to durable treatment responses in oncology. In lung adenocarcinoma, KRAS inhibitors are hampered by incomplete clinical responses and acquired resistance. Here we treated genetically engineered mouse models of Kras-driven lung adenocarcinoma with KRAS inhibitors to model these conditions. Initial treatment response was rapid but incomplete, with residual tumor burden transcriptionally resembling alveolar epithelial cells. With continued treatment, we invariably observed genetic Kras amplification as a resistance mechanism. To model oncogene-independent resistance, we used functional CRISPR approaches to promote squamous lineage transformation. We found that ∆Np63 was sufficient to transform alveolar organoids to a squamous state in vitro, conferring insensitivity to KRAS inhibition. In vivo, Nkx2-1 loss and/or ectopic Sox2 expression poised tumors for squamous lineage commitment. Squamous-transformed tumors did not exhibit evidence of KRAS/MAPK reactivation, underscoring the role for lineage transcription factors and histologic transformation in mediating KRAS independence.

title: Reactivation of the embryonic ζ-globin gene ameliorates severe forms of α-thalassemia.
abstract: Hemoglobinopathies are the most common inherited anemias worldwide. While most carriers are asymptomatic or mildly affected, severe forms of α-thalassemia, including severe hemoglobin H (HbH) disease and surviving individuals with Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis syndrome (BHFS), require lifelong transfusion support or stem cell transplantation. Reactivating the silenced embryonic α-like globin (ζ-globin) gene is a promising approach for treating these diseases. Here we identify the key cis-regulatory elements responsible for silencing the ζ-globin gene in definitive erythroid cells and subsequently develop gene-editing strategies that reactivate ζ-globin expression to therapeutically relevant levels. In a preclinical mouse model of BHFS, we show that this strategy rescues the otherwise prenatal lethal condition until late in development (E17.5). Using primary erythroid cells derived from patients with HbH disease and BHFS, we show that these approaches reactivate ζ-globin expression to levels exceeding those achieved in the mouse model, producing therapeutic levels of α-like globin.

title: Behavioral genomics identifies Creld1 as a cross-modal regulator of somatosensation.
abstract: Somatosensation is mediated by dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons, which convert physical and chemical stimuli into electrical signals. However, the full repertoire of molecular components underlying somatosensation remains incompletely identified. Here we developed an efficient postnatal CRISPR-Cas9 knockout platform for interrogating DRG-expressed genes (such as Piezo2, Trpv1 and Scn9a) in mice using AAV9-mediated single-guide RNA delivery. Combining this approach with somatosensory behavioral assays, we performed a targeted screen of 20 genes and identified Creld1 as a cross-model regulator of somatosensation. Either single-guide RNA-mediated postnatal knockout or tamoxifen-induced Cre-mediated deletion of Creld1 in DRG neurons resulted in profound behavioral deficits in touch, temperature, pain and itch, whereas its overexpression enhanced touch and thermal responses. Mechanistically, CRELD1 functions as an auxiliary regulator of voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav) for controlling DRG neuron excitability. Together, this work establishes a robust postnatal screening platform for behavioral genomics and identifies Creld1 as a master regulator of somatosensory function.

title: Intramuscular self-amplifying RNA and adenoviral RSV vaccines program distinct systemic and respiratory mucosal immune architectures.
abstract: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) remains a major cause of severe lower respiratory tract disease in infants, older adults, and immunocompromised individuals, underscoring the need for vaccine strategies that balance systemic protection with frontline respiratory immunity. Although adenoviral and RNA-based RSV are both promising platforms, how the platform itself shapes systemic versus respiratory mucosal immunity under the same antigenic context remains insufficiently defined. We conducted a head-to-head comparison of an LNP-delivered saRNA vaccine (LNP-RSV-preF saRNA) and a recombinant Ad5-vectored vaccine (Ad5-RSV-preF) in mice using intramuscular prime-boost immunization. The two platforms drove distinct immune architectures rather than just differences in response magnitude. LNP-RSV-preF saRNA preferentially promoted respiratory mucosal immunity, including elevated BALF IgG, pulmonary antibody-secreting cells, CD69+ T cells, and lung-resident memory T (TRM) cells, as well as cycling and memory-associated CD8+ T-cell states and durable lung IgA memory. In contrast, Ad5-RSV-preF induced stronger systemic immunity, featured by higher early serum IgG, splenic polyfunctional effector T cells, enhanced germinal center/TFH responses, and effector-polarized CD8 + T cells, with sustained systemic humoral memory. Ad5-vectored and LNP-saRNA vaccine platforms induce distinct compartmentalized immune responses to the same RSV preF antigen. This study establishes a framework for rational platform selection in RSV vaccine design, enabling tailored strategies to balance systemic immunity and respiratory mucosal memory.

title: An aptamer-regulated CRISPR/Cas12a system based on split crRNA for theophylline and tobramycin detection.
abstract: Most existing CRISPR/Cas12a methods for small molecules detection employ DNA aptamers as an intermediary, while RNA aptamers remain underexplored. The conventional CRISPR/Cas12 system offers limited programmability due to its partially conserved crRNA sequence. In this study, we developed an aptamer-regulated CRISPR/Cas12a system based on split crRNA. We divided the full crRNA into a crRNA handle segment (RH) and a crRNA spacer segment that is identical to the RNA aptamer sequence of target (RS-Apt). RS-Apt was endowed with dual functions: activating the activity of Cas12a and binding to target small molecules, ingeniously linking non-nucleic acid targets with the CRISPR system. The strong affinity between the target and RS-Apt reduces the amount of RS-Apt available to participate in the CRISPR system, resulting in a decrease in the fluorescence signal of the system. Within 1.5 h, the system for theophylline (TP) exhibited a linear range from 50 nM to 200 µM and a detection limit (LOD) of 2 nM, while the system for tobramycin (TOB) showed a linear range of 200 nM to 100 µM with an LOD of 63 nM. Notably, visual semi-quantitative detection of TP and TOB was achieved via lateral flow strips. Moreover, the system achieved satisfactory recovery and visual detection of TP using lateral flow strips in TP-spiked serum samples. This system can detect different targets simply by changing the sequence of the RS-Apt and activator, without the need for complex sequence design of the chains or large-scale instruments, providing a new strategy for CRISPR/Cas12a in the detection of small molecules.

title: A programmable aptamer-triggered B-PER/CRISPR cascade amplification platform for ultrasensitive detection of Staphylococcus aureus.
abstract: Rapid and sensitive detection of Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) is critical for food safety and public health. Herein, this work developed an ABC (aptamer-B-PER-CRISPR) cascade detection platform, where B-PER stands for bidirectional primer exchange reaction, that integrates aptamer-mediated target recognition, B-PER isothermal amplification, and CRISPR/Cas12a trans-cleavage for highly sensitive and specific detection of S. aureus. Upon target recognition, the trigger strand T is released from the aptamer-T duplex, initiating B-PER to generate abundant products containing sequences recognized by the guide RNA (gRNA), which activate Cas12a to cleave the reporter probe, generating a detectable fluorescence signal. Under optimized conditions, the platform exhibited a linear range of 102 to 1010 CFU per mL with a regression equation of F520 nm = 575.36 log C + 3246.47 (R2 = 0.9992) and a limit of detection of 13 CFU per mL. The assay showed excellent specificity for S. aureus, with negligible cross-reactivity toward Vibrio parahaemolyticus and Salmonella. Recovery tests in spiked milk samples yielded average recoveries of 98.9-100.7%. Overall, the ABC platform offers high sensitivity, excellent specificity, robust anti-interference capability, and operational simplicity, demonstrating great potential for rapid and reliable detection of foodborne pathogens in complex matrices.

title: Advances in the development and delivery of nucleic acid-based therapeutics.
abstract: Recent advancements in experimental and computational methods along with growing gene sequencing libraries have enabled rapid development of nucleic acid-based therapeutic design for a wide variety of diseases. New drugs, delivery tools and methods have enabled precise and efficient therapy at a molecular scale. This review covers the current landscape and future directions of methods for gene and cell therapies, as well as their applications, advantages, and limitations. We present self-amplifying RNA, circular RNA, CRISPR systems, antisense oligonucleotides, and antibody-oligonucleotide conjugates, as well as CAR modification of T-cells, natural killer cells, and macrophages, with a brief discussion of modified stem cells. We also discuss developments in viral and non-viral delivery systems for their applications in cell and gene therapies.

title: Polycation chain length determines the in vivo mRNA delivery efficiency of block copolymer micelles.
abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA)-based therapeutics hold great promise by enabling in situ expression of therapeutic proteins. The success of these therapies in vivo critically depends on the design of safe and efficient delivery systems. Polymeric micelles formed by block catiomers can encapsulate mRNA, protect it from degradation, and facilitate intracellular delivery. Polycation chain length has been proposed as a design parameter of micelles, yet how it governs stabilizing interactions to define mRNA delivery performance remains unestablished. Here, we systematically investigate this relationship using a series of poly(ethylene glycol)-poly(glycidyl-phenylalanate) (PEG-PG(Phe)) block copolymers with varying PG(Phe) chain lengths. These polymers interact with mRNA via polyion complexation and π-π stacking. Our findings revealed that the block catiomers having PG(Phe) segments with 90 units formed micelles with superior stability and enhanced endosomal escape, while micelles with shorter segments were rapidly dissociated and micelles with longer blocks showed impaired PEG shielding. Moreover, the polymer with a PG(Phe) block of 90 units achieved 2-fold higher protein expression in vivo compared to shorter or longer chain variants. These findings reveal that tuning polycation chain length with core π-π interactions is key to unlocking highly efficient mRNA delivery.

title: Microfluidic channel engineering for mRNA-LNPs: a systematic review of mixing strategies, nanostructures, and biological performance.
abstract: mRNA-lipid nanoparticles (mRNA-LNPs) have revolutionized nucleic acid therapeutics, yet their clinical success relies heavily on precise manufacturing processes. This review comprehensively explores the critical intersection between microfluidic channel design, lipid self-assembly biophysics, and the subsequent biological performance of mRNA-LNPs. First, we analyze the fundamental fluid mechanics driving representative microfluidic mixers, elucidating how different channel architectures dictate solvent exchange rates and nanoparticle assembly kinetics. We then systematically examine how these specific mixing regimes modulate essential physicochemical characteristics, including lipid distribution, internal nanostructure, particle morphology, size distribution, and overall colloidal stability. Crucially, we bridge the gap between manufacturing and pharmacology by evaluating how mixing-induced physicochemical differences directly translate into distinct biological outcomes, such as cellular uptake mechanisms, endosomal escape efficiency, and systemic pharmacokinetics. By integrating microfluidic engineering principles with biological evaluation, this review provides a mechanistic framework for understanding how continuous-flow assembly processes program the functional behavior of mRNA-LNP systems. Ultimately, we highlight emerging design principles essential for developing the next generation of robust, highly efficient nucleic acid delivery platforms.

title: A surface-mediated hydrogel patch for localized CRISPR genome editing in inflammatory wound therapy.
abstract: The NLRP3 inflammasome is a central driver of inflammatory tissue injury and delayed repair in bacteria-infected wounds, yet local genome editing in such lesions remains limited by nonspecific release and off-target exposure. Here, we report a pH-gated surface-mediated hydrogel patch for infection-responsive delivery of CRISPR-Cas9 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes. Rather than embedding the cargo within the bulk matrix, polymer-coated NLRP3-targeting RNPs are reversibly anchored on the hydrogel surface, enabling localized presentation under physiological conditions and rapid detachment in the acidic microenvironment of Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus)-infected wounds. In vitro studies demonstrated an NLRP3 editing efficiency of 57% in J774A.1 cells and 69% in L929 cells surpassing or matching the performance of the commercial transfection reagent Lipofectamine CRISPRMAX (50% in J774A.1; comparable in L929). In a murine full-thickness skin defect model with S. aureus infection, topical administration of the patch achieved >20% NLRP3 editing efficiency in wound tissue, accompanied by a statistically significant reduction in inflammatory cell infiltration. Consequently, this pH-responsive surface anchoring and release strategy establishes a novel paradigm for localized, precision gene therapy and holds strong translational promise for the treatment of chronic inflammatory wounds.

title: Exploiting inosine as a distinctive cleavage site for deriving a highly specific RNA-cleaving DNAzyme.
abstract: Most RNA-cleaving DNAzymes are limited to cleaving between combinations of the four canonical ribonucleotides. Through in vitro selection, we isolated ICD11-1T, a DNAzyme that selectively cleaves at inosine, a non-canonical RNA modification generated by adenosine deamination. ICD11-1T cleaves inosine-containing substrates with a rate constant of 0.1 min-1 and achieves >103-fold selectivity over adenosine, discriminating between nucleosides that differ at the C6 and N1 positions of the purine ring. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed that the inosine positions the cleavage site near the catalytic core, whereas the adenosine complex sequesters it away, accounting for the stringent specificity. Using ICD11-1T, we constructed a fluorescent biosensor that enabled imaging of endogenous ADAR (adenosine deaminase acting on RNA) editing activity in fixed and permeabilized cells. This work provides a proof-of-concept tool for studying adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing and establishes a strategy for expanding the functionality of DNAzymes.

title: A targeting delivery platform for the mapping of responses to p53-independent intervention in heterogeneous patient cancer cells.
abstract: Developing new cancer therapeutic strategies has become a central focus in precision oncology. However, a major challenge is the lack of robust models to accurately assess target vulnerability in patient-specific heterogeneous cancer cells, which limits the translation of research findings into effective clinical therapies. In this study, we developed an ex vivo blood-based model utilizing a versatile nano-delivery platform to evaluate the responsiveness of MDM2 knockout as a representative therapeutic approach in circulating malignant cells (CMCs) from patients stratified by their p53 status. In our genome editing plasmid delivery system (p@RPA), protamine sulfate was combined with a cell-penetrating peptide to condense the CRISPR-Cas9 plasmid into nano-cores. These nano-cores were then coated with chondroitin sulfate shells functionalized with the AS1411 aptamer, enabling the selective recognition of CD44 and/or nucleolin overexpressing malignant cells. Using the same vector, a molecular beacon delivery system (MBs@RPA) co-loaded with MBMDM2 for probing MDM2 mRNA, MBTP53 for probing TP53 mRNA and MBTP73 for probing TP73 mRNA was constructed for the in situ evaluation of biomarker changes induced by genome editing. p@RPA demonstrates satisfactory efficacy in mediating gene editing for MDM2 knockout in malignant cells. Notably, the knockout of MDM2 induces cell cycle arrest and leads to a marked upregulation of anti-tumor TAp73 irrespective of their p53 status. With efficient gene editing and mRNA probing achieved in patient-derived CMCs, we establish an ex vivo platform capable of in situ therapeutic efficacy assessment at single-cell resolution to explicitly reveal the underlying cellular heterogeneity across individual CMCs.

title: Targeting CLK1 by CRISPR tools and pharmacological inhibition modulates the innate immune response and dengue virus replication.
abstract: Alternative splicing is a key regulatory mechanism known to be altered upon viral infection. These alterations can arise both from direct viral interference with the splicing machinery and from cellular responses such as activation of innate immunity. Here, we investigated splicing changes shared between dengue virus (DENV) infection and interferon (IFN) treatment in cultured cells, the latter serving as a model for virus-independent innate immune activation. Among the common events, we identified an increased production of non-coding mRNA isoforms from the CLK1 gene, which gives rise to a kinase that phosphorylates splicing factors including SR proteins and spliceosomal components. Consistent with this finding, IFN treatment led to a reduction in CLK1 protein levels. Using stable cell lines with CRISPR/dCas9-mediated modulation of CLK1 expression, we found that silencing CLK1 enhanced the induction of immune response genes, while its over-expression attenuated it. Inhibition of CLK1 kinase activity with the pharmacological inhibitor TG003 further potentiated IFN-induced gene expression and reduced DENV replication. Altogether, these results identify CLK1 as a proviral negative regulator of IFN-stimulated gene expression and suggest that its inhibition could enhance antiviral defenses and become a target for therapeutic strategies.

title: Histone demethylase Kdm2a aggravates pressure overload-induced myocardial fibrosis through global and locus-specific H3K36me2 chromatin remodeling.
abstract: Subclinical hypertensive heart disease (SHHD) is a precursor to heart failure and ultimately progresses to impaired left ventricular systolic function, which is characterized by myocardial hypertrophy leading to compromised contractility and by myofibroblast proliferation and activation leading to decreased myocardial compliance. However, the epigenetic mechanisms that coordinate fibroblast-mediated fibrosis during pressure overload remain incompletely understood. Here, we identified the histone demethylase Kdm2a as an important regulator of cardiac remodeling in a mouse transverse aortic constriction (TAC) model. Kdm2a was up-regulated and enriched in activated cardiac fibroblasts during TAC-induced remodeling. Fibroblast-enriched Kdm2a knockdown improved cardiac function, reduced myocardial hypertrophy, and markedly attenuated interstitial and perivascular fibrosis in TAC hearts. In cultured primary cardiac fibroblasts, profibrotic stimulation increased Kdm2a expression, whereas CRISPR-mediated Kdm2a knockout suppressed fibroblast activation, collagen production, and extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition. Conversely, Kdm2a overexpression enhanced profibrotic responses. RNA sequencing and network analyses further showed that Kdm2a modulates ECM-associated pathways and remodeling-related gene programs. Mechanistically, Kdm2a modulation was associated with both global and locus-specific remodeling of H3K36me2. Kdm2a up-regulation was accompanied by altered bulk H3K36me2 levels, while CUT&RUN-qPCR demonstrated locus-specific changes in H3K36me2 enrichment at remodeling-associated genes, including Col1a1, Col4a1, and Cdkn2b/p15. These findings suggest that Kdm2a reshapes the H3K36me2 chromatin landscape in a context- and locus-dependent manner to promote fibroblast activation and ECM remodeling and identify Kdm2a as an epigenetic driver of fibroblast-mediated cardiac remodeling and a potential therapeutic target for sustained pressure overload-induced heart failure.

title: Small interfering RNA targeting protein Z-dependent protease inhibitor improves hemostasis in Von Willebrand factor- and Factor X-deficient mice.
abstract: Non-factor therapeutics have transformed the treatment paradigm in hemophilia A. Owing to their mode of action, these agents may also provide benefit for other rare bleeding disorders (RBDs) such as von Willebrand disease (VWD)-type 3 and Factor X (FX) deficiency. Targeting protein Z-dependent protease inhibitor (ZPI), a natural anticoagulant, is a novel strategy to enhance hemostasis. We evaluated the effects of ZPI post-transcriptional silencing using a GalNAc-conjugated siRNA (mTGM-148) in von Willebrand factor-deficient (VwfKO) mice and in mice with strongly reduced factor X levels (< 1%; f10low-mice). mTGM-148 reduced plasma ZPI antigen below 15% in both models. In VwfKO-mice, mTGM-148 significantly enhanced contact activation-initiated thrombin generation and normalized INTEM clotting parameters. In f10low-mice, thrombin generation was minimally affected, but EXTEM clotting parameters were significantly ameliorated. Importantly, mTGM-148 treatment significantly reduced blood loss in the tail clip model for both VwfKO-mice and f10low-mice. These data suggest that ZPI post-transcriptional silencing is a viable strategy to improve the hemostatic potential in both VWD-type 3 and FX deficiency. As such, ZPI inhibition represents a promising non-factor therapeutic approach for selected RBDs.

title: Molecular dynamics simulation and QM/MM study of IscB-ωRNA complex.
abstract: The CRISPR-Cas9 system's gene-editing fidelity relies on the HNH nuclease domain's ability to hydrolyze DNA via metal-ion catalysis. While IscB-ωRNA variants offer advantages for viral delivery due to their small size, their editing efficiency is much lower than that of Cas9. The understanding of how HNH-domain dynamics and metal-ion selection jointly control catalysis is essential for its rational improvement. Here, we employ molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) simulations, and free energy perturbations (FEP) to study the conformation dynamics of the IscB-ωRNA-target DNA complex and cation binding energy in the core HNH(IscB)-DNA region. Our MD simulations revealed that the IscB-ωRNA-DNA complex is overall stable. However, the core HNH(IscB)-DNA region shifts to a larger separation, consistent with recent findings of coupling between HNH motion and activation in IscB-ωRNA-DNA. However, the HNH domain motion may be decreased by Cas9-like H246D/H270N mutations. QM/MM and FEP studies found that three Cas9 activating ions, Mg2+, Mn2+, and Co2+, also have higher binding energy in the mutated HNH(IscB)-DNA region, suggesting that the catalytic efficiencies of IscB-ωRNA could be subjected to the balance between stabilizing ion binding and domain motions.

title: IGF2BP1 in 17q-gain cooperates with MYCN to regulate purine biosynthesis and immunotherapy efficacy in neuroblastoma.
abstract: Concurrent chromosomal 17q-gain and MYCN amplification define a subset of neuroblastoma associated with particularly adverse clinical outcomes. However, how these genetic alterations synergize to promote tumor progression and whether their cooperation confers therapeutic vulnerabilities remain elusive. We herein performed a CRISPR-based functional screen targeting 17q-gain genes and identified the RNA m6A reader IGF2BP1 as a critical MYCN collaborator to promote aggressive neuroblastomas via activation of phosphoribosylaminoimidazole succinocarboxamide synthetase (PAICS), a key enzyme involved in de novo purine biosynthesis. Rewiring of PAICS-mediated nucleotide metabolism enabled tumor cells to sustain necessary purine pools for productive transcription of replicative stress-responsive genes, including CHK1, to cope with the exacerbated replication stress. Pharmacological inhibition of CHK1 elicited a robust immune reprogramming, leading to activation of cGAS-STING signaling, upregulation of Major Histocompatibility Complex class I expression, and synergistic tumor suppression with immune checkpoint blockade. Altogether, we identify an IGF2BP1/MYCN-PAICS-CHK1 axis that drives aggressive neuroblastoma phenotypes and constitutes an actionable vulnerability for therapeutic intervention.

title: P-body-mediated RNA decay controls neural crest EMT.
abstract: Neural crest cells, a multipotent vertebrate stem cell population, undergo a tightly regulated epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) to delaminate from the neural tube and initiate migration. Neural crest EMT is controlled by a transient pulse of Draxin, which acts as a molecular rheostat of canonical Wnt signaling, and is then rapidly downregulated by unknown mechanisms. To address this, here we use in vivo reporter assays and live RNA imaging to show that Draxin mRNA is rapidly degraded posttranscriptionally via its 3' untranslated region. We found that Draxin transcripts are targeted to cytoplasmic processing bodies (P-bodies), which are membrane-less sites of RNA processing and decay. Disruption of P-bodies by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated depletion of the RNA helicase DDX6 prevented posttranscriptional downregulation of Draxin and impaired neural crest EMT in vivo. These findings parallel observations in human patients carrying DDX6 mutations, who exhibit defects in P-body assembly and craniofacial abnormalities associated with neural crest dysfunction. Together, our results identify P-bodies as regulators of Draxin mRNA decay and reveal a spatially organized mechanism of RNA turnover that controls neural crest EMT during vertebrate development.

title: Late-onset preeclampsia is characterized by accelerated placental aging.
abstract: Late-onset preeclampsia (LOPE) is a major pregnancy complication characterized by hypertension and placental dysfunction, resolving only upon delivery. Here, we show that LOPE placentae undergo accelerated molecular aging, marked by telomere attrition, DNA damage, and trophoblast senescence. Using primary placental tissue and trophoblast organoids, we demonstrate oxidative stress as a driver of telomere shortening and angiogenic imbalance. Inflammation did not alter placental aging trajectories. Antioxidant treatment (superoxide dismutase) preserved telomere length, reduced DNA damage, and restored angiogenic balance, highlighting oxidative stress as a modifiable determinant of placental aging. We identify reduced expression of telomeric repeat-containing RNAs (TERRAs) as a molecular hallmark of LOPE, and show that antisense oligonucleotide-mediated TERRA depletion exacerbates telomere erosion and senescence. Together, these findings delineate oxidative stress and TERRA loss as mechanisms driving placental decline, establish trophoblast organoids as a tractable model of placental aging, and reveal potential therapeutic avenues for mitigating preeclampsia-associated placental dysfunction.

title: Desulfinylation of the deubiquitinase USP7 by SRXN1 attenuates oxidative acute liver injury.
abstract: Protein S-sulfinylation is a reversible oxidative cysteine modification, but its contribution to acute liver injury such as those induced by acetaminophen (APAP) overdose has not been reported. Sulfiredoxin-1 (SRXN1) is the only oxidoreductase known to reduce the sulfinylated proteins, yet the substrates and mechanisms through which it protects against acute liver injury are unclear. Here, we show that hepatic protein S-sulfinylation was markedly upregulated in APAP-overdose patients and mice. Hepatocyte-specific knockout or pharmacological inhibition of Srxn1 sensitized mice to APAP-induced acute liver injury. In contrast, overexpression of SRXN1, but not its oxidoreductase-dead C99S mutant, protected mice from APAP-induced liver injury. Mechanistically, we identified the deubiquitinase ubiquitin-specific protease 7 (USP7) as an SRXN1 substrate required for hepatoprotection. USP7 inhibition worsened APAP-induced liver injury, whereas its overexpression alleviated injury by stabilizing its deubiquitinase substrate heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1). Loss of SRXN1 enhanced S-sulfinylation of USP7 at Cys315, promoting its ubiquitination and degradation. SRXN1 expression correlated with USP7 levels in human liver samples. Delayed lipid nanoparticle (LNP) delivery of SRXN1 messenger RNA (mRNA) mitigated established APAP-induced liver injury beyond the therapeutic window of N-acetylcysteine. These findings define an SRXN1-USP7-HO-1 axis as a promising therapeutic target for oxidative liver injury and highlight LNP-mediated SRXN1 mRNA delivery as a potential treatment approach.

title: Precision Medicine in Sickle Cell Disease: From Molecular Pathways to Curative Strategies.
abstract: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a monogenic β-globin disorder characterized by hemoglobin S polymerization, hemolysis, and vaso-occlusion, yet it exhibits remarkable clinical heterogeneity. Despite advances in supportive care and disease-modifying therapies, substantial variability in severity, treatment response, and long-term outcomes persists. Therefore, this review aims to examine the biological and clinical foundations of precision medicine in SCD, emphasizing genomic modifiers, molecular pathways, and phenotype-driven therapeutic strategies. Key pathogenic pathways including hemoglobin polymerization, vascular adhesion, and inflammatory and oxidative amplification have enabled the development of targeted agents such as hydroxyurea, voxelotor, crizanlizumab, and L-glutamine, each demonstrating domain-specific targets. Pharmacogenomic insights, particularly involving fetal hemoglobin regulatory loci (e.g. BCL11A and HBS1L-MYB), further elucidate variability in disease expression and therapeutic response. Emerging curative approaches, including allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, lentiviral gene addition, and CRISPR-Cas9-mediated genome editing, represent transformative applications of precision hematology. Collectively, these advances support a paradigm shift from generalized symptom management toward biologically informed, individualized care. Continued integration of genomic profiling, biomarker stratification, and equitable implementation frameworks will be essential to translate precision strategies into sustainable improvements in global SCD outcomes.

title: Toward point-of-care CRISPR-based diagnostics using split crRNA and split activator/target systems.
abstract: Split crRNA and split activator/target strategies have enhanced and advanced CRISPR-based diagnostics (CRISPR/Dx) by requiring a conditional assembly of components. The split crRNA involves dividing the guide RNA (crRNA) itself into multiple inactive fragments that only reassemble to become functional crRNA upon binding to a specific target. The split activator/target involves dividing the target or activator substrate into two reconfigurable segments that trigger Cas activation only upon proper assembly. These evolved CRISPR/Dx systems have enabled: direct quantification of miRNA and ultrashort RNA sequences, amplification-free and attomolar-level detection, single-base discrimination, protospacer adjacent motif (PAM)-free recognition, one-pot analysis, multiplex diagnostics, non-nucleic acid target detection, and constructing biochemical circuits and logic gates. Herein, we critically discuss the advances, pitfalls, challenges, and future perspectives of these CRISPR/Dx systems for field-deployable point-of-care diagnostics. Different split crRNA and split activator/target strategies and applications for CRISPR/Dx are highlighted.

title: Genome-wide CRISPR screens identify shared and context-specific regulators of podocyte resistance to oxidative injury.
abstract: Podocyte injury is a convergent driver of glomerular disease progression, yet the genetic determinants that govern podocyte vulnerability to oxidative stress remain incompletely defined. Here, we performed genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 knockout screens in differentiated human podocytes exposed to two complementary injury models: Adriamycin (ADR), a clinically relevant inducer of podocyte damage, and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), a direct oxidative stress challenge. Human podocytes were transduced with a genome-wide sgRNA library, differentiated under non-permissive conditions and subjected to optimized stress conditions that imposed selective pressure while preserving library complexity. Across five independent replicates per condition, sequencing-based sgRNA profiling demonstrated high reproducibility, balanced library representation and clear treatment-specific selection. The ADR screen identified 819 depleted and 456 enriched genes, whereas the H2O2 screen identified 277 depleted and 215 enriched genes. Integrated analysis revealed both model-specific dependencies and 27 shared depleted genes across the two injury conditions, implicating stress adaptation, chromatin regulation, mitochondrial metabolism, inflammatory signaling and cytoskeletal organization as candidate processes required for podocyte survival. These genome-wide screens provide a functional framework for prioritizing genes that regulate podocyte resilience to oxidative injury and offer a resource for mechanistic studies of glomerular disease.

title: Progress in polymeric nanoparticle-based treatment approaches for Wnt β-catenin pathway modulation and adenomatous polyposis coli mutant colorectal cancer.
abstract: About 80-90% of sporadic instances of colorectal cancer (CRC) are caused by mutations in the adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) gene, which is one of the earliest and most common molecular events. The constitutive activation of the Wnt/β-catenin signalling pathway caused by APC dysfunction promotes unchecked cellular proliferation, tumour initiation, progression, and treatment resistance. Systemic toxicity, insufficient tumour selectivity, and acquired drug resistance continue to restrict treatment results for advanced colorectal cancer (CRC) despite advancements in surgery, chemotherapy, targeted treatments, and immunotherapy. Novel treatment approaches that can address the molecular anomalies linked to APC dysfunction are therefore desperately needed. In this context, a number of treatment modalities have been studied, including small interfering RNA (siRNA), microRNA, CRISPR/Cas-based gene-editing systems, chemotherapeutic drugs, and combination therapy. Polymeric nanoparticles (PNPs) are among the strategies that have shown promise as preclinical delivery systems and have the potential to be translated into clinical settings. Poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA), chitosan, and PEG-based polymeric nanoparticles (PNPs) offer biocompatibility, controlled release, enhanced tumour accumulation, and protection of therapeutic cargo. In addition to critically assessing PNP-mediated medication and gene delivery techniques that target APC-associated Wnt/β-catenin signalling, this review explores the mechanistic significance of APC in colorectal carcinogenesis. The promise of PNPs to enhance APC-focused treatment in colorectal cancer is highlighted by emphasising targeted delivery, therapeutic precision, biomarker-guided techniques, translational hurdles, and future clinical prospects.

title: Liver-Targeted DGAT2 siRNA Ameliorates Steatosis and Fibrosis in a High-Fat Diet-Induced MASH Mouse Model.
abstract: Diacylglycerol O-acyltransferase 2 (DGAT2), a key enzyme in hepatic triglyceride (TG) synthesis, is considered a promising therapeutic target for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH). Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) targeting conserved regions of human and mouse DGAT2 mRNA were designed, synthesized, and screened in vitro, leading to the identification of a GalNAc-conjugated siRNA, VX093L, which mediates potent DGAT2 mRNA knockdown in both human and mouse hepatocytes and exhibits sustained hepatic DGAT2 silencing in healthy mice. In a high-fat diet (HFD)-induced MASH mouse model, the effects of VX093L (1 or 3 mg/kg, biweekly) were evaluated in comparison with the approved drug resmetirom (10 mg/kg, daily). Eight-week treatment with VX093L potently silenced hepatic DGAT2 (>80%, p < 0.0001), thereby inhibiting hepatic TG synthesis, resulting in significantly ameliorating hepatic steatosis. Notably, the improvement in steatosis translated into effective attenuation of fibrosis, with 1 mg/kg VX093L exhibiting better anti-fibrotic efficacy compared to resmetirom, and this benefit was not accompanied by increased inflammation. In conclusion, VX093L represents a promising siRNA-based therapeutic for the treatment of MASH.

title: Redefining intranasal brain delivery: from nasal entry to meaningful parenchymal and cellular exposure.
abstract: Nose-to-brain (N2B) delivery is a promising noninvasive strategy to circumvent the blood‒brain barrier (BBB). However, the clinical translation of N2B platforms remains hindered by a conceptual oversimplification that equates crude central nervous system (CNS) exposure with effective therapeutic delivery. This review reconceptualizes the N2B pathway as a stage-resolved sequential transport cascade extending from nasal entry to meaningful parenchymal and cellular access. We identify a critical imbalance in current formulation strategies, which have advanced two extreme poles, namely initial mucosal retention and epithelial permeation at one end and final target-cell engagement at the other, while leaving the intermediate post-epithelial gateways, including cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and perivascular space (PVS)-mediated redistribution and deep intraparenchymal diffusion, as structural and interpretive blind spots. To bridge this gap, we propose an integrated engineering paradigm with three core design principles. First, multistage-aware design harmonizes sequential spatiotemporal functionalities within a single vehicle architecture. Second, disease-informed design integrates pathologically remodeled barrier states and glymphatic hydrodynamics into the formulation rationale. Third, cargo-informed design establishes the distinct biophysical identity and inherent liabilities of each payload, from small molecules to viral vectors and CRISPR machinery, as the primary engineering starting point. Finally, we advocate for a methodological standard demanding stage-specific validation of vehicle integrity, cross-boundary penetration, and functional target engagement, beyond compartment-blind whole-brain readouts. We further underscore the biofate and clearance of delivery systems as an emerging axis of safety and regulatory evaluation. Collectively, this framework provides a systematic basis for transitioning N2B engineering into a viable clinical modality.

title: Glycan recognition by DC-SIGN, Galectins, and Siglecs: structural insights and ligand-based drug design strategies- a review.
abstract: Glycan-mediated communication between immune cells and their environment is orchestrated by a structurally diverse set of lectin receptors whose exquisite ligand specificity governs both protective immunity and pathological immune evasion. Among these, the C-type lectin DC-SIGN, the proto- and chimera-type Galectins, and the immunoglobulin-like Siglecs occupy central positions in shaping innate and adaptive immune responses. Understanding the molecular basis of these interactions including the thermodynamics and kinetics of binding, the roles of multivalency and avidity, and the structural dynamics of recognition pockets is essential for both decoding immune regulation and developing precision therapeutics. This review presents a mechanistic and comparative analysis of glycan recognition across all three lectin families. We discuss how pathogens exploit these receptors to evade immunity, how tumors deploy hypersialylation and galectin secretion as non-canonical immune checkpoints, and how structural knowledge has enabled rational ligand-based drug design. Current therapeutic strategies including glycomimetic inhibitors, monoclonal antibodies, clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-mediated glycoengineering, and chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) cell approaches are critically evaluated alongside emerging technologies in AI-assisted glycochemistry, single-cell glycomics, spatial glycoproteomics, and glycan nanoparticle delivery. We conclude by outlining a framework for precision glycoimmunotherapy in cancer, infection, fibrosis, and autoimmunity, positioning lectins as dynamic immune checkpoints whose structural plasticity makes them compelling and tractable drug targets.

title: Evaluating the potential of treatment options for chronic hepatitis B.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) remains a leading cause of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma worldwide, but long-term or even lifelong viral suppression with nucleos(t)ide analogues (NAs) seldom clears hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), so-called 'functional cure.' In recent years, a shift in treatment strategy from viral suppression toward cure has emerged, catalyzed by three revised international hepatitis B guidelines (2025-2026) and the first-in-class phase 3 evidence that a finite antiviral therapy, the antisense oligonucleotide bepirovirsen, can achieve a functional cure in about one in five NA-suppressed CHB patients with baseline HBsAg below 3000 IU/mL.
AREAS COVERED: We evaluated the spectrum of established and emerging treatment options for CHB, organized around quantitative HBsAg (qHBsAg) as the axis for selecting and sequencing therapy. Coverage spans backbone NAs and pegylated interferon-α, an HBsAg-guided roadmap, finite NA therapy and off-treatment outcomes, bepirovirsen, other virus-targeting and immunomodulatory agents, and genome-directed covalently closed circular DNA silencing and editing.
EXPERT OPINION: Bepirovirsen's approaching approval is an inflection point. qHBsAg should guide personalized, sequential therapy, with partial cure (HBsAg < 100 IU/mL) as a potential intermediate target when functional cure is unlikely. Durability, standardized biomarkers, rational combination design, metabolic co-management and equitable access are the priorities; a sterilizing cure remains distant.

title: "The pharmacological potential of CRISPR-Cas9: Revolutionizing gene therapy and drug development".
abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 has entered the mainstream of genetic research and therapeutic development, offering a level of programmable and targeted gene editing that has substantially expanded the possibilities of genetic manipulation. This review focuses on the discovery to development of CRISPR-Cas9 and its recent practice in pharmacological and biotechnology field. We discuss further advancements in CRISPR technology such as high-fidelity CRISPR and new systems Cas12 and Cas13 which increases efficiency of editing and opens more opportunities. CRISPR technology has been further advanced when combined with Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning; guide RNA is now optimized while the off-target effects are predicted. The review also focuses on the new targets for therapy, recent trials, the legal and the social and ethical relevance of the CRISPR approach. With the development of CRISPR-Cas9 promising and revolutionary preliminary achievements in the fields of drug development and disease management and tissue engineering are anticipated. Although, in its application, there are questions that have been raised concerning side effects, carriers, and ethics, it is important to take advantage of it in the right manner. As seen in this review, CRISPR-Cas9 plays the crucial part of the development of biomedical studies and therapeutic paradigms.

title: In silico design and molecular docking evaluation of antisense oligonucleotides targeting IDO1 mRNA in the context of depression.
abstract: Depression is a prevalent mental disorder worldwide, often accompanied by severe complications that significantly impair patients' daily lives. Indoleamine-2,3-dioxygenase 1 (IDO1), a key metabolic enzyme in the kynurenine pathway, is considered a promising therapeutic target for depression treatment. Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) are small nucleic acid drugs characterized by high specificity, high potency, minimal drug-drug interactions, a prolonged duration of action, and a low risk of off-target activity, making them effective tools for targeting molecules previously considered undruggable. Consequently, this study designed a novel ASO targeting the IDO1 gene using a computational approach as a fundamental basis for further investigation. Based on rational design criteria, five candidate ASOs were screened and utilized for molecular docking simulations with their corresponding IDO1 mRNA fragments. Furthermore, the intermolecular interactions and binding affinities of the resulting complexes were comprehensively evaluated. The results demonstrated that strong interactions were established across the five complexes. Among them, ASO1 displayed the strongest binding affinity. Notably, its binding site is located within the coding region (CDS) of the mRNA, suggesting its potential to effectively inhibit IDO1 gene expression and exert therapeutic efficacy for depression.

title: RNA base-modification and A-to-I editing landscapes of oxidatively stressed human retinal pigment epithelium under Quantum Molecular Resonance electrotherapy and blood-derived secretome.
abstract: Chemical modifications of RNA bases and adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) editing are regulatory layers essentially unexplored in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), whose oxidative dysfunction underlies age-related macular degeneration. We mapped both layers in ARPE-19 cells exposed to tert-butyl hydroperoxide under two non-pharmacological interventions, Quantum Molecular Resonance (QMR) electrotherapy and a patient blood-derived secretome, across 56 libraries spanning four arms, three time points and matched stressed and stress-free conditions (GEO: GSE328981). Base modifications were called with HARMLNC and A-to-I editing screened with a transition-signal caller, then re-analysed with REDItools3, JACUSA2 and LoDEI. The high-confidence set comprised 241 calls at 15 sites, all of classes canonical to tRNA and rRNA. The most prevalent was an adenosine modification at chrM:2617 in mitochondrial 16S rRNA (MT-RNR2), detected in 51 of 56 libraries and in every arm. Two positions 1 bp apart lie in an EZR/SYTL3 overlap region, whereas a third chromosome 6 site maps to HLA-C, 127.5 Mb away. No position of either layer differed between treatment arms: 7 testable modification sites (minimum p = 0.19) and, at single-nucleotide resolution under dedicated callers agreeing to r = 0.975-0.992, 15 curated editing positions (minimum q = 0.169). Two one-sided tests bound any change in substitution composition within 1.4% and in mean editing frequency within 10% for secretome and combination and 20% for QMR. Against a stress-free baseline internal to the cohort, only chrM:13710 (MT-ND5) changed detectably (q = 0.03). These layers are therefore small, largely constitutive and quantifiably undisturbed by either intervention at the resolution available.

title: Severity-dependent and sex-biased dysregulation of A-to-I RNA editing in COVID-19 reveals CTSS as a key regulatory target.
abstract: SARS-CoV-2 infection causes diverse clinical outcomes, with men facing higher risks of severe disease. Adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing mediated by ADAR enzymes governs innate antiviral immunity, yet its contribution to COVID-19 severity and sex-biased disease remains unclear. We performed epitranscriptomic profiling on 126 blood samples from non-COVID controls and COVID-19 patients spanning different disease severities. We detected 1,466 differentially RNA-edited sites in 514 genes linked to clinical outcomes. Although ADAR expression increased in COVID-19 patients overall, it was strongly reduced in ICU patients compared with non-ICU patients, and this shift was far more prominent in males. This severity-associated and sex-biased ADAR/ADARB1 downregulation coincided with decreased global RNA editing and perturbed expression of immune-related edited transcripts. Cathepsin S (CTSS) was identified as a central regulatory node: elevated A-to-I editing within its 3' UTR in ICU patients stabilizes CTSS mRNA. Without stratifying by disease severity, ADAR expression and global editing showed no significant sex differences; the large sex divergence only appeared among ICU patients. This indicates severity-dependent, not infection-innate, disruption of A-to-I editing, disproportionately amplified in critically ill males. CTSS 3'UTR editing may serve as a biomarker for patient stratification, revealing a mechanistic connection between epitranscriptomic changes and male-biased severe COVID-19.

title: siRNA therapeutics: from hepatic delivery to extrahepatic targeting.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Small interfering RNA (siRNA) has progressed from an experimental gene-silencing tool to an established therapeutic modality through advances in chemical modification and delivery. Lipid nanoparticles (LNP) and N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc)-siRNA conjugates have driven this clinical translation, particularly for liver-directed applications. Extending comparable delivery efficiency and selectivity to non-hepatocyte cell populations and extrahepatic tissues remains a major challenge.
AREAS COVERED: This review examines approved and late-stage siRNA therapeutics and the delivery principles underlying their clinical development. Relevant publications and clinical trial records from 1998 to 2026 were identified through PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov, supplemented by regulatory agency reports. LNP-based delivery, GalNAc-mediated hepatocyte targeting, and emerging strategies for non-parenchymal liver cells and extrahepatic tissues are discussed, with emphasis on the factors governing cell-selective and productive delivery. Next-generation delivery technologies and the therapeutic distinctions between siRNA and antisense oligonucleotides are also considered.
EXPERT OPINION: The next phase of siRNA therapeutics will require a transition from organ-level accumulation toward functional cell-selective delivery. Improved receptor targeting, intracellular trafficking, and endosomal escape, together with rationally designed delivery systems, may extend RNA interference beyond hepatocytes and broaden its therapeutic applications in inflammatory, fibrotic, metabolic, and malignant diseases.

title: Donidalorsen for the treatment of hereditary angioedema.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Hereditary angioedema (HAE) is a rare disorder with a prevalence of approximately 1 in 50,000. Management of HAE brings challenges including the frequency of delivery of the medication, routes of medication delivery, cost of treatment and significant impact on quality of life for patients with HAE. Donidalorsen is the newest FDA-approved long-term prophylaxis medication for HAE that offers substantial benefits over its competitors.
AREAS COVERED: A search of the current literature on donidalorsen was conducted using the PubMed and Cochrane libraries. In this review, we discuss the mechanism and clinical efficacy of donidalorsen. We also explore the comparison between donidalorsen and other agents on the market for the long-term prophylaxis of HAE. The safety profile of donidalorsen as well as a discussion on the economic impact of donidalorsen is also reviewed.
EXPERT OPINION: Donidalorsen offers a promising option for treatment of HAE, with substantial attack reduction, infrequent dosing, and improved quality of life. Continued long-term safety data are needed, but donidalorsen may become a leading prophylactic option for HAE worldwide.

title: Targeting fibroimmune remodeling in androgenetic alopecia: emerging opportunities for RNA-based drug discovery.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Current treatments for androgenetic alopecia (AGA) primarily suppress androgen signaling or stimulate hair growth. Recent single-cell and spatial transcriptomic studies identify fibroimmune remodeling as a potential source of new AGA targets.
AREAS COVERED: This review integrates transcriptomic and mechanistic evidence linking androgen-responsive fibroblasts, immune-cell recruitment, and extracellular matrix remodeling, in male and female pattern hair loss. Herein, the authors assessed published human scalp, cell and animal studies of JAK/STAT, TGF-β, CXCL12-CXCR4/ACKR3, and DKK3-CKAP4, and evaluated RNA therapeutic modalities and delivery barriers. Literature was identified primarily through PubMed in the last 20 years.
EXPERT OPINION: Fibroimmune remodeling should be viewed as a complementary, rather than alternative, framework to androgen biology. The most promising drug discovery strategy is to identify molecularly defined patient subsets and locally inhibit nodal mediators that couple fibroblast activation to inflammation and matrix remodeling. RNA therapeutics are well suited to otherwise difficult-to-drug intracellular targets, but progress will require human spatial validation, rigorous target prioritization, reproducible delivery, and pharmacodynamic biomarkers demonstrating restoration of the regenerative follicular niche.

title: From oncogenesis to approval: the lentiviral gene therapy revolution in Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.
abstract: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS) is an X-linked primary immunodeficiency caused by pathogenic variants in the WAS gene, resulting in absent or dysfunctional WAS protein (WASp) and a clinical triad of eczema, recurrent infections, and micro-thrombocytopenia. Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation has historically represented the only curative option, but outcomes are constrained by donor availability, graft-versus-host disease, and transplant-related toxicity. Autologous gene therapy emerged as a compelling alternative. Early gammaretroviral vector trials confirmed that ex vivo correction of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells could restore WASp expression and produce meaningful clinical benefit. However, insertional oncogenesis exposed an unacceptable genotoxic liability and drove the field toward self-inactivating lentiviral vectors. Clinical trials employing lentiviral platforms demonstrated durable, multi-lineage engraftment, sustained WASp expression, and robust immune reconstitution, with no reported cases of vector-related leukemia. These outcomes culminated in the FDA approval of WASKYRA (etuvetidigene autotemcel) in December 2025, establishing autologous gene therapy as a licensed standard of care for WAS patients lacking a suitable HLA-matched related donor. Next-generation precision gene-editing strategies and in vivo delivery platforms offer a path toward safer and more accessible correction. This review traces the full arc of WAS gene therapy, from early preclinical proof of concept through regulatory approval.

title: Engineering stem cell-derived islets for type 1 diabetes: genetic strategies for immune evasion and stress resilience.
abstract: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is characterized by autoimmune-mediated destruction of pancreatic β-cells, resulting in lifelong insulin dependence and disease burden. Stem cell-derived islet (SCI) replacement therapies have emerged as a promising strategy to restore endogenous insulin production; however, immune rejection, inflammatory stress, and intrinsic β-cell vulnerability remain major barriers to durable graft survival. Recent advances in gene editing and stem cell engineering have accelerated the development of next-generation SCIs designed to evade immune recognition while enhancing resistance to diabetogenic stress pathways. In this review, we examine genetic engineering strategies aimed at improving β-cell protection through modulation of antigen presentation, immune checkpoint signaling, cytokine responsiveness, and cellular stress adaptation. We discuss established immune-evasive targets including beta-2-microglobulin (B2M), class II major histocompatibility complex transactivator (CIITA), cluster of differentiation 47 (CD47), programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1), and cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4-immunoglobulin (CTLA4-Ig), alongside emerging stress-resilience pathways involving renalase (RNLS), thioredoxin-interacting protein (TXNIP), and unfolded protein response regulators. We further highlight how β-cell stress can amplify immune recognition and graft dysfunction. Collectively, these approaches support multifunctional engineered SCIs designed to overcome immune-mediated and intrinsic stress-related barriers to durable β-cell replacement. Literature was identified through PubMed and Google Scholar searches conducted from February through September 2026.

title: Targeting phenol-soluble modulins: eco-friendly theragnostic strategies against Staphylococcus aureus biofilms.
abstract: The growing resistance to antibiotics by Staphylococcus aureus and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a global health threat. Traditional antibiotics act on the viability of bacteria, whereas new ones are now increasingly targeting virulence factors. Phenol-soluble modulins (PSMs) are essential virulence factors that play important roles in inflammation, neutrophil lysis, cytotoxicity and biofilm formation. PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and Google Scholar were used for literature search of articles published between 2010 and 2026. Green-synthesized metal nanoparticles (NPs) have been found to be capable of altering these mechanisms by inducing reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, membrane damage, and by interfering with the quorum-sensing mechanism of the bacteria, along with inhibiting the Agr system. Optimization of NP-based interventions can be supported by multi-omics approaches such as genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics and metabolomics. Other potential methods of targeted PSM pathway and Agr pathway suppression are also available, such as CRISPR-Cas9 and dCas9, but there are delivery difficulties. The potential use of combining nanotechnology, gene editing, multi-omics, artificial intelligence, and synthetic biology could allow for development of more advanced anti-virulence strategies against S. aureus infections targeted at PSM.
