title: The advances and challenges of mRNA-LNP application in fields of hematology and oncology therapeutics.
abstract: The rapidly global deployment of COVID-19 mRNA-LNP vaccines established the clinical feasibility of combining RNA medicine with LNP delivery systems, transforming a long-standing experimental concept into a scalable therapeutic modality, previously considered impossible. Currently, the value of mRNA-LNPs has been expanding from infectious disease vaccines to cancer immunotherapy, personalized neoantigen vaccination, in vivo immune-cell engineering, protein replacement therapy, mRNA-encoded biologics and genome editing, with particular relevance to hematology and oncology. However, in hematologic and oncologic settings, therapeutic success is constrained by biological barriers that less prominent in prophylactic vaccination. Systemically administered LNPs are strongly influenced by hepatic sequestration, protein corona formation and mononuclear-phagocyte clearance; solid tumors additionally present heterogeneous vasculature, variable enhanced permeability and retention, dense extracellular matrix, elevated interstitial pressure and limited intratumoral diffusion. Hematologic applications face a different set of constraints, including access to spleen and bone marrow, selective delivery to T cells, NK cells and hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs), and preservation of the normal marrow niche. In this Review, we therefore discuss the molecular and principles of formulation that underpin mRNA-LNP performance in hematology and oncology, including mRNA engineering, lipid nanoparticle architecture, intracellular trafficking and selective organ targeting(SORT) delivery strategies, oncology applications spanning neoantigen vaccines, tumor-microenvironment reprogramming, mRNA-encoded biologics, gene editing and combination therapy; and hematology applications including in vivo CAR-T, CAR-NK and HSPC engineering. We further consider how inefficient extrahepatic delivery, limited endosomal escape, context-dependent reactogenicity, repeat-dosing constraints and the manufacturing complexity of individualized products continue to limit broader clinical translation. Emerging strategies, including artificial-intelligence-guided RNA and lipid design, self-amplifying RNA, circular RNA and next-generation thermostable formulations, may help address these application limitations in the fields of hematology and oncology.

title: Klhl41b orchestrates sarcomere assembly and growth to drive skeletal muscle hypertrophy in vivo.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Nemaline myopathy (NM) is a clinically and genetically heterogeneous disease caused by mutations in sarcomere-associated genes, with congenital forms representing the most severe end of the spectrum. Recessive mutations in KLHL41 underlie a severe congenital NM characterized by sarcomeric disorganization and impaired muscle growth. The in vivo mechanisms by which KLHL41 governs sarcomere assembly and growth remain poorly understood.
METHODS: We generated zebrafish models of KLHL41 deficiency by the CRISPR-Cas9 approach to examine the temporal and molecular basis of sarcomere assembly defects in NM. The phenotypic and physiological characterization of skeletal muscle defects was investigated by birefringence, spontaneous coiling, spontaneous swimming behavior, and force generation assays. Structural analyses by electron microscopy and immunofluorescence assessed myofibril organization and sarcomere structures across developmental time points. Quantitative proteomics and biochemical assays were performed to identify perturbations in sarcomeric proteins and associated molecular pathways.
RESULTS: We show that Klhl41b is essential for the formation and organization of sarcomeres, supporting both radial and longitudinal muscle growth. Loss of Klhl41b resulted in reduced sarcomere size, defective sarcomere assembly followed by progressive destabilization of sarcomeres, nemaline body formation, and reduced muscle function. Proteomic analysis in Klhl41b-deficient zebrafish revealed reduced abundance of the sarcomeric troponin complex proteins, altered abundance of components of the translational machinery, and increased abundance of components of atrophy-associated pathways.
CONCLUSIONS: These data show that Klhl41b is required for sarcomere assembly and growth, and its deficiency drives a cascade of structural and molecular changes underlying skeletal muscle hypotrophy and NM pathology. These findings advance our understanding of disease mechanisms and may inform targeted therapeutic strategies to restore sarcomere integrity and muscle function.

title: Innovations and emerging trends in adoptive cell therapies for solid tumors: engineering strategies and clinical translation.
abstract: Cancer remains a formidable challenge in global oncology, with conventional treatments often failing to achieve durable responses in advanced stages. Adoptive cell therapy (ACT), despite its revolutionary success in hematological malignancies, faces critical bottlenecks in solid tumors, including a hostile immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), restricted cellular trafficking, and the rapid onset of T-cell exhaustion. This review systematically explores the evolution of ACT platforms, ranging from foundational tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) to precision-engineered chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T and T-cell receptor (TCR)-T therapies. We highlight how innovative engineering strategies such as the integration of "armored" CARs, synthetic gene circuits, and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing have been employed to enhance the persistence and polyfunctionality of effector cells. Beyond T-cell-centric approaches, we examine the emerging landscape of diverse immune effector cells, including CAR-natural killer (NK) cells, and CAR-macrophages (CAR-M), which offer unique advantages in antigen recognition and safety profiles. Furthermore, we detail the synergistic potential of multimodal combination regimens, where ACT is paired with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), localized radiotherapy, or nanotechnology-based delivery systems to dismantle TME barriers and achieve systemic anti-tumor immunity. By tracing the journey of therapeutic cells from ex vivo expansion to intratumoral infiltration and cytotoxicity, this review illuminates the molecular mechanisms governing therapeutic efficacy. Finally, we discuss the current clinical trial landscape, manufacturing hurdles, and the regulatory pathways essential for transitioning these sophisticated cellular products from bench to bedside.

title: ZNF292 mutations impair RNA and protein biosynthesis defining an adverse prognostic subset in early-stage chronic lymphocytic leukemia.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: ZNF292 alterations are recurrently detected in patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), occurring in 3%-6% of patients as mutations and in 2% as 6q deletions. Although preliminary evidence suggested an independent prognostic role for ZNF292 mutations, their specific clinical relevance in early-stage CLL and the underlying biological mechanisms remain poorly defined.
METHODS: 488 CLL patients were analyzed using targeted Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS) to characterize the landscape and clinical significance of ZNF292 mutations. CRISPR/Cas9-genome editing was employed to introduce the most prevalent ZNF292 variants into CLL cellular models. Their biological and functional implications were evaluated by integrating RNA-sequencing data from these isogenic cellular models with transcriptomic data from primary patient samples, complemented by functional validation and drug response assays.
RESULTS: ZNF292 mutations were associated with shorter time to first treatment (TTFT; median 25 vs. 52 months, P = 0.009) and inferior overall survival (OS, median 93 vs. 148 months, P = 0.004). Importantly, when restricting the analyses to early-stage cases, ZNF292 alterations were independently associated with shorter TTFT and OS, identifying a high-risk subgroup. Mechanistically, transcriptomic analyses revealed that ZNF292 mutations suppress global protein biosynthesis and modulate cell cycle progression in both primary CLL samples and CRISPR/Cas9-edited cells. Furthermore, ZNF292 deficiency impaired replication stress responses via defective CHK1 activation, resulting in DNA damage accumulation. Evaluating potential therapeutic vulnerabilities, ZNF292-mutated cells exhibited enhanced in vitro sensitivity to ibrutinib and venetoclax.
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings propose ZNF292 alterations as an independent prognostic factor in early-stage CLL and unveil their role in disease progression.

title: RNA N4-acetylcytidine modification in health and cancer: molecular mechanisms, cellular plasticity, and therapeutic opportunities.
abstract: N⁴-acetylcytidine (ac⁴C) is an evolutionarily conserved RNA modification that was initially identified in transfer RNA (tRNA) and ribosomal RNA (rRNA). Increasing evidence has subsequently expanded its functional landscape to messenger RNA (mRNA) and multiple classes of non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs). As the best-characterized ac⁴C writer in mammals, N-acetyltransferase 10 (NAT10) orchestrates RNA structure, stability, processing, and translation, thereby governing fundamental physiological processes, including ribosome biogenesis, translational fidelity, proteostasis, cell fate determination, hematopoiesis, reproduction, and embryonic development. Cancer cells exploit the NAT10-ac⁴C axis to selectively stabilize or enhance the translation of oncogenic transcripts, reprogram tRNA and rRNA-dependent translational programs, and cooperate with non-canonical NAT10 functions, including R-loop regulation, protein acetylation, and RNA binding, to sustain uncontrolled proliferation, cancer stemness, metabolic reprogramming, DNA damage repair, invasion and metastasis, resistance to regulated cell death, and immune evasion. Consequently, the NAT10-ac⁴C axis has emerged as a central molecular hub linking RNA fate, the translational machinery, and adaptive tumor reprogramming. Therefore, phenotypes resulting from NAT10 depletion or pharmacological inhibition should not be indiscriminately attributed to reduced ac⁴C deposition in the absence of catalytic rescue experiments and site-specific validation. In this Review, we comprehensively summarize the molecular basis of ac⁴C, its substrate landscape, catalytic mechanisms, and determinants of substrate selectivity, as well as its physiological functions in normal tissues and pathological roles in cancer. We further compare the shared and context-dependent mechanisms by which the NAT10-ac⁴C axis drives malignant progression and therapeutic resistance across diverse cancer types. In addition, we critically evaluate current ac⁴C detection technologies, the hierarchy of substrate evidence, NAT10 inhibitors, targeted protein degradation strategies, rational combination therapies, biomarker-guided patient stratification, and therapeutic windows. Finally, we propose that future research should move beyond broad NAT10 inhibition toward identifying tumor-specific NAT10 dependencies and selectively disrupting oncogenic NAT10-RNA regulatory circuits through high-confidence ac⁴C atlases, site-specific RNA editing technologies, and precision delivery strategies.

title: CRISPR-enhanced microalgae for carbon sequestration and carotenoid production: opportunities and fundamental constraints.
abstract: Microalgae represent a promising biological platform for CO2 sequestration and the sustainable production of high-value metabolites, particularly carotenoids such as lutein and astaxanthin. However, industrial performance remains constrained by low carbon conversion efficiency, reduced photosynthetic performance, and competing metabolic fluxes that limit product yield. The emergence of CRISPR/Cas-based genome engineering has enabled precise and multiplexed modulation of microalgal metabolic networks, offering new opportunities to overcome these limitations. This review critically evaluates CRISPR-enabled engineering strategies for improving carbon assimilation, photosynthetic efficiency, and carotenoid biosynthesis in microalgae. We discuss advances in transformation and delivery systems across diverse species, CRISPR interference, CRISPR activation, and multiplexed pathway rewiring. Targeted modifications of light-harvesting complexes, carbon concentrating mechanisms, and key carotenoid biosynthetic enzymes are discussed with their reported impacts on biomass accumulation, CO2 fixation, and pigment productivity. Emerging evidence indicates that while pathway-specific genetic interventions can significantly enhance metabolic accumulation, these improvements are often not proportionally reflected in whole-cell carbon fixation, revealing underlying constraints imposed by energy allocation, redox balance, and regulatory network coupling. Finally, we highlight the potential of synthetic regulatory circuits and programmable transcriptional control as next-generation tools for dynamic regulation of metabolic fluxes rather than static gene-level modifications. By integrating molecular engineering strategies with physiological and system-level constraints, this review provides a critical framework for developing robust microalgal cell factories for sustainable bioproduction and climate mitigation.

title: Antifungal resistance landscapes in major fungal pathogens in Zhejiang, China.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Invasive fungal infections caused by Aspergillus fumigatus and other pathogenic fungi represent a major global health threat, with treatment increasingly complicated by the emergence of antifungal drug resistance. Azole antifungals serve as the first-line therapy for aspergillosis, but resistance rates vary substantially across geographical regions. This study aimed to characterize the antifungal resistance landscape among clinical fungal isolates from Hangzhou and Yiwu cities in Zhejiang Province, Eastern China, and to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying azole resistance in Aspergillus fumigatus.
RESULTS: We analyzed 110 Aspergillus clinical isolates for antifungal susceptibility. Among A. fumigatus strains, 8.6% exhibited azole resistance, with half of these harboring the tandem repeat mutation TR34/L98H in the cyp51A gene. One resistant strain carried the TR46/Y121F/T289A mutation combination. Minimum inhibitory concentration testing revealed that 8.6% of A. fumigatus isolates were resistant to amphotericin B We identified one resistant isolate without known resistance mutations and characterized it through whole-genome sequencing and transcriptomic analysis. Novel mutations S437F in cyp51A and P298T in hmg1 were discovered; however, functional validation using CRISPR-Cas9 demonstrated these mutations do not directly confer resistance. Instead, transcriptomic profiling revealed significant upregulation of ergosterol biosynthesis pathway genes and efflux transporter genes, suggesting alternative resistance mechanisms. Among non-A. fumigatus species, all A. niger isolates displayed resistance to itraconazole and posaconazole.
CONCLUSIONS: This comprehensive regional surveillance reveals concerning patterns of antifungal resistance among major human pathogenic fungi in Zhejiang Province, China. The identification of both classical resistance mutations and novel transcription-mediated resistance mechanisms highlights the complex and evolving nature of antifungal resistance. These findings emphasize the critical need for continued surveillance programs and rapid resistance detection methods to inform clinical treatment strategies and improve patient outcomes.

title: Next-generation CAR-T cell therapy against cancer: precision engineering, programmable immunity, and emerging clinical frontiers.
abstract: While chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy has revolutionized the treatment of hematological malignancies, there are significant hurdles to overcome, such as antigen escape, T-cell exhaustion, limited persistence in the body, severe toxicities, manufacturing complexity, high costs, and low effectiveness in the treatment of solid tumors. There are many reviews describing novel CAR-T technologies, the evidence strength, clinical maturity and unmet translational risks of each are largely included in those reviews. This review highlights the ways in which next-generation engineering increases the safety, efficacy and programmability of CAR-T. The primary and authoritative clinical, regulatory and preclinical evidence on recent advances from 2022 to 2026 was carefully evaluated, including the quality and quality control of the evidence for each strategy. New innovations are Armored CARs, dual-target and logic-gated/synNotch systems, universal and switchable platforms, CRISPR/Cas9 and base/prime editing, allogeneic CAR-Ts, non-viral manufacturing, and lipid-nanoparticles in vivo CAR-T generation. Additionally, the engineering and combination approaches for the treatment of solid tumors with checkpoint inhibitors, radiotherapy, oncolytic viruses, nanotechnology, and artificial intelligence are discussed. An evidence-to-maturity framework separates the clinically proven methods from the emerging technologies and highlights some of the critical translation hurdles related to safety, immunogenicity, durability, manufacturing and scale. Precision Immunotherapy is becoming more and more possible with the next generation CAR-T engineering, however the validation and translational optimization of these cells is dominant to their eventual clinical use.

title: Cancer nanomedicine and RNA/Lipid nanoparticle platforms in oncology: developmental evolution, translational barriers, and precision-therapy opportunities.
abstract: Nanomedicine has become an important translational platform in oncology by enabling altered pharmacokinetics, controlled exposure, reduced systemic toxicity, intracellular delivery of nucleic acids, and improved handling of complex therapeutic payloads. Early cancer nanomedicines, including pegylated liposomal cytotoxics and albumin-bound drug products, demonstrated that nanoscale formulation design could improve the clinical utility of established anticancer agents. More recently, lipid nanoparticles, RNA therapeutics, individualized neoantigen vaccines, gene-regulatory approaches, and immune-modulating delivery systems have expanded the role of nanoparticles from passive drug carriers to programmable oncology platforms. This narrative review examines the developmental evolution of cancer-focused pharmaceutical nanoparticles, with emphasis on liposomes, lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), albumin-bound systems, polymeric particles, polymeric micelles, nanocrystals, nanoemulsions, solid lipid nanoparticles, inorganic particles, extracellular vesicles, and hybrid delivery technologies. Each platform class is treated systematically, covering representative approved products, formulation characteristics, route of administration, clinical evidence, and the specific development risks that limit it. There view connects platform design with oncology-specific barriers, including tumor heterogeneity, variable enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effects, dense extracellular matrix, abnormal tumor vasculature, mononuclear phagocyte clearance, protein-corona formation, endosomal escape, immune activation, and the difficulty of translating animal tumor models into clinical benefit. These barriers are organized as a sequential delivery cascade, and the behavior of each platform class is compared step by step rather than described as a set of universal phenomena. Nanoparticle candidates that accumulated well in preclinical tumors but failed in clinical trials are examined alongside approved products, because the contrast between the two is where most of the transferable lessons sit. A product-development perspective is used to discuss critical quality attributes (CQAs), manufacturing scalability, potency testing, sterility strategy, stability, release methods, regulatory expectations, commercial feasibility, and clinical differentiation. A development-to-translation framework is proposed for comparing cancer nanomedicine platforms across formulation maturity, analytical maturity, manufacturing maturity, biological rationale, clinical evidence, regulatory readiness, and commercial feasibility; regulatory and commercial maturity are scored separately, the criteria behind each level are defined explicitly, and the resulting rankings are presented as a heuristic aid to discussion rather than a validated quantitative metric. Future progress in oncology nanomedicine will depend not only on novel materials or targeting claims, but also on disciplined product design, biologically meaningful potency assays, scalable manufacturing, patient-selection strategies, and clear integration with precision oncology.

title: Precision base-editing of the cryptic 3' acceptor site to correct the RNA splicing defect of β654-thalassemia.
abstract: β-Thalassemia is one of the most common inherited disorders worldwide and is caused by mutations affecting β-globin production. β654 mutation (IVS2-654, C > T) is one of the most frequently occurring β-thalassemia alleles in Han Chinese population, which activates a cryptic 3' splice site and leads to aberrant RNA splicing. Previous studies demonstrated that direct base editing of the IVS2-654 mutation is challenging because suitable single-guide RNAs (sgRNAs) cannot effectively target this site. Here we investigated an alternative therapeutic strategy by targeting the mutation-activated cryptic 3' splice acceptor site, rather than the disease-causing mutation itself. We first introduced base substitutions into the cryptic splice acceptor site in a β654-thalassemia mouse model using CRISPR-Cas9-mediated homology-directed repair, which restored normal RNA splicing and validated the therapeutic rationale of this approach. We then generated base-edited β654 mice by microinjecting Td-CBEmax mRNA together with sgRNAs targeting the cryptic splice acceptor site into one-cell embryos. Base editing was successfully achieved in 78% of live-born β654 mice, of which 86% produced correctly spliced β-globin transcripts. Restoration of normal RNA splicing was accompanied by marked improvement of hematological parameters and tissue pathology in most base-edited founder mice and their offspring compared with non-edited β654 mice. Together, these findings demonstrate that mutation-activated cryptic splice sites are therapeutically actionable targets for precision base editing and provide proof of concept for a precise and effective strategy to correct aberrant RNA splicing in β654-thalassemia.

title: Lipid nanoparticle-mediated transcription factor EB mRNA delivery for the treatment of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a prevalent disorder characterized by excessive hepatic lipid accumulation, frequently progressing to steatohepatitis, fibrosis, and cirrhosis. Transcription factor EB (TFEB) coordinates lysosomal biogenesis, autophagy, and lipid catabolism, and therefore represents a potential therapeutic target; however, safe and direct strategies for selectively enhancing hepatic TFEB activity remain limited. Here, liver-targeted lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) were developed to deliver mRNAs encoding wild-type TFEB or the constitutively active TFEB S211A mutant, and their efficacy was evaluated in cellular and choline-deficient, L-amino acid-defined high-fat diet (CDAHFD)-induced mouse models of MASLD. LNP-mediated delivery increased hepatic TFEB expression, enhanced autophagic flux, and reprogrammed metabolic pathways toward fatty acid oxidation (e.g., CPT1A and ACOX1) while suppressing the expression of lipogenic genes (e.g., FASN, ACC, and SREBP1). Consequently, targeted TFEB mRNA therapy significantly reduced hepatic triglyceride content, attenuated steatosis, lowered MASLD activity scores, and decreased fibrotic remodeling. Mechanistically, transcriptomic profiling, ChIP-qPCR, promoter-reporter assays, and targeted knockdown models indicated that TFEB exerts its protective effects against lipid accumulation at least partly by transcriptionally activating the fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) signaling pathway. Collectively, these findings establish LNP-mediated TFEB mRNA delivery as a useful preclinical approach for investigating hepatic biology and provide a targeted, transient, and non-integrating genetic strategy with potential for the treatment of MASLD.

title: A patient-derived missense mouse model of Kabuki syndrome 1.
abstract: Kabuki syndrome type 1 (KS1) is a rare cause of intellectual disability resulting from heterozygous pathogenic variants in the gene encoding the histone methyltransferase KMT2D. A previously established loss-of-function mouse model of KS1 exhibits key phenotypic features, and therapeutic trials in this mouse model suggest postnatal malleability of neurological symptoms. However, 15-30% of individuals with KS1 carry missense variants. To investigate whether missense variants lead to similar phenotypic presentation in mice, we used CRISPR-Cas9 to introduce the KS1 patient variant R5179H, corresponding to R5230H in mice, into C57BL/6NTac animals. Computational and in vitro testing suggested that the R5230H variant does not impair protein stability or enzyme function of KMT2D. Despite a distinct mechanistic basis, our new mouse model (Kmt2d+/R5230H) recapitulated most phenotypes of our prior loss-of-function model, including growth deficiency, craniofacial anomalies and IgA deficiency, but not altered neurological function. Kmt2d+/R5230H mice showed perinatal lethality and a high frequency of unilateral kidney agenesis, a novel phenotype in KS1 mouse models. Kmt2d+/R5230H mice provide a unique opportunity to understand the impact of missense variants on KMT2D function and uncover developmental and perinatal abnormalities in KS1.

title: Human-relevant disease models to accelerate the development of nucleic acid-based therapies and other advanced therapeutics.
abstract: Advanced therapeutics, including programmable nucleic acid-based therapies (NATs), such as small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), CRISPR-Cas 9 editing systems, modified in vitro transcribed messenger RNAs (mRNAs) and Adeno-associated viruses (AAVs), have the potential to transform healthcare. However, while there have been considerable successes, there have also been notable clinical failures in early-stage human trials, which slowed down the progression of these therapeutic platforms. Multiple trials of NATs have been halted or discontinued, or approved products carry black box warnings as unforeseen or underestimated toxicities and poor efficacy have been observed in humans. There are a variety of reasons for failure of NATs, one of which is that many preclinical studies lack disease modelling in a human-relevant manner and, therefore, do not capture disease-specific effects on therapy tolerability and efficacy. This Perspective provides a short overview of why better human disease modelling is required to understand the potential therapeutic liabilities of NATs across modalities.

title: Diverse RNA Editing Systems Across Heterolobosea (Discoba).
abstract: Mitochondrial RNA editing events were previously reported in only three unrelated species within the phylum Heterolobosea (Discoba): Naegleria gruberi and Acrasis kona (which performs C-to-U substitutions) and Pharyngomonadida sp. BB2 (which inserts single nucleotides by a yet unknown mechanism). We present novel high-quality genome assemblies obtained via a combination of whole-genome and targeted sequencing approaches and predicted proteomes for two species, Paravahlkampfia ustiana and Heteramoeba clara, representing an understudied clade of the phylum. Surprisingly, we discovered RNA editing events of C-to-U substitutions and mononucleotide insertions co-existing in the mitochondria of P. ustiana, while the two systems were both absent in H. clara. In addition, P. ustiana also exhibits A-to-I editing sites in rRNA transcripts encoded in multicopy circular rDNA plasmids. RNA editing events in P. ustiana were verified by proteomics, Illumina short RNA reads, ONT long cDNA and direct RNA reads. We elaborate on the potential mechanisms of mitochondrial insertional editing by investigating several aspects of the RNA transcription machinery and base modifications in template DNA and mRNA products. We report additional cases of C-to-U RNA editing in other species of Heterolobosea and explore the distribution of various putative components of the C-to-U editosome, including the DYW domain-containing pentatricopeptide repeat (PPR) proteins, across the phylum expanding the understanding of the evolutionary dynamics underlying this phenomenon, which remains understudied outside land plants. The comparative analysis of available sequence data from Heterolobosea revealed that C-to-U RNA editing was acquired relatively deep in the evolution of Heterolobosea and subsequently underwent repeated losses.

title: Improving the dynamic range of a trimethoprim-responsive self-amplifying RNA.
abstract: Self-amplifying mRNA (SAM) is a potential platform for protein replacement, as it enables recipients to transiently produce a therapeutic protein for 4-8 weeks. To obtain external control over the level and duration of protein expression, synthetic SAM constructs that switch OFF in the presence of a small molecule such as trimethoprim (TMP) have been developed in the past. Here, we increase the ON-state protein expression of such a TMP-responsive SAM by fusing the effector protein L7Ae to a TMP-responsive destabilizing domain (DD) on both terminals. We also lower the OFF-state by adding a duplicate of the SAM 3'UTR downstream from the DD-L7Ae subgenomic ORF. We demonstrate that fusing two DDs to L7Ae has a beneficial effect on the response rate and level of protein production after removal or addition of TMP. We further demonstrate that overexpression of DD-L7Ae results in microscopic abnormalities. These insights are implemented in a mechanistic model, and further improvements of the platform are highlighted.

title: Cellular signal-responsive m5C editing by an inducible split CRISPR platform.
abstract: RNA 5-methylcytidine (m5C) modification plays an essential role in regulating RNA metabolism and functions in cellular processes. Tools to achieve temporal and transcript-specific m5C editing for functional studies are still limited. Furthermore, methods enabling m5C editing triggered by specific cellular signals to study m5C functions are currently lacking. Here, we present a temporally and conditionally controlled m5C writing platform engineered through integrating abscisic acid (ABA)-mediated chemically induced proximity with split-dCas13b-NSUN2/NSUN6 technology. This system enables the writing of m5C by reconstituting the split dCas13b-based m5C editing complex at the guide RNA (gRNA)-targeted RNA transcript sites under the control of the inducer ABA. The deposition of m5C is inducible, reversible and selective. The deposited m5C is biologically active and influences the stability of endogenous mRNA transcripts. Moreover, by incorporating ABA prodrugs, the m5C writing can be triggered by signals associated with distinct physiological or disease conditions (e.g., tumor microenvironment and senescence). This conditional m5C editing strategy provides a new programmable tool for studying m5C biology in a context-dependent manner and expands the repertoire of RNA modification editing technologies.

title: PNLDC1 deadenylase affects translational rate and cell proliferation in mESCs.
abstract: PNLDC1 is a member of the DEDD deadenylases, known for its specificity in poly(A) tail removal during mRNA turnover. While initially characterized for its function in pre-piRNA trimming critical to spermatogenesis and transposon silencing, its broader deadenylase activity which is especially pronounced during early development and silenced during differentiation, remains poorly understood. In this study, we mapped the epigenetic regulation of Pnldc1 during mESC differentiation, uncovering its promoter methylation pattern associated with transcriptional repression. Pnldc1-knockout mESC models established via CRISPR/Cas9 were shown to retain viability and pluripotency. RNA-seq and subsequent polysome profiling revealed that Pnldc1 deficiency leads to the downregulation of gene networks involved in translation and a lower overall translational rate. Notably, PNLDC1 has been linked to epigenetic changes in various cancers and is associated with oncogenic signaling pathways. Using a homology model based on the related PARN deadenylase, we conducted virtual screening of compound libraries and selected 12 candidates for experimental testing. Experimental validation revealed that two compounds significantly impacted genes involved in stress response and signal transduction, while also suppressing aberrant proliferation. These findings highlight PNLDC1's role in regulating mRNA stability during differentiation and proliferation and as a candidate for targeted therapeutic intervention.

title: Detection of the RNA-Editing Enzyme ADARB1 in Primary Auditory Neurons and Anti-ADARB1 Immunofluorescence as a Means for Automated Counting.
abstract: Spiral ganglion neurons (SGNs), the primary auditory afferents in the inner ear, are vulnerable to degeneration from neuropathies, concussion, and aging, among other causes. Accurate quantification of SGNs is critical for assessing degeneration and therapeutic interventions, but manual counting is arduous due to dense cellular crowding and unreliable nuclear markers. Because SGNs receive input from GluA2-containing AMPA receptors, the transcripts for which must be RNA-edited for calcium impermeability, we hypothesized that SGNs express high levels of the RNA-editing enzyme ADARB1. Here, we confirm enriched expression of Adarb1 transcripts in SGNs and show that anti-ADARB1 antibodies robustly label the nuclei of type I and type II SGNs from young and aged mice, adult macaques, and adult humans. Neuronal versus glial specificity was confirmed using antibodies against neurofilament heavy chain (NFH), human antigen D (HuD), GATA binding protein 3 (GATA3), and SRY-box 2 (SOX2). A blinded investigator manually counted mouse SGNs via NFH, and these were compared to automated counts of ADARB1-positive nuclei using the analyze particles function in ImageJ. A concordance correlation coefficient and Bland-Altman analysis demonstrated strong agreement between the manual and automated counts. Together, these results suggest broad utility of ADARB1 immunolabeling for automated counts of SGNs across species.

title: A binding-activated CRISPR/dCas13X imaging system enables precise RNA tracking in plants.
abstract: Visualizing the spatiotemporal dynamics of native RNA molecules with single-transcript-level sensitivity in living plant cells remains a formidable challenge due to the high background noise caused by the unique cellular architecture of plants. Here, using transiently transformed Nicotiana benthamiana cells and stable Arabidopsis thaliana lines, we present a high-signal-to-noise RNA imaging platform that couples CRISPR-dCas13X with a binding-associated fluorescence stabilization strategy. We identified a novel plant-specific degron that selectively targets unbound probes for proteasomal degradation while preserving target-associated signal in a manner consistent with binding-dependent protection, enabling high-fidelity detection of endogenous mRNA puncta with minimal perturbation. Leveraging this platform, we characterized dynamics of FT mRNA trafficking in living plant cells, including plasmodesmata-targeting, cell-to-cell trafficking, and long-distance movement. Loss-of-function analysis further identified the established RNA-binding protein GRP7 as a factor that contributes to efficient FT mRNA transport. This work establishes a useful toolkit for investigating plant RNA biology and provides mechanistic insight into the systemic transport of florigenic signals.

title: Deficiency of placental GDF15 causes fetal growth restriction by inhibiting fetal hepatic STAT3-IGF2 axis.
abstract: Fetal growth restriction (FGR) is a major cause of perinatal morbidity and mortality, yet its underlying mechanism remains elusive. Here, we show that growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15) levels are significantly reduced in the placenta and fetal circulation in mouse and pig FGR models and correlate positively with fetal weight. Placenta-specific GDF15 deficiency causes FGR, while placenta-specific Gdf15 mRNA delivery through targeted lipid nanoparticle (LNP) effectively alleviates FGR. Mechanistically, placental GDF15 is a major contributor to the fetal circulating GDF15 pool and enters the fetal compartment, where it activates the hepatic STAT3 signaling pathway to stimulate IGF2 production during pregnancy. Placental GDF15 deficiency decreases hepatic STAT3 phosphorylation and IGF2 levels in fetuses. Inhibition of STAT3 in primary mouse fetal hepatocytes blocks GDF15-induced IGF2 upregulation. Placenta-specific Gdf15 mRNA-LNP administration rescues the decreased hepatic p-STAT3 and IGF2 levels in FGR fetuses. Collectively, our findings identify a placenta-fetal liver metabolic axis where placental GDF15 promotes fetal growth by activating the fetal hepatic STAT3-IGF2 pathway, revealing a potential therapeutic target for FGR.

title: Immunoinformatics and reverse vaccinology design of self-amplifying RNA vaccine against marburg virus with structural dynamics and immune simulation analysis.
abstract: Marburg virus disease (MVD), a deadly zoonotic illness in humans, is caused by the Marburg virus (MARV), a single-stranded RNA virus belonging to the Orthomarburgvirus genus of the Filoviridae family. There are currently no approved vaccines or efficient antiviral therapies for MARV, despite high morbidity and fatality rates of the virus, particularly in Africa. Recognizing its epidemic potential and its inclusion on the WHO list of blueprint priority pathogens, an immunoinformatics approach was used to design novel multi-epitope saRNA vaccine candidates (MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII) targeting the viral GP, NP, VP40, and VP35 via CD8 + , CD4 + , and B cell epitopes. These epitopes were derived from target protein sequences and incorporated into MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII after validation for antigenicity, non-allergenicity, non-toxicity, and conservation. Additionally, the selected epitopes were conjugated to suitable adjuvants via various linkers, thereby enabling the design of a potentially stable vaccine. Additionally, the designed MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII were incorporated into the standard saRNA model, in which ORF-2 encodes the target vaccine peptide. Moreover, biophysical analyses unveiled that the developed vaccines are basic (pI < 7), soluble (GRAVY < 0), and stable (aliphatic index < 80). Subsequently, docking of MB-saVaxI to TLR2 (-938.3) and TLR4 (-902.4), and MB-saVaxII to TLR3 (-1485.4) and TLR7 (-1543.6) demonstrated significant affinity, with detailed hydrogen-bond interactions validated by MM-GBSA and molecular dynamics simulations. Furthermore, MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII were effectively cloned in-silico into Escherichia coli, and immune simulations indicated that the vaccines triggered robust innate and adaptive immunity, with a sustained memory response and TH cell activation, as evidenced by IFN-γ and IL-2 production. Additionally, the mRNA structure of MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII remained stable throughout the expression pathway in the host. However, extensive in-vitro and in-vivo studies are needed to establish the safety and efficacy of this vaccine candidate conclusively.

title: The Mitochondrial ubiquitin ligase MARCHF5 cooperates with MCL1 to inhibit Apoptosis in KSHV-transformed primary effusion lymphoma cell lines.
abstract: Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV) causes several malignancies in people with HIV including Kaposi's sarcoma and primary effusion lymphoma (PEL). We have previously shown that PEL cell lines require myeloid cell leukemia-1 (MCL1) to inhibit apoptosis. MCL1 is an oncogene that is amplified in cancers and causes resistance to chemotherapy regimens. MCL1 is thus an attractive target for drug development. The emerging clinical relevance and therapeutic potential of MCL1 motivated us to study the roles of this oncogene in PEL in depth. Using a systems biology approach, we uncovered an unexpected genetic interaction between MCL1 and MARCHF5 indicating that they function in the same pathway. MARCHF5 is an E3 ubiquitin ligase most known for regulating mitochondrial homeostasis and antiviral signaling, but not apoptosis. We thus investigated how MCL1 and MARCHF5 cooperate to promote PEL cell survival. CRISPR knockout (KO) of MARCHF5 in PEL cell lines resulted in a significant increase in apoptosis despite the presence of MCL1. The anti-apoptotic function of MARCHF5 was dependent on its E3 ligase and dimerization activities. Loss of MARCHF5 or inhibition of the 26S proteasome furthermore stabilized the MCL1 antagonist NOXA without affecting levels of MCL1. Interestingly, NOXA KO provides a fitness advantage to PEL cells suggesting that NOXA is the pro-apoptotic signal that necessitates the anti-apoptotic activities of MCL1 and MARCHF5. Finally, endogenous reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation experiments show that MARCHF5 and NOXA are found in the same protein complex. Our findings thus provide the mechanistic link that underlies the genetic interaction between MCL1 and MARCHF5. We propose that MARCHF5 induces the degradation of the MCL1 antagonist NOXA thus reinforcing the pro-survival role of MCL1 in these tumor cells. This newly appreciated interaction of the MCL1 and MARCHF5 oncogenes may be useful to improve the design of combination therapies for KSHV malignancies.

title: Integrative ALS therapy: gene targeted therapy by base editing and potential exercise rehabilitation as synergistic strategies for functional recovery.
abstract:
PURPOSE: A key pathological hallmark of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is transactive response DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43, encoded by TARDBP) proteinopathy. Mutations in TARDBP and cellular stress can drive nuclear clearance and cytoplasmic aggregation of TDP-43. TDP-43 is an essential nuclear RNA-binding protein that regulates RNA metabolism, and cytoplasmic TDP-43 aggregation leads to aberrant splicing of essential neuronal transcripts including stathmin-2 (STMN2) and unc-13 homolog A (UNC13A). Dysregulated RNA splicing causes cryptic exon (CE) inclusion in STMN2 and UNC13A mRNA, resulting in non-functional proteins and disruption of axonal regeneration and synaptic integrity. Splice-switching antisense oligonucleotides and gene-editing platforms can correct STMN2 and UNC13A mis-splicing defects. However, restoring STMN2 and UNC13A expression alone is not sufficient to regenerate neuromuscular junctions or reverse skeletal muscle atrophy, both of which are crucial for functional recovery in patients with ALS.
METHODS: We reviewed gene-targeted treatment strategies and rehabilitative mechanisms that inhibit ALS progression and reverse neuromuscular degeneration by analyzing databases, including Google Scholar, PubMed, and ScienceDirect. We proposed a dual-modality therapeutic approach integrating base-editing-mediated gene therapy with exercise-based rehabilitation.
RESULTS: Antisense oligonucleotides and genome editing can restore transcript fidelity by preventing cryptic exons inclusion in STMN2 and UNC13A, thereby stabilizing neuronal function. Gene-targeted therapies halt ALS progression; however, these treatments alone are insufficient to reverse neuromuscular degeneration or achieve functional recovery needed for patients with ALS to return to daily life.
CONCLUSION: Integrated rehabilitation is a crucial step in gene-targeted therapy for ALS. This strategy halts disease progression and restores neuromuscular function, thereby improving the lifespan and quality of life of patients with ALS.

title: Pharmacological Myristoylation Inhibition by Zelenirstat Disrupts Growth Signalling, Energy Metabolism, and Migration in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer Cells.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Metastatic breast cancer cells rely on oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) for energy production, yet selectively targeting mitochondrial metabolism in cancer cells remains a major therapeutic challenge. Myristoylation, the modification of proteins with the 14-carbon fatty acid myristate by N-myristoyltransferases NMT1 and NMT2, dually impacts cancer cell signalling and metabolism. The pan-NMT inhibitor zelenirstat selectively inhibits these enzymes to prevent the myristoylation of target proteins.
METHODS: We assessed the effects of zelenirstat on the protein levels and metabolic activity of multiple triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) cell lines. NDUFAF4 knockout (KO) MDA-MB-231 cells were engineered using CRISPR/Cas9. Functional assays included multiple types of respirometry, cell migration measurements, and spheroid formation.
RESULTS: Zelenirstat treatment depleted myristoylated complex I assembly factor NDUFAF4 levels in four different TNBC cell lines. This loss effectively abrogated mitochondrial OXPHOS through impairment of complex I, resulting in reduced cellular energy production. Zelenirstat treatment resulted in NADH accumulation, loss of AMPK, and decreased glycolysis. Given that zelenirstat impacted cell signalling and OXPHOS, we further demonstrated that it also significantly impaired migration and invasion. Importantly, both zelenirstat treatment and NDUFAF4 KO TNBC MDA-MB-231 cells dramatically reduced mammosphere formation, indicating potent activity against breast cancer stem cells (BCSCs).
CONCLUSION: In addition to the previously shown inhibitory effect of zelenirstat on TNBC cell growth in vitro and in vivo, our new data demonstrate the widespread effects of zelenirstat on both aggressive TNBC cells and BCSCs. These findings highlight the potential of zelenirstat as an anti-metastatic agent, warranting further clinical trial evaluation in patients with TNBC.

title: The Dual Role of Piezo1 in Cancer: Mechanotransduction, Microenvironment Remodelling, and Therapeutic Opportunities.
abstract: The mechanosensitive ion channel Piezo1 translates physical cues from the tumor microenvironment-including extracellular matrix stiffness, fluid shear stress, and compressive forces-into intracellular calcium signals and downstream cascades, playing a pivotal role in cancer. Piezo1 exhibits pronounced tumor-type dependency: it acts as an oncogene in multiple solid tumor types (eg, glioma, pancreatic cancer, esophageal squamous cell carcinoma) but exerts tumor-suppressive effects in lung cancer and clear cell renal cell carcinoma. This context-dependent duality poses fundamental challenges for clinical translation. This review systematically dissects the molecular mechanisms by which Piezo1 regulates proliferation, migration, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, cancer stem cell maintenance, and Piezo1-mediated ferroptosis via the TfR1/DMT1/NCOA4/GPX4 axis, which couples iron overload and lipid peroxidation to mechanical cues, is also discussed as a novel therapeutic vulnerability. It further analyzes its role in tumor microenvironment remodelling, including extracellular matrix stiffening, cancer-associated fibroblast activation, angiogenesis, lymphangiogenesis, and metabolic reprogramming. Moreover, the bidirectional immunomodulatory functions of Piezo1 are highlighted: it enhances T cell and natural killer cell antitumor activity but may also promote immunosuppression through regulatory T cells, tumor-associated macrophages, and dendritic cells. Regarding Piezo1-targeted therapies, advances in small-molecule modulators, ultrasound-based physical modulation, nanotechnology, combination regimens, and antibody-drug conjugates are summarized. Five translational bottlenecks are critically appraised: tissue specificity, cancer type-dependent functional differences, limitations of pharmacological tools, clinical translation barriers of mechanical force stimulation and drug resistance and tumor heterogeneity. Finally, future directions are discussed, including structure-guided drug design, organ-on-a-chip screening, CRISPR-based editing, and emerging modalities. As a critical hub linking mechanical cues to tumor biology, precise Piezo1 modulation promises to establish a new "mechanomedicine" paradigm-an emerging field that leverages mechanical force-based diagnostics and therapeutics for disease management. Future efforts should focus on highly selective modulators, patient stratification based on Piezo1 expression and mechanical signatures, and spatiotemporally synergistic strategies combining Piezo1 targeting with chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and metabolic interventions.

title: Potential Therapeutic Applications of Spherical Nucleic Acids (SNAs) in Cancer: Key Observations and Insights.
abstract: Spherical nucleic acids (SNAs) are a unique class of nucleic acid nanotherapeutics characterized by densely packed, radially arranged oligonucleotides surrounding a nanoparticle or molecular core, or core-free nanoscale structures. Compared with conventional linear nucleic acids, SNAs exhibit excellent cellular uptake, resistance to nuclease degradation, and efficient target recognition without the help of transfection agents. This review summarizes SNAs' structural diversity, design principles, and the multiscale delivery barriers they encounter. We mainly focus on liposomal SNAs (LSNAs) as programmable platforms for cancer immunotherapy. We emphasize how lipid chemistry, membrane architecture, and anchor stability control lymphoid distribution, immune-cell uptake, antigen presentation, and strong antitumor immunity, rather than seeing lipids as inert carriers. Furthermore, we also discuss current developments in gene silencing, CRISPR-based genome editing, and stimulus-responsive multimodal therapies, highlighting the significant therapeutic advancements of SNAs like clinical trial NU-0129 and LSNAs like cavrotolimod. Finally, we describe present translational obstacles and potential prospects by using SNAs as next-generation precision immunotherapeutics.

title: Nanoparticle-Mediated Brain-Targeted Drug Delivery for Methamphetamine Use Disorder: Advances, Challenges and Translational Perspectives.
abstract: Methamphetamine use disorder (MUD) poses a significant global health challenge, lacking FDA-approved pharmacotherapies. Despite extensive exploration of therapeutic targets and interventions, effective treatment remains scarce due to challenges in delivering therapeutic agents to relevant brain regions at effective concentrations. Nanoparticle-mediated delivery offers a promising approach for transporting various therapeutic cargos to the central nervous system, including small molecules, nucleic acids, peptides, proteins, and gene-editing systems. However, the application of nanomedicine strategies in addressing the unique pathophysiological characteristics of MUD has not been systematically assessed. This review presents a problem-focused analysis of how lipid-based, polymeric, inorganic, biological, and hybrid nanocarriers tackle successive delivery obstacles such as systemic stability, blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration, brain region-specific distribution, and controlled release of intracellular cargo. We compare preclinical nanotherapeutic approaches encompassing small-molecule neuroprotective agents, anti-METH vaccines, gene-silencing RNAs, neurotrophic proteins, and emerging gene-editing methods, outlining their respective benefits, limitations, and design considerations. Additionally, we explore key factors influencing nanomedicine performance in MUD, including protein corona formation, the impact of METH-related BBB dysfunction and neuroinflammation on nanoparticle distribution, and the disparity between acute animal models and chronic human MUD with relapse tendencies. In conclusion, we present a systematic framework for aligning nanocarrier characteristics with distinct delivery obstacles and therapeutic needs. We also emphasize forthcoming avenues such as disease-triggered nanocarriers, targeted delivery to specific regions, combined nanomedical approaches, theranostic strategies, and standardized assessments of biodistribution, effectiveness, safety, and translational potential.

title: Integration of Nanotechnology with ctDNA: New Advances for Monitoring Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy.
abstract: The evaluation of tumor response in the neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NACT) is still difficult as traditional imaging techniques can only provide morphological information at discrete intervals, and pathological response is usually assessed only after surgery. Although circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) has the potential to provide a minimally invasive approach to monitor molecular response during treatment, its clinical use is hampered by low presence, high fragmentation, rapid clearance and the presence of high levels of non-tumor cell-free DNA (cfDNA). In this review, we aim to discuss the challenges of ctDNA detection in analytical and biological settings and how nanotechnology may be able to help address these challenges, particularly during the NACT window. The analytical performance and the potential integration of nanotechnology platforms, including gold nanoparticle plasmonic sensing, magnetic nanoparticle (MNP) extraction and microfluidic integration, fluorescent quantum dots for multiplexing, carbon-based electrochemical sensors and nano‑based CRISPR biosensing, enable a rapid detection of ctDNA. Benefits of these nanotechnological platforms are not just that technologies exist, but that early ctDNA clearance predicts response, persistence signals resistance, and nanotechnology makes routine, sensitive, and rapid monitoring feasible, provided certain translational hurdles are cleared. While there is great promise for the use of nanotechnology to enable fast, sensitive detection of ctDNA during NACT, significant issues remain in standardization of assays, reproducible manufacturing, prospective validation, and cost-effectiveness before clinical use is a reality.

title: Nanotechnology-Enabled Immunotherapy for Colorectal Cancer: Overcoming the "Cold" Tumor Microenvironment in Microsatellite-Stable Disease.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed the management of mismatch repair-deficient/microsatellite instability-high (dMMR/MSI-H) colorectal cancer (CRC), yet the ~95% of patients with mismatch repair-proficient/microsatellite-stable (pMMR/MSS) disease derive little benefit owing to an immunologically "cold" tumor microenvironment (TME), poor T-cell infiltration, myeloid dominance, TGF-β-enriched stroma, and the systemically immunosuppressive milieu imposed by hepatic metastases. Clinically tested combinations-multikinase inhibitor plus anti-PD-1, Fc-enhanced dual checkpoint blockade, chemotherapy- or antiangiogenic-ICI regimens-have so far produced modest, largely non-durable response rates that are further attenuated in liver-metastatic disease, motivating approaches that pharmacologically remodel the TME rather than only release checkpoint restraint.
OBJECTIVE: To provide an evidence-stratified synthesis of nanotechnology-enabled immunotherapy in CRC that explicitly separates (a) clinically established evidence, (b) strategies under early-phase clinical investigation, and (c) concepts that remain preclinical or are extrapolated from other tumor types, and to derive from this appraisal a biomarker-enriched translational research agenda.
METHODS: Narrative, integrative (non-systematic) review. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ASCO/ESMO/AACR proceedings were searched from January 2010 through April 2026. Each strategy was appraised according to the highest available level of evidence, the tumor type and model system in which the evidence was generated, and its demonstrated CRC specificity.
RESULTS: In current clinical practice, nanomedicine in CRC is essentially limited to nanoparticle-formulated cytotoxics exploited for pharmacokinetic advantage (e.g. liposomal irinotecan), whereas nano-enabled immunotherapy is confined to a small number of early-phase trials-most notably lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-formulated individualized neoantigen mRNA vaccines in ctDNA-positive resected CRC and hafnium-oxide nanoparticle radioenhancers-none of which has yet demonstrated a progression-free or overall survival benefit in MSS CRC. Against this background we critically appraise six classes of strategy: (i) LNP-based mRNA neoantigen vaccines; (ii) polymeric and inorganic nanocarriers for STING and TLR agonists; (iii) tumor-associated macrophage-repolarizing nanoparticles; (iv) nano-radiosensitizers and photothermal/photodynamic platforms priming immunogenic cell death; (v) nano-formulated checkpoint inhibitor delivery; and (vi) locoregional nano-strategies directed at hepatic metastasis-specific immunosuppression. For categories (ii)-(vi) the supporting evidence is predominantly murine (largely subcutaneous CT26/MC38 models) or extrapolated from immunologically "hot" tumors such as melanoma and non-small-cell lung cancer, in which both the underlying biology and the checkpoint backbone differ materially from MSS CRC. Recurrent translational barriers include low, highly heterogeneous nanoparticle accumulation in human tumors, dense TGF-β-rich stroma and elevated interstitial pressure, mononuclear phagocyte system clearance, liver-metastasis-specific tolerance that subcutaneous models do not reproduce, unresolved manufacturing/CMC and regulatory pathways, and the absence of validated pharmacodynamic biomarkers of intratumoral immune conversion.
CONCLUSION: Nanotechnology offers a mechanistically coherent and experimentally testable-but at present clinically unproven-set of strategies for converting "cold" MSS CRC into immune-responsive disease. We therefore position nano-enabled immunotherapy as a research priority rather than an imminent standard of care, and argue that its clinical value can only be established through biomarker-enriched, paired-biopsy early-phase trials with pharmacodynamic endpoints of immune conversion and prospective stratification by metastatic site (particularly hepatic involvement) and consensus molecular subtype.
LIMITATIONS: This is a narrative rather than systematic review; it is therefore subject to selection and publication bias, and much of the evidence synthesized is preclinical and of limited direct translational certainty.

title: The Role of TXNIP in Skeletal Muscle Physiology and Related Diseases: Current Perspectives.
abstract: Thioredoxin-interacting protein (TXNIP) is a multifunctional regulatory protein of the α-arrestin family that acts as a redox sensor, an energy-responsive molecule, and a transcription-associated regulator. TXNIP has emerged as a key regulator of skeletal muscle homeostasis and has been implicated in the pathogenesis of multiple muscle disorders. Skeletal muscle is a principal site of systemic glucose disposal, accounting for more than 70% of insulin-stimulated glucose uptake in the human body. TXNIP has been implicated in sarcopenia, obesity-related insulin resistance, limb ischemia-induced muscle injury, disuse muscle atrophy, and hereditary muscular dystrophy through multiple mechanisms, including glutathione metabolic regulation, ferroptosis, NLRP3 inflammasome activation, impaired GLUT4 membrane translocation, and altered mitochondrial substrate oxidation. Recent advances in gene editing, single-cell sequencing, metabolomics, and human clinical research have enabled a more detailed characterization of TXNIP-related molecular mechanisms in skeletal muscle. This review provides a systematic synthesis of recent evidence on TXNIP in skeletal muscle, organized around seven themes: its molecular characteristics, expression and regulatory patterns in skeletal muscle, physiological functions, disease-specific pathogenic mechanisms, intervention-related regulatory networks, current limitations, and future perspectives. This review aims to provide a mechanistic rationale for targeting TXNIP as a potential strategy for the prevention and treatment of skeletal muscle-related diseases.

title: FZD10 and Diseases: From Molecular Mechanisms to the Potential of Targeted Therapy.
abstract: Frizzled class receptor 10 (FZD10) is a member of the Frizzled family of seven-transmembrane receptors. It mediates Wnt signaling through both canonical (β-catenin) and non-canonical (planar cell polarity and Ca²⁺) pathways, thereby regulating cell proliferation, differentiation, migration, apoptosis, and stem cell self-renewal. Dysregulation of FZD10-resulting from altered expression, aberrant promoter methylation, or functional impairment-has been linked to multiple human diseases, including cancers, metabolic and inflammatory disorders, and neurodegenerative conditions. In malignant tumors, FZD10 shows tissue-specific oncogenic activity. It is overexpressed in synovial sarcoma, colorectal cancer, gastric cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, cervical cancer, ovarian cancer, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, non-small cell lung cancer, and renal cell carcinoma, but downregulated in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. This restricted expression pattern makes FZD10 a potential biomarker for diagnosis and prognosis, as well as a candidate for targeted therapy. This review summarizes current knowledge on FZD10, covering its gene and protein structure, signaling mechanisms, and roles in various diseases. We also discuss its diagnostic and prognostic value in different cancers, and review recent progress in FZD10-targeted strategies, including antibodies, radioimmunotherapy, small-molecule inhibitors, drug repurposing, exosome-based delivery, and gene editing. Current limitations, such as the context-dependent functions of FZD10 and the safety issues associated with targeted agents, are also discussed. Future studies are needed to clarify the mechanistic basis of FZD10 action and to develop biomarkers for patient stratification.

title: Biotechnological Approaches to Biofilm-Targeted Antifungal Therapy in Recurrent Vulvovaginal Candidiasis.
abstract: Recurrent Vulvovaginal Candidiasis (RVVC) is increasing worldwide, with biofilm persistence and antifungal resistance limiting treatment options. The combined use of antifungal treatments with antibiofilm agents has become a promising strategy. This review explores advanced therapeutic approaches, their limitations, and prospects. Overgrowth of vaginal Candida inflames the mucosa, causing itching, dryness, and whitish discharge. Biofilm formation worsens the condition, contributing to treatment failure, resistance, and recurrence. Conventional antifungal modalities are often inadequate against these multidimensional biofilm assemblies. Combining natural and synthetic antifungal agents with antibiofilm adjuncts has shown improved outcomes by targeting Candida cells within biofilms. This review compiles studies on multicomponent approaches to managing vaginal Candida infections, focusing on pan-Candida species to clarify species-specific resistance and persistence. Host factors in non-virgin women, a highly affected population, are examined alongside regional data on recurrence and treatment failure. Together, these insights highlight the microbiology of Candida biofilms, host and regional influences, and the socio-economic burden of RVVC, while emphasising the translational importance of combination therapy and biotechnology-driven innovations such as molecular docking, nanocarriers, CRISPR-based gene modulation, and engineered probiotics.

title: Stimuli-responsive Graphene Nanoplatforms Co-delivering Self-amplifying RNA, circRNA, and cGAMP for Cancer Immunotherapy: A Narrative Review.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Cancer immunotherapy has emerged as a transformative therapeutic strategy; however, its efficacy remains limited by tumor heterogeneity, immune suppression, and inefficient delivery of nucleic acid therapeutics. Graphene-based nanomaterials have attracted considerable attention as multifunctional carriers because of their high surface area, tunable surface chemistry, and stimuli-responsive properties.
METHODS: This narrative review critically summarizes recent advances in stimuli-responsive graphene nanoplatforms for the co-delivery of self-amplifying RNA (saRNA), circular RNA (circRNA), and cGAMP. A conceptual multifunctional graphene-based delivery framework is proposed to guide future experimental research in cancer immunotherapy. Particular emphasis is placed on graphene functionalization strategies, RNA conjugation approaches, tumor-responsive release mechanisms, and synergistic immune activation pathways.
RESULTS: Graphene nanoplatforms demonstrate significant potential to protect nucleic acid therapeutics from degradation while enabling controlled release in response to pH, redox, enzymatic, and near-infrared stimuli. The integration of saRNA, circRNA, and cGAMP provides complementary therapeutic benefits, including prolonged antigen expression, enhanced molecular stability, and potent activation of the STING pathway. This combination promotes coordinated activation of innate and adaptive immunity, resulting in improved dendritic cell maturation, T-cell priming, and antitumor immune responses.
DISCUSSION: The multifunctional nature of graphene-based nanocarriers offers opportunities for simultaneous delivery of multiple immunotherapeutic agents while reducing systemic toxicity. Nevertheless, challenges related to biosafety, biodegradability, large-scale manufacturing, and regulatory approval remain barriers to clinical translation.
CONCLUSION: Stimuli-responsive graphene nanoplatforms co-delivering saRNA, circRNA, and cGAMP represent a promising next-generation strategy for precision cancer immunotherapy. Continued advances in graphene engineering and translational nanomedicine may facilitate their future clinical application.

title: Heat Shock Protein 90 as a Master Regulator of Multidrug Resistance: Small-molecule Inhibitors, Prodrugs, Hybrid Molecules, Antibody-drug Conjugates, and Nanotechnology-based Delivery Systems.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION/OBJECTIVE: Multidrug Resistance (MDR) remains a major obstacle to effective cancer chemotherapy, driven by multiple interconnected mechanisms, including overexpression of ATP-binding Cassette (ABC) transporters, enhanced DNA repair, apoptosis evasion, and protumorigenic microenvironmental factors. Heat Shock Protein 90 (HSP90) has emerged as a master regulator of MDR by chaperoning multiple client proteins involved in drug efflux, survival signaling pathways, and cellular stress responses. These mechanisms collectively decrease intracellular drug accumulation and promote tumor cell survival, leading to therapeutic failure. This review aims to summarize HSP90-targeted therapeutic strategies for overcoming MDR in cancer and evaluate their mechanistic basis, efficacy, and translational potential.
METHODS: A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar up to 2010-2026. Keywords included "HSP90," "multidrug resistance," "cancer," "HSP90 inhibitors," "prodrug," "ADC," and "nanotechnology," combined using Boolean operators. Relevant preclinical and clinical studies on HSP90-targeted strategies to overcome MDR were included, while duplicates and studies that were irrelevant or insufficiently detailed were excluded. Eligible studies were screened and analyzed for mechanisms, therapeutic outcomes, and limitations.
RESULTS: Small-molecule HSP90 inhibitors, including geldanamycin derivatives and resorcinol-based compounds, demonstrate potential in destabilizing MDR-associated client proteins such as P-glycoprotein, MRP1, BCRP, and survival kinases, thereby restoring sensitivity of resistant cancer cells to chemotherapy. Prodrug strategies improve bioavailability and reduce systemic toxicity while preserving HSP90 inhibitory activity. Hybrid molecules that integrate HSP90 inhibition with complementary mechanisms, such as HDAC inhibition and kinase inhibition, provide synergistic multi-targeted effects against resistance pathways. Antibody-drug conjugates facilitate tumor-selective delivery of HSP90 inhibitors, enabling receptormediated internalization and reducing the impact of efflux mechanisms. Furthermore, nanotechnology-based delivery platforms, including liposomes, polymeric nanoparticles, and stimuli-responsive carriers, enhance pharmacokinetics, enable co-delivery of HSP90 inhibitors with chemotherapeutic agents, and support controlled intratumoral drug release.
DISCUSSION: HSP90-targeted strategies represent a promising approach for reversing MDR by simultaneously regulating multiple resistance-associated pathways. The ability of HSP90 inhibitors to disrupt drug efflux transporters, survival signaling networks, and stress adaptation mechanisms provides a strong rationale for their integration with conventional chemotherapy and emerging targeted therapies. However, clinical translation remains challenging due to tumor heterogeneity, biological barriers, dose-limiting toxicities, and variations in patient response. Rational combination strategies, biomarker-guided patient selection, and advanced delivery technologies are essential to maximize therapeutic benefits and improve clinical outcomes.
CONCLUSION: HSP90-targeted therapeutic approaches offer significant potential for overcoming MDR in cancer by restoring drug sensitivity and enhancing treatment efficacy. Future progress will depend on optimized combination therapies incorporating MDR modulators, personalized treatment strategies guided by predictive biomarkers, and innovative technologies such as artificial intelligence-assisted drug design and CRISPR-based gene editing. Continued interdisciplinary research is required to translate HSP90- targeted innovations into effective clinical interventions for patients with drug-resistant cancers.

title: SMART Nanocarriers for siRNA Delivery: Stimuli-Responsive Platforms for Targeted Gene Silencing.
abstract: Despite the remarkable specificity of small interfering RNA (siRNA)-based treatments for gene silencing, biological limitations like poor stability, rapid systemic clearance, immunogenicity, and inefficient intracellular delivery hinder their clinical translation. A promising strategy for overcoming these challenges and enabling precise, site-specific gene silencing is the use of SMART nanocarriers, including stimuli-responsive, adaptable, and multifunctional delivery platforms. Controlled siRNA release, enhanced cellular uptake, and effective endosomal escape are enabled by these novel nanocarriers' ability to respond dynamically to exogenous triggers such as light, ultrasound, and magnetic fields as well as endogenous stimuli such as pH gradients, redox potential, enzymatic activity, and hypoxia. Recent advances have combined rational material design, surface functionalization with targeted ligands, and modular architectures to gain spatiotemporal control over gene silencing while limiting unintended targets and systemic toxicity. This study examines the critical design concepts, fabrication methodologies, and molecular pathways governing SMART nanocarrier-mediated siRNA distribution, with a focus on polymeric, lipid-based, inorganic, and bioinspired platforms. The article highlights key preclinical and emerging clinical breakthroughs, as well as issues with scalability, repeatability, immunocompatibility, and regulatory translation. This review emphasizes the critical significance of stimulus-responsive nanocarriers in developing siRNA treatments towards precision medicine applications in oncology, neurological disorders, and inflammatory illnesses by consolidating recent studies and future prospects.

title: Crossing the Blood-brain Barrier: Emerging Nanotechnological Approaches for Neurodegenerative Disease Therapy.
abstract: Neurodegenerative disorders such as Parkinson's Disease (PD), Alzheimer's Disease (AD), Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), and Huntington's Disease (HD) are characterized by progressive neuronal degeneration and severe therapeutic limitations due to the Blood-Brain Barrier (BBB). Recent advances in nanotechnology have enabled the development of nanoscale drug delivery systems capable of improving BBB penetration and enhancing therapeutic efficacy. This review discusses recent progress in Lipid Nanoparticles (LNPs), polymeric nanoparticles, exosomes, magnetic nanoparticles, gold nanoparticles, graphene quantum dots, and RNAloaded nanocarriers for brain-targeted delivery. Special emphasis is placed on receptor-mediated transcytosis, intranasal delivery, magnetic targeting, and ionizable lipid nanoparticle systems for nucleic acid delivery. Recent nanoformulations including curcumin-loaded nanoparticles, siRNA- loaded lipid nanoparticles, dopamine-loaded liposomes, and lactoferrin-functionalized polymeric nanoparticles are critically compared based on BBB penetration, therapeutic efficacy, toxicity, and translational potential. Furthermore, current clinical challenges including nanotoxicity, pharmacokinetics, large-scale manufacturing, and regulatory barriers are discussed. Nanotechnology- based therapeutics represent a promising strategy for improving diagnosis and treatment of neurodegenerative disorders and may facilitate the future development of precision nanomedicine.

title: Fungal Keratitis: A Narrative Review with a Focus on Antifungal Resistance and Emerging Therapies.
abstract: Corneal infection that can cause blindness, fungal keratitis has shown an increasing prevalence worldwide, especially in tropical and subtropical areas, where it significantly increases the risk of unilateral corneal blindness. The epidemiology, molecular etiology, diagnosis, antifungal resistance, and changing treatment of fungal keratitis are all reviewed in this article. Geographic diversity is evident in epidemiological patterns, with filamentous fungi such as Aspergillus and Fusarium predominating in warm climes, and an increasing number of reports of Candida species in temperate and healthcare-associated settings. Disease incidence and outcomes have been further affected by post-COVID-19 changes in ophthalmic treatment, extensive corticosteroid exposure, delayed presentations, and environmental factors, including climate fluctuations and increased airborne spore loads. Rapid stromal invasion, enzyme-mediated tissue damage, biofilm development, and host immune dysregulation are key factors determining severity, according to molecular findings. For improved detection, including in culture-negative and polymicrobial cases, diagnostic advancements focus on combining traditional microscopy and culture with in vivo confocal microscopy, MALDI-TOF MS, targeted PCR, and metagenomic next-generation sequencing. Time to treatment is being reduced by rapid point-of-care techniques like tear β-D-glucan tests, LAMP, CRISPR/Cas platforms, and AI-based image analysis. The necessity for systematic susceptibility testing and antifungal management is supported by rising antifungal resistance, particularly rising MIC trends in Fusarium and Aspergillus species, which exhibit variable susceptibility to azoles and amphotericin B, highlighting the need for species-specific antifungal susceptibility testing. The evolving epidemiology, molecular etiology, and new developments in fungal keratitis diagnosis are covered in this article. Additionally, it emphasizes new therapeutic approaches, including advanced drug delivery systems, advances in antifungal resistance management, and potential avenues for improved management. The article presents a narrative review focusing on recent developments in the epidemiology, molecular mechanisms, diagnosis, antifungal resistance, and treatment options for fungal keratitis.

title: Targeted Delivery of RNA-based Therapeutics by Lipid Nanoparticles.
abstract: Lipid Nanoparticles (LNPs) have emerged as adaptable and effective delivery systems for RNA-based therapies, transforming contemporary medicine. This article covers the design, processes, and therapeutic potential of LNPs for RNA delivery. LNPs improve RNA encapsulation, stability, and targeted cellular delivery. Lipid nanoparticles protect RNA molecules from enzymatic degradation, enable endosomal escape, and allow cytoplasmic release for gene control or functional translation. Various RNA types are delivered using LNPs for specific therapeutic applications, such as mRNA for vaccines and protein replacement, siRNA for gene silencing in diverse genetic and oncological conditions, miRNA for gene expression modulation, and CRISPR/Cas9 components for targeted gene editing. LNP-mediated RNA therapies have demonstrated efficacy across a diverse array of diseases. The design and optimization of LNPs depend on several factors. In vivo studies and preclinical models have confirmed their safety and efficacy, leading to successful clinical trials and FDA-approved RNAbased therapies. However, challenges encompass immunogenicity, limited tissue selectivity, substantial production requirements, and longer safety duration. Recent advancements in ionizable lipid chemistry, microfluidic formulation, and targeted delivery techniques are broadening the therapeutic potential of LNPs, reinforcing their significance as essential carriers in the forthcoming era of precision RNA medicine.
