title: Translational Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamics of a Cationic mRNA-Lipid Nanoparticle from Mice to Non-Human Primates
abstract: Cationic lipid nanoparticles have demonstrated unique potential for extrahepatic mRNA delivery, particularly enabling selective targeting of the pulmonary endothelium. However, their translational development has been hampered by reports of infusion-related immune reactions and innate immune system activation, most notably transient complement activation. Here, we present a case study illustrating the discovery and translational advancement of a selected cationic LNP into non-human primates (NHPs) for initial pharmacokinetic assessment and evaluation of potential immunostimulatory side effects. We show surface charge dependent organ-selective expression of reporter mRNAs from different LNPs in vivo. An mRNA encoding the Tie2 agonist COMP-Angl, was formulated with LNP002, and respective pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic readouts were analyzed in two independent non-human primate studies. Notably, dose-dependent transient complement activation could be abrogated by extending the infusion time. Finally, we identified the blood-borne pharmacodynamic biomarker PDGFB for LNP002/mRNA-76 treatment reflecting activated Tie2-signalling in healthy pulmonary endothelium in vivo supported by single cell sequencing and cluster-alignment of downstream effector genes with the same spatial profile as the delivered mRNA.

title: BI-TfR1 CapX rapidly transits the blood-brain barrier for efficient, low-dose gene delivery throughout the CNS.
abstract: Safe, efficient gene delivery throughout the CNS remains a central obstacle to treating genetic diseases of the brain and spinal cord. We describe BI-TfR1 CapX, a human transferrin receptor (TfR1)-binding AAV capsid that, after a low intravenous dose in adult humanized TFRC mice, transduced more than 80% of cortical and spinal neurons and ∼60% of cortical astrocytes, with reduced distribution and expression in several peripheral tissues relative to AAV9. Unlike other engineered BBB-crossing capsids, CapX bound the CNS vasculature within minutes and a large fraction of its genomes reached parenchymal nuclei within 24 hours. Delivering a Prnp -targeted epigenetic silencer ( Prnp -CHARM), CapX reduced brain Prnp mRNA by over 95% requiring 18-fold fewer vector genomes per brain cell than AAV-PHP.eB for 50% lowering. A CapX delivered dual-vector cytosine base editor installed a protein-truncating PRNP stop codon lowering brain prion protein by 80%. These properties make CapX an attractive vehicle for human CNS gene therapy.

title: Thiomorpholino antisense oligonucleotides inhibit telomerase and limit cancer cell proliferation
abstract: Reactivation of telomerase confers immortality to approximately 90% of human tumors by enabling continuous elongation of the DNA at chromosome ends, or telomeres. The telomerase catalytic subunit TERT adds TTAGGG repeats using a portion of the telomerase RNA component hTR as a template. Because telomerase is inactive in most normal somatic cells, it remains an attractive therapeutic target; however, no telomerase inhibitor has yet demonstrated robust clinical efficacy with acceptable safety. Here we evaluate thiomorpholino oligonucleotides (TMOs) as a new class of antisense oligonucleotides targeting the template region of hTR. TMOs incorporate morpholino rings and phosphorothioate linkages, which enhance nuclease resistance, RNA binding and nuclear uptake. Two anti-hTR TMOs inhibited telomerase activity in vitro with an IC50 below 1 nM, whereas two control TMOs were at least 100-fold less active. HeLa cells treated with anti-hTR TMOs showed progressive telomere shortening, detectable after one week of treatment. Growth inhibition was observed after substantial telomere erosion, and both telomere length and proliferation recovered upon withdrawal of TMOs. These findings establish TMOs as a promising new chemistry for telomerase-targeted therapeutics.

title: A tRNA-derived small RNA orchestrates cardioprotection through distinct cell-type-specific mechanisms.
abstract: Pathological cardiac fibrosis and hypertrophy, key contributors to adverse remodeling that drives heart failure (HF), are not adequately targeted by current therapies. We identified tRNA-Asp-GTC-3'tDR, an ischemia-induced tRNA-derived small RNA (tDR), as an endogenous regulator of both remodeling processes across cardiac fibroblasts and cardiomyocytes. In murine models of myocardial ischemia- and pressure overload-induced HF, cardiac delivery of tRNA-Asp-GTC-3'tDR reduced fibrosis and hypertrophy, preserved cardiac function, and improved survival, with limited three doses conferring durable protection after ischemia, whereas silencing it worsened both. Strikingly, tRNA-Asp-GTC-3'tDR acts through distinct mechanisms in different cell types: in fibroblasts, it assembles stress granules that sequester ribosome-loaded profibrotic transcripts, whereas in cardiomyocytes it engages pseudouridine synthase PUS7 to activate RNA autophagy. Its regulation and functions were confirmed in human cardiac cells and tissues. These findings demonstrate that a single tDR coordinates cell-type-specific protective programs in the heart, suggesting a new therapeutic axis to mitigate HF progression.

title: Programming primary human T cells to deliver gene editing machinery.
abstract: Clinical applications of gene editors including CRISPR-Cas9 are limited by the cell-type specificity and tissue penetrance of current in vivo delivery options. Cell-mediated gene editor delivery could overcome these obstacles. To date, systems utilizing immortalized cell lines have demonstrated gene editor delivery in vitro . Because T cells traffic throughout the organism and engage in intercellular communication with individual target cells, we wondered whether they could be engineered to deliver gene editing machinery. Here, we demonstrate that primary human T cells can produce retroviral-based enveloped delivery vehicles (EDVs) packaging functional Cas9 ribonucleoproteins. When paired with fusogenic VSV-G, T cell-generated Cas9-EDVs edited a diverse array of target cells. We developed a miniaturized Moloney murine leukemia virus-based system that proved superior to existing architectures in this context and optimized both lentiviral and site-specific knock-in approaches for T cell engineering. These Enveloped Particle Information Courier-(EPIC-) T cells offer key advantages as delivery systems.

title: RAPTOR-targeted Antisense Oligonucleotides Restrict Pathological mTORC1 Activity in GATOR1-dependent Disease
abstract: Loss-of-function mutations in the GATOR1 complex (NPRL2, NPRL3, and DEPDC5) are among the most common genetic causes of epilepsy. These mutations impair amino acid-dependent regulation of mTORC1 and cause hyperactive signaling, neuronal hyperexcitability, astrocytic metabolic remodeling, seizures, and early mortality. Here, we report the development of antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) targeting RAPTOR, an mTORC1 scaffolding subunit, to correct pathological mTORC1 hyperactivity caused by defective upstream regulation. RAPTOR-targeted ASO treatment reduced RAPTOR expression in mouse and human systems and dampened mTORC1 signaling in GATOR1-deficient models. ASO-mediated RAPTOR reduction rescued neuronal hyperexcitability, corrected astrocytic mitochondrial dysfunction, and suppressed spontaneous seizures in vivo. A single treatment significantly extended longevity across neuronal and astrocytic models of GATOR1 deficiency. Collectively, these findings establish RAPTOR-targeted ASOs as a mechanism-based therapeutic approach that durably corrects cellular and circuit-level consequences of GATOR1 deficiency. By tuning RAPTOR abundance, this strategy provides a therapeutic framework for mTORC1-driven epilepsies and related diseases.

title: Structural engineering of dual-targeting antisense oligonucleotides enhances exon 44 skipping for treating Duchenne muscular dystrophy
abstract: Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) inducing exon-skipping during pre-mRNA splicing offer promising treatment for diseases such as Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Recently, dual-targeting ASOs that simultaneously bind two splicing regulatory sequences have been shown to improve exon-skipping efficiency. Current ASOs are designed to interact with target RNAs solely based on Watson-Crick base pairing. Here we report the development of dual-targeting three-dimensional bridge (3D-bridge) ASOs in which tertiary interactions are engineered to increase target-binding affinity and the number of target residues occupied. We designed a 3D-bridge ASO for skipping exon 44 of dystrophin mRNA and biochemically validated its enhanced binding affinity for the target RNA over a similar ASO with the tertiary interactions disrupted. We subsequently optimized the 3D-bridge ASO by varying its ends and ribose chemical modifications using patient-derived induced directly reprogrammed myotubes and identified an LNA/DNA mixmer as the most potent. We further demonstrate enhanced exon-skipping efficacy and potency of the 3D-bridge ASO compared to previously reported ASOs in myotubes differentiated from patient-derived primary myoblasts and MyoD-reprogrammed fibroblasts harboring mutations amenable to reframing through exon 44 skipping. In conclusion, the 3D-bridge ASO technology improves the current dual-targeting design, demonstrating the utility and power of structure-based ASO design methods.

title: The RNA helicase KREH2 directly binds the RESC1-RESC2 complex in trypanosomatid mitochondrial RNA editing.
abstract: Trypanosomatids are medically important single-celled eukaryotic protists with exceptional RNA biology. They display highly unusual RNA biogenesis pathways, notably mitochondrial RNA editing, an essential post-transcriptional process transforming cryptic primary transcripts into functional mRNAs. Large multiprotein assemblies coordinate the RNA editing process, in which small guide RNAs (gRNAs) anneal to the pre-mRNAs and serve as templates for uridine insertion or deletion. Kinetoplast RNA Editing Helicases (KREHs) are important components of the RNA editing process that modifies large portions of pre-mRNA via the sequential annealing and dissociation of multiple gRNAs. However, how KREH helicases interact with components of the editing machinery, and which subunits mediate these interactions, remain unresolved. Here, we examined an association between the DEAH/RHA RNA helicase KREH2 and the RESC1-RESC2 protein heterodimer using proximity labeling and co-immunoprecipitation coupled to quantitative mass spectrometry in vivo . We reconstituted a minimal trimeric KREH2 peptide-RESC1-RESC2 complex in vitro and characterized novel direct binding of a KREH2 peptide to RESC1 using cryo-electron microscopy. These results establish a mechanistic link between the RNA helicase KREH2 and the RESC1-RESC2 module at the 5'-end of gRNAs, providing new avenues for studying the orchestration of RNA remodeling in trypanosomatid mitochondrial RNA editing.

title: KSHV upregulates the long non-coding RNA PURPL via p73 to suppress p53
abstract: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) are a class of regulatory RNAs with lengths exceeding 200 nucleotides. The lncRNA PURPL (p53 upregulated regulator of p53 levels) is a p53-regulated gene. PURPL is an oncogenic lncRNA that represses p53 function; it is upregulated in many tumors and promotes cancer cell proliferation. Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV) is the causative agent of all forms of Kaposi sarcoma (KS) and is tightly associated with primary effusion lymphoma (PEL). We found upregulation of PURPL in both de novo and chronically KSHV-infected cells. We found that p73 (a p53 homolog) associates with the PURPL promoter and upregulates PURPL expression. Previously, it has been shown that KSHV-encoded latency-associated nuclear antigen (LANA) stabilizes p73. We found that ectopic expression of LANA increased both p73 protein levels and PURPL expression. p73 knockdown abrogates PURPL upregulation following KSHV infection. Antisense oligonucleotides (ASO) targeting PURPL reduced PEL cell proliferation and increased acetylated p53 levels. In contrast to p53, p73 is not repressed by PURPL RNA. In summary, our study reveals how an oncogenic virus can utilize p73 to upregulate the oncogenic lncRNA PURPL as an additional way to repress p53. Moreover, we propose another mechanism by which p73 may promote tumor growth.

title: Angiotensin II Promotes Mitral Valve and Left Atrial Pathology in Fibrillin-1C1041G/+ Mice
abstract: Background: Activation of the renin-angiotensin system (RAS) contributes to aortic diseases caused by fibrillin-1 haploinsufficiency (Fbn1C1041G/+). However, whether RAS activation influences mitral valve disease associated with FBN1 variants remains undefined. This study determined whether inhibition or augmentation of the RAS affects mitral valve pathology in Fbn1C1041G/+ mice. Methods: Angiotensinogen (AGT) antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) were administered for 12 weeks to inhibit the RAS in male and female Fbn1C1041G/+ mice. To augment the RAS, mice were infused with angiotensin II (AngII; 1,000 ng/kg/min) for 28 days. Mitral valve and heart function were monitored by ultrasound. At termination, hearts were dissected free and tissue sectioned to assess mitral valve leaflet thickness and pathology. Results: Mitral valve leaflet thickness was significantly increased in Fbn1C1041G/+ mice compared to Fbn1+/+ littermates of both sexes. ASO-mediated AGT inhibition did not alter this phenotype despite markedly reduced plasma AGT concentrations. AngII infusion increased mitral valve leaflet thickness in Fbn1C1041G/+ mice with increased proteoglycan and collagen content, while exerting minimal effects in Fbn1+/+ mice. Twenty-five percent of AngII-infused Fbn1C1041G/+ mice died of non-vascular causes. Ultrasound showed mitral valve dysfunction in AngII-infused Fbn1C1041G/+ mice. Grossly expanded left atria were common in AngII-infused Fbn1C1041G/+ mice. These markedly enlarged left atria contained increased fibrosis, macrophage accumulation, and platelet-rich masses. Conclusions: Mitral valves of Fbn1C1041G/+ mice did not respond to AGT inhibition but were markedly more susceptible to AngII infusion, with greater increases in thickness and compositional changes than mitral valves of Fbn1+/+ mice. In addition, AngII promoted mitral valve dysfunction that were associated with pronounced left atrial pathology.

title: Establishment and characterization of LNCaP-TR-BoM, a bone metastasis-derived prostate cancer cell line with an intermediate AR-attenuated phenotype.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Progression of prostate cancer under androgen receptor (AR) pathway-targeted therapy spans a phenotypic spectrum, from tumors that sustain AR pathway output to tumors that become independent of AR signaling. Experimental models that occupy the intermediate portion of this spectrum, in which AR is still expressed but pathway output is reduced, are comparatively scarce.
METHODS: LNCaP cells expressing a triple-modality reporter (LNCaP-TR) were injected into nude mice by the intracardiac route, and a bone lesion that arose in the middle spine of one animal was recovered and propagated as LNCaP-TR-BoM. The subline and its parental line were compared by two-dimensional and three-dimensional culture assays, RNA-seq, qRT-PCR, and immunoblotting. AR pathway output was assessed using KLK3 expression under AR antagonist treatment. Public prostate cancer datasets provided clinical context. A CRISPR-Cas9 EPHA3 -edited derivative was evaluated in aggregation and spheroid assays.
RESULTS: Relative to parental LNCaP-TR, LNCaP-TR-BoM formed more numerous and larger cell aggregates in monolayer culture and larger, less circular spheroids in both suspension and Matrigel three-dimensional culture. AR mRNA was modestly reduced and AR protein remained readily detectable, whereas KLK3 mRNA and protein were reduced disproportionately more than those of AR. Residual KLK3 expression remained suppressible by AR inhibitors enzalutamide and darolutamide. Transcriptome-based pseudotime placed LNCaP-TR-BoM between the parental line and the androgen-refractory LNCaP-RF variant. Subsequent differential gene expression (DGE) and pathway enrichment analysis revealed that LNCaP-TR-BoM exhibits transcriptomic rewiring concordant with that of clinical mCRPC, thus evidencing LNCaP-TR-BoM as a potentially clinically relevant model cell line. Finally, EPHA3 showed the largest fold change among the most significant differentially expressed genes in LNCaP-TR-BoM compared with the parental line. Therefore, EPHA3 was explored to demonstrate the utility of the LNCaP-TR-BoM cell line as a discovery system for genes that potentially drive the malignancy of bone-metastatic prostate cancer at the intermediate AR-attenuated progression stage. An EPHA3 -silenced derivative of LNCaP-TR-BoM lacking detectable EPHA3 protein formed smaller aggregates and smaller, more circular spheroids, suggesting EPHA3 may play a role in driving the malignancy of AR-intermediate bone-metastatic prostate cancer. This finding provides support for the potential utility of the LNCaP-TR-BoM cell line as a discovery system for genes relevant to driving AR-intermediate bone-metastatic prostate cancer.
CONCLUSIONS: LNCaP-TR-BoM is a bone lesion-derived prostate cancer cell line in which AR expression is retained but AR pathway output is attenuated, accompanied by an mCRPC-concordant transcriptomic shift and altered multicellular organization. It provides a paired discovery system for candidate genes such as EPHA3 .

title: Dual-Antigen CCHFV Vaccine Induces Neutralizing Immunity and Protection Against Lethal Challenge
abstract: Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) is a WHO-priority pathogen with high mortality and wide global distribution. A major challenge in CCHFV vaccine development is identifying antigens that induce functional cellular and humoral immunity. We previously showed that the CCHF nucleoprotein (NP) elicits protective responses in mice and non-human primates but does not induce neutralizing antibodies. We therefore systematically screened six chimeric DNA vaccines expressing different CCHF glycoproteins combined with NP. A construct comprising the ectodomain of the glycoprotein Gc and NP elicited robust antibody and T-cell responses to both antigens. The Gc-NP gene was subsequently developed as a lipid nanoparticle-formulated mRNA vaccine using a scalable manufacturing pipeline. Gc-NP mRNA-LNP induced robust antigen-specific humoral and cellular responses comparable to those elicited by the corresponding DNA vaccine, despite the substantially lower dose. Both vaccine approaches generated Gc-directed neutralizing antibody responses against CCHFV pseudovirus and protected mice against homologous Hoti and heterologous IbAr10200 strain challenge. These findings demonstrate that systematic antigen screening combined with genetic vaccine platforms can identify a potent multi-antigen CCHF vaccine candidate.

title: Engineered mRNA-packaging virus-like particles enable efficient and precise mitochondrial base editing in vitro and in vivo.
abstract: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) base editors (mtBEs) are promising tools for studying and correcting pathogenic mtDNA mutations. However, the application of mtBEs is often hindered by substantial mtDNA-wide off-target editing that accumulates with prolonged mtBE expression resulting from plasmid DNA or viral delivery. To overcome this limitation, we developed mtBE-VLPs, a virus-like-particle (VLP) platform for transiently delivering mtBEs in vitro and in vivo with minimal off-target effects. While canonical protein-packaging VLPs yielded undetectable mtDNA base editing, engineered mRNA-packaging VLPs enabled efficient but transient mtBE cargo delivery. By iteratively engineering mRNA-packaging VLP compositions, we improved mtBE-VLP-mediated base editing efficiencies from less than 1% to greater than 50% across multiple target mtDNA loci in bulk populations of treated cultured cells. To further improve the packaging and delivery of certain mtBEs, we developed a strategy to selectively reduce mtBE cargo expression in VLP producer cells but not transduced cells, which increased VLP-mediated base editing efficiencies for certain mtBEs by 7.1-fold. Compared to plasmid DNA delivery in vitro , mtBE-VLPs exhibited equivalent on-target editing but 23- to 41-fold lower mtDNA-wide off-target editing, highlighting the improved editing specificity offered by transient mtBE delivery. mtBE-VLPs efficiently installed a pathogenic mtDNA mutation in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (88% efficiency) and corrected a pathogenic mtDNA mutation in a human patient-derived cell line (41% efficiency). Additionally, a single subretinal injection of mtBE-VLPs yielded 6-20% (average 12%) mtDNA base editing in the mouse retinal pigment epithelium with minimal mtDNA-wide off-target editing. These findings establish mRNA-packaging mtBE-VLPs as promising vehicles for efficient and precise mitochondrial base editing via transient mtBE delivery.

title: SLC25A28 is a synthetic lethal vulnerability in nucleotide excision repair-deficient cancers.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Approximately 10% of bladder, upper urinary tract, and endometrial cancers harbor deleterious somatic alterations in nucleotide excision repair (NER) pathway genes. Although platinum-based chemotherapy is the standard treatment for NER-deficient tumors, its utility is limited by nephrotoxicity, motivating alternative strategies that avoid direct DNA targeting. Here, we employed a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screen to identify synthetic lethal vulnerabilities in NER-deficient cancer cells. An ERCC4 -null RT112/84 bladder cancer cell line was generated and validated by Sanger sequencing and Western blotting, and functional NER deficiency was confirmed using a host cell reactivation assay. Parallel screens in ERCC4 -deficient and isogenic wild-type cells. nominated SLC25A28 as the top-ranked synthetic lethal candidate in ERCC4 -deficient cells, an interaction further supported by DepMap dependency. Clonogenic assays confirmed that loss of SLC25A28 selectively impaired cell viability in cells deficient for ERCC2 , ERCC3 , ERCC4 , or ERCC5 and inducible knockout selectively suppressed ERCC4 -deficient xenograft growth in-viv o. Mechanistically, RNA sequencing followed by gene set enrichment analysis revealed enrichment of oxidative stress-related pathways, including cellular responses to reactive oxygen species (ROS) and DNA damage signatures, upon SLC25A28 loss. These transcriptional changes are consistent with increased oxidative stress and DNA damage, placing heightened demand on NER-mediated repair. Direct measurement confirmed increased intracellular ROS. Collectively, our nominates SLC25A28 as a previously unrecognized synthetic lethal vulnerability in NER-deficient cancers and implicate mitochondrial iron homeostasis as a candidate metabolic dependency that may be targeted independently of platinum-based chemotherapy.
SIGNIFICANCE: This study identifies SLC25A28 as a synthetic lethal vulnerability in nucleotide excision repair-deficient cancers, linking mitochondrial iron homeostasis and oxidative stress to selective DNA damage intolerance and therapeutic opportunity.

title: The Spliceosome Scaffold Component BCAS2 Promotes Pancreatic Cancer Progression through Weak 5' Splice Site-Dependent Splicing Regulation.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the deadliest malignancies. Dysregulated RNA splicing has emerged as a critical mechanism contributing to PDAC progression. However, whether structural components of the spliceosome regulate oncogenic alternative splicing was not known. Here, we identify the nineteen complex (NTC) component BCAS2/SPF27 as a critical regulator of PDAC progression. Elevated expression of BCAS2 in PDAC is associated with poor patient outcomes. Transcriptomic analyses revealed that BCAS2 specifically regulates alternative exons with weak splice sites. In particular, BCAS2 promotes SOS1 exon 21 inclusion and consequently RAC-signaling activation. Furthermore, splice-switching antisense oligonucleotide (ASO)-mediated skipping of SOS1 exon 21 suppressed PDAC proliferation and migration. Our findings uncover a role of BCAS2 in the regulation of weak splice-site usage and identify the BCAS2-SOS1-RAC signaling axis as a potential therapeutic vulnerability in pancreatic cancer.

title: A transient third metal ion shapes the catalytic cycle of a group I intron ribozyme.
abstract: The self-splicing group I intron ribozyme from Tetrahymena thermophillia (THr) is a prototypical example of how RNA overcomes its limited chemical repertoire to form complex, negatively charged junctions and catalyze chemical reactions. Despite over 30 years of bio-chemical and structural characterization, questions still remain regarding the requirements for THr catalysis that may inform structure based drug design against group I introns, as well as the use of THr as an RNA editing tool. Recent cryo-EM structures have provided an unprecedented window into the first and second steps of splicing, enabling detailed mechanistic investigation at the atomistic level. In this work, we leverage solvation theory, molecular dynamics, alchemical free energy simulations, and machine learning accelerated QM/MM to probe outstanding questions related to 1) the role of a possible third Mg 2+ binding in the active site, 2) differences in catalytic requirements between G exo cofactors and between the first and second steps of splicing, 3) the potential role of an acid or base, and 4) restrictions on the identity of the 5 ' exon splice site nucleotide, U(-1). We propose that a transient, cofactor dependent, interaction with a third metal participates in the first step, while a higher affinity interaction with this third ion is required in the second step. We also propose that the presence of a phosphate on the G exo in the first step, and analogously the G ω in the second step, forms a metal ion binding site not present when guanosine is bound. Finally, we propose and computationally test design modifications of G22 (isofunctional substitutions of 2,6-diaminopurine that tune the p K a at the N1 position) that we predict will enable the accommodation of C(-1) in a crucial wobble-like pair at physiological pH. This design would provide a potential strategy for expanding the sequence space accessible to programmable trans-splicing ribozymes in RNA editing applications.

title: One Scaffold, Many Targets: Fully Modified RNA Nanostructures for Multi-Gene Silencing Beyond the Liver.
abstract: Therapeutic siRNAs are a major clinical modality for hepatic gene silencing, but efficient extrahepatic delivery and multi-gene modulation remain significant barriers. Nucleic acid nanotechnology offers programmable assembly, but conventional structures suffer from enzymatic instability in vivo . Here we report fully chemically modified RNA nanostructures (FMRNs)-a vehicle-free platform entirely composed of stabilized therapeutic nucleic acids that integrate structural precision with metabolic durability. Following systemic administration, FMRNs exhibit enhanced pharmacokinetics and extrahepatic accumulation, with in vivo behavior influenced greatly by hydrodynamic size rather than molecular weight. Using triangular and square geometries, we demonstrate programmable control over siRNA stoichiometry to achieve sustained, simultaneous silencing of up to four genes from a single entity. Nanostructure assembly alone drives productive delivery, especially to heart and muscle, matching lipophilic conjugation. Furthermore, cerebrospinal fluid administration reveals that larger FMRNs improve central nervous system distribution and retention revealing physicochemical parameters that impact brain exposure. FMRNs establish a modular and effective platform combining improved pharmacokinetics, extrahepatic delivery, and multi-gene silencing for complex diseases.

title: Rational Design of 5' UTRs for Optimized mRNA Expression and Cost-Effective, Rapid Analysis of Capped mRNA
abstract: In vitro-transcribed (IVT) messenger RNA (mRNA) therapeutics require rigorous quality control of 5' capping efficiency and 3' poly(A) tail length, both of which constitute critical quality attributes (CQAs). Current analytical workflows for these CQAs rely on hybridization with nucleic acid probes and biotin-based affinity purification, which constrain throughput and increase per-assay cost. Here, we report a rationally designed 5' untranslated region (5' UTR) that sustains high translational efficiency while enabling probe-free, one-step purification for rapid quantification of capping efficiency and poly(A) tail length distribution. This approach exploits a strategically engineered 5' UTR incorporating a purine-only RNase A-resistant fragment terminating at a single pyrimidine cleavage site, together with a translation-enhancing element comprising an N6-methyladenosine (m6A) deposition motif and an 18S rRNA complementarity sequence. This dual-function design accommodates GA-rich sequence segments without compromising mRNA translational output. Compared with conventional probe- and biotin-dependent workflows, the present method substantially reduces cost and processing time and is compatible with simultaneous detection of segmented AmGn poly(A) tail variants. This integrated platform provides a simplified, probe-free and construct-universal for high-throughput in-process control (IPC) of mRNA therapeutics.

title: Neonatal Delivery of Exon Skipping Therapeutics Maximizes Brain Dystrophin Rescue in the Mdx52 Mouse Model of Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy
abstract: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is caused by mutations in the DMD gene, resulting in the loss of dystrophin expression. Beyond progressive muscle degeneration, nearly half of patients exhibit cognitive and behavioral impairments, highlighting the need for effective central nervous system (CNS) therapies. In this study, we investigated whether neonatal delivery could maximize brain dystrophin rescue in mdx52 mice using exon 51 skipping strategies. We compared systemic and intracerebroventricular (ICV) delivery of an antisense oligonucleotide (ASO-51) and an AAV9-mediated U7snRNA approach (scAAV9-U7-Ex51), administered neonatally. Neonatal intravenous ASO-51 induced widespread but transient exon skipping, resulting in limited brain dystrophin restoration. ICV administration markedly increased CNS exon skipping but did not overcome the limited persistence of ASO, leading to progressive loss of exon skipping and dystrophin rescue. In contrast, neonatal ICV delivery of scAAV9-U7-Ex51 achieved robust, widespread, and sustained exon 51 skipping throughout the brain, including the hippocampus, cortex, and cerebellum, resulting in 20-50% restoration of Dp427 expression. These findings demonstrate that early CNS-directed delivery enhances brain dystrophin restoration and establish AAV-U7-mediated exon skipping as a promising strategy for addressing CNS comorbidities in DMD.

title: Apical-Out Ileal Organoids: A Versatile Platform for Probing Gut-Nanomaterial Interactions
abstract: The human ileal epithelium forms a critical interface governing interactions with luminal microorganisms and nanomaterials, yet physiologically relevant in vitro models with accessible apical surfaces remain limited. Here, human apical-out ileoids derived from healthy ileal biopsies are established as a platform that recapitulates the architecture and complexity of the native ileal epithelium. Assessment of donor- and passage-dependent variability identifies a representative ileoid line and a robust culture window. Integrated proteomic, imaging, ultrastructural, and functional analyses demonstrate preservation of key epithelial features, including brush-border organization, barrier integrity, absorptive capacity, and multiple endocytic pathways. Intact ileoids internalize nanoparticles of distinct surface charge, including empty lipid nanoparticles compositionally matched to approved mRNA vaccine formulations, establishing that uptake can be quantified across an unperturbed apical surface. This uptake is restrained by a retained mucin-rich glycocalyx. Cleavage of surface-attached mucins selectively enhances uptake of negatively charged nanoparticles, leaving near-neutral and positively charged nanoparticles unchanged, and increasing entry of Salmonella bacteria. These findings reveal the glycocalyx as a charge-selective regulator of epithelial uptake. In conclusion, our study provides a foundation for nanoparticle-epithelium investigations using human apical-out ileoids, and a versatile, translationally relevant platform for nanomedicine delivery, host-microbe interactions, and epithelial transport.

title: PINPOINT enables non-destructive nanoscopic quality control of individual lipid nanoparticles and their mRNA cargo
abstract: Quality control of lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) is central to development of mRNA therapeutics, yet ensemble measurements obscure critical heterogeneity in particle morphology and mRNA cargo loading. Here we introduce PINPOINT (Profiling Individual Nanoparticles with Precise Observation of INternalized Therapeutics), a single-particle nanoscopy platform for non-destructive, multiparametric profiling of preformulated LNP samples. Super-resolution imaging with Nile Red resolves size and morphology, while an optimized permeabilization strategy provides selective access to encapsulated mRNA without compromising LNP integrity. Single-particle fluorescence measurements, including RiboGreen and sequence-specific probes, enable quantification and validation of mRNA loading and identity. Comparative analyses of bare and encapsulated mRNA reveal kinetic and structural features, exposing heterogeneity masked by bulk assays. By integrating structural and molecular readouts at the single-particle level, PINPOINT establishes a quantitative framework for assessing of LNP composition and payload distribution, offering actionable insights for improving batch consistency and guiding the rational design of next-generation mRNA delivery systems.

title: Progranulin deficiency promotes neuroinflammation through cathepsin B-mediated activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome
abstract: Haploinsufficiency of progranulin (resulting from mutations in the GRN gene) is a major genetic cause of frontotemporal dementia (FTD), which is characterized by profound changes in personality and behavior, progressive impairments in executive function, speech, language and/or movement, TDP-43 pathology, lysosomal dysfunction, and neuroinflammation. Studies in progranulin-deficient mouse models have demonstrated the critical role of neuroinflammation in disease pathogenesis, as deletion of NF-kB or complement factors prevents FTD-associated behavioral deficits. While progranulin is known to be anti-inflammatory, the precise molecular mechanism by which its deficiency triggers inflammatory cascades remain unclear. Here, we investigate the involvement of the NLRP3 inflammasome in progranulin-deficient models, including mice, human microglial cells, and patient fibroblasts. In Grn mice, we found increased levels of several inflammasome-related proteins, including procaspase-1 and cleaved IL-1{beta}. Similarly, GRN knockout (KO) microglia cells showed significant increases in levels of procaspase-1, NLRP3, and cleaved IL-1{beta}. Moreover, KO cells had increased NLRP3 oligomerization, suggesting that progranulin negatively regulates inflammasome assembly. We also investigated the potential link between lysosomal dysfunction and NLRP3 inflammasome activation in progranulin deficiency. We found that pharmacological inhibition of cathepsin B reduced NLRP3 inflammasome oligomerization as well as inflammatory cytokine expression in GRN KO cells. Additionally, siRNA knockdown of cathepsin B reduced levels of procaspase-1 and cleaved IL-1{beta} in GRN KO cells. Finally, we found that heterozygous GRN fibroblasts exhibited similar increases in procaspase-1 and cleaved IL-1{beta} levels, and these increases were corrected by treatment with an antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) that increase progranulin protein levels. Overall, our results demonstrate that progranulin deficiency promotes NLRP3 inflammasome assembly and activity through cathepsin B-mediated signaling, thereby establishing a mechanistic link between lysosomal dysfunction and increased inflammation. The ability of the GRN-targeting ASO to correct NLRP3-mediated inflammation highlights a promising therapeutic strategy for FTD-GRN and inflammation in other neurodegenerative disorders linked to progranulin deficiency.

title: An Injectable Antisense Oligonucleotide (ASO) Approach to Treat Obesity in Preclinical Models
abstract: Obesity leads to metabolic dysregulation and thus drives complications including type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, steatotic liver disease and some cancers. Obesity is primarily driven by lifestyle factors, which impacts individuals differently depending on their genetic susceptibility. Studies on this genetic risk have provided major insights into gene networks that modulate obesity development, including incretins and their regulatory circuits. Indeed, incretin-based therapeutics (i.e. GLP1 RA) have proven to be enormously successful in promoting weight loss, but do so with several ongoing challenges including significant weight rebound upon cessation, loss of lean mass, and side effects that reduce therapeutic longevity. Thus, ongoing research is necessary to identify additional interventions that overcome or minimise these concerns. To this end, in our previous work we have identified a novel lipid regulatory protein with potential to influence lipid storage. In the current study, we use antisense oligonucleotides (ASO) to silence this protein in mouse models of diet induced obesity, and demonstrate that once weekly IP injections of ASO prevents the development of obesity, and defends against the progression of existing obesity. This is shown to be effective in multiple mouse strains fed different diets over various time frames, with gene targeting ASOs leading to reductions in fat mass, no change in lean mass, along with improvements in whole body glucose tolerance and steatotic liver disease. Additional studies demonstrate that this phenotype is likely driven by effects in adipose tissue, but not liver, and is not linked to activation of the Type 1 Interferon response, a previously implicated off target effect of ASO administration. Thus, these studies demonstrate that our injectable ASO approach in mice can successfully treat obesity in the absence of major change in lean mass, thus positioning this intervention as a therapeutic program that works alternatively to, or in conjunction with current weight loss medicines.

title: Chimeric archaeal BHB-human pre-tRNA scaffold HARBOR system enables versatile production of functional circular RNA modalities
abstract: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) exhibit superior intrinsic stability and lower immunogenicity compared with linear RNAs, rendering them promising modalities for biomedical and biotechnological applications. Here, we establish the HARBOR (Human-Archaeal RNA Backbone for Overexpression of circular RNA) system, an engineered endogenous circRNA expression platform integrating a human precursor transfer RNA (pre-tRNA) scaffold with an archaeal Bulge-Helix-Bulge (BHB) motif. HARBOR repurposes the endogenous tRNA splicing machinery to generate chimeric pre-tRNA intermediates, which are rapidly degraded following processing, while producing circRNAs ranging from hundreds of nucleotides to 8 knt in cells and in vivo. Notably, it enables robust production of large-sized circRNAs with yields nearly 80-fold than the intronic complementary sequence-mediated back-splicing (3D5) system and can drive protein expression from translatable circRNAs at an efficiency close to 20-fold than the Tornado system. Such prominent properties support diverse applications of HARBOR, including producing therapeutic aptamers targeting PKR-associated neuroinflammation and pathological TDP-43 condensation, as well as protein-coding circRNAs encoding adenine base editors for genome editing and MYOD1 for fibroblast-to-myocyte trans-differentiation. Collectively, HARBOR represents a versatile, scalable, and user-friendly platform that unifies circRNA-based aptamer and protein expression applications, advancing circRNA-enabled engineering and biomedical applications.

title: A Humanized Mouse Model of DRPLA Recapitulates Epilepsy and Demonstrates Antisense Oligonucleotide-Mediated Disease Modification
abstract: Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy (DRPLA) is an ultra-rare progressive myoclonus epilepsy caused by a glutamine-coding CAG repeat expansion in atrophin-1 (ATN1). Mutant ATN1 (mATN1) expression results in symptoms that inversely correlate to CAG-expansion size: young-onset cases have the most CAG repeats and developmental delay, high-frequency treatment-resistant seizures, and early mortality. We sought to characterize the seizure susceptibility of a fully humanized ATN1 mouse expressing human mATN1 with 112 CAG repeats to then assess therapeutic antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) intervention on seizure-related outcomes. Atn1Q112/+ or wild-type (WT) mice were treated with investigational ASO targeting human, CAG-expanded, ATN1 or saline (P2 and then again at 4 weeks-old) before acute seizure testing, ataxia profiling, and chronic in vivo video-EEG recording for spontaneous seizures up to 8 weeks-old. Saline-treated Atn1Q112/+ mice were more seizure prone with early death. However, ASO administration to Atn1Q112/+ mice normalized seizure threshold, decreased ataxia, and protected against early death. Atn1Q112/+ mice exhibited spontaneous behavioral seizures recorded over 2 weeks, which were absent in ASO-treated Atn1Q112/+ and WT mice, with a specific mATN1 expression-driven decrease in delta and theta EEG frequencies. Atn1Q112/+ mice are highly seizure prone, validating this model for DRPLA epilepsy. ATN1 represents a novel epilepsy-related risk factor for therapeutic investigation.

title: Cowpea Chlorotic Mottle Virus virus-like particles as DNA or RNA delivery vehicle to fish cells
abstract: Cowpea Chlorotic Mottle Virus (CCMV) is an icosahedral plant virus composed of 180 monomeric units of the capsid protein. Virions encapsulate the viral RNA genome, which can be removed from the virion by changing pH conditions, after which the capsid proteins can be reversibly assembled to form empty CCMV virus-like particles (VLPs), or VLPs that have encapsulated either heterologous DNA or RNA. Earlier research has shown that CCMV VLPs are suitable as delivery vehicles for heterologous DNA/RNA molecules into mammalian cells, leading to subsequent expression of their encoded genes. In this study, we evaluated the potential of CCMV VLPs to encapsulate nucleic acids and transfer them to fish cells in vitro, and to zebrafish larvae and juveniles in vivo. VLPs containing pVax-GFP plasmid (3690 bp) were stable for up to 5 weeks in buffer at pH 7.2 and pH 5, whereas VLPs containing GFP-mRNA (1168 nt) were stable for up to 3 weeks, but only when stored in a buffer at pH 4.5. When administered directly to the culture medium, VLPs were readily taken up by fish as well as mammalian cell lines but could not unpack and transfer nucleic acids to the cells. VLPs delivered by transfection however, could transfer nucleic acids to the cells, leading to reporter gene expression. When VLPs were administered directly to the culture medium along with the cell-penetrating peptide dfTAT, only VLPs containing pVax-GFP in pH 7.2 buffer were able to transfer DNA to mammalian but not fish cells. In vivo however, upon intramuscular injection, the same VLPs were able to transfer plasmid DNA to myocytes of zebrafish larvae and juveniles as efficiently as when injecting naked plasmid DNA. Altogether, these findings provide the foundation for future studies on the use of CCMV VLPs as delivery vehicles for DNA or RNA to fish cells.

title: VO659, a CAG repeat-targeting antisense oligonucleotide, lowers multiple neurotoxic mutant huntingtin proteins in Huntington's disease
abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is caused by a CAG repeat expansion in the huntingtin (HTT) gene, encoding an elongated polyglutamine stretch in the corresponding mutant HTT (mHTT) protein. HD pathogenesis is driven by multiple neurotoxic mHTT protein species, including HTT1a and repeat-associated non-AUG translation (RAN) proteins, which increase in expression as mutant CAG repeats lengthen due to somatic expansion. VO659 is an investigational CAG repeat-targeting antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) that lowers mHTT protein levels by blocking translation. Here, we show that VO659 allele-preferentially lowers levels of multiple neurotoxic mHTT protein species in a CAG repeat length-dependent manner, relatively sparing wild-type HTT, while becoming more efficacious as somatic expansion occurs. VO659 reduced HTT1a mRNA levels in HD fibroblasts with an ultra-long CAG repeat, blocked the translation of HTT1a and polyalanine-containing RAN proteins derived from HTT exon 1 overexpression constructs, and displayed a long tissue half-life in mouse brain, supporting an infrequent dosing regimen. A first-in-human, open-label phase 1/2a clinical trial (NCT05822908) is currently ongoing in HD patients. VO659's unique CAG repeat-dependent and allele-preferential mechanism of action holds promise for its therapeutic effect in HD patients by targeting multiple core neurotoxic proteins derived from (somatically) expanded mHTT CAG repeats, while sparing wild-type HTT expression.

title: Deletion of LRP1 in Smooth Muscle Cells Induces Infrarenal Aortic Aneurysms in Mice
abstract: Background: Low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 1 (LRP1) in smooth muscle cells (SMCs) is essential for maintaining aortic wall integrity. This study investigated whether deletion of LRP1 in SMCs induces region-specific aortic pathology and evaluated a potential therapeutic strategy. Methods: Lrp1-floxed mice were bred with Sm22-Cre+/0 mice to generate mice with SMC-LRP1 deletion (SMC-LRP1-/-) and wild-type littermates (SMC-LRP1+/+). Micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) was used to visualize the aorta, and aortic tissue sections were characterized histologically. To evaluate a potential therapeutic strategy, antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) targeting hepatocyte-derived angiotensinogen (AGT) were administered to inhibit AGT synthesis. Results: Immunostaining and Western blotting confirmed LRP1 deletion in aortic SMCs. At 40 weeks of age, micro-CT revealed marked increases in aortic width and volume. Although dilatation occurred throughout the aorta, the infrarenal region exhibited the greatest expansion in both male and female SMC-LRP1-/- mice compared with SMC-LRP1+/+ littermates; subsequent analyses therefore focused on this region. LRP1 deletion in SMCs caused pronounced SMC loss and increased collagen deposition in the infrarenal aorta. Inhibition of hepatocyte-derived AGT with ASO attenuated infrarenal aortic dilatation and preserved aortic wall integrity in both male and female mice. Conclusions: Deletion of LRP1 in SMCs causes progressive aortic dilatation that includes the infrarenal aorta. Pharmacologic inhibition of hepatocyte-derived AGT attenuates infrarenal aortic dilatation.

title: Fibronectin silencing remodels the fibrotic bone marrow niche
abstract: Bone marrow (BM) fibrosis is a defining feature of Primary Myelofibrosis, yet the extracellular matrix (ECM) that sustains the fibrotic niche remains largely untargeted therapeutically. Fibronectin (FN), a key organizer of ECM architecture and growth factor signaling, accumulates in the fibrotic BM niche and correlates with disease severity. Here, we investigated whether systemic FN depletion can disrupt pathological remodeling of the BM niche. We developed a chemically modified antisense oligonucleotide targeting FN1 (FN ASO), which reduced FN expression and assembly and impaired transforming growth factor-{beta}1 (TGF-{beta}1)-induced activation of mesenchymal stromal cells. Systemic FN ASO administration efficiently depleted circulating and BM FN in mice and was well tolerated during short-term treatment. In two complementary models of BM fibrosis, FN silencing reduced FN matrix organization, stromal activation, active TGF{beta}-1, reticulin, and collagen deposition. In Jak2V617F-driven disease, transcriptomic profiling further revealed attenuation of ECM, TGF-{beta}1, and mesenchymal remodeling programs, accompanied by changes in inflammatory signaling. Collectively, these findings identify FN as an active organizer of the fibrotic BM niche and show that its systemic silencing uncouple ECM organization from profibrotic stromal signaling, providing rationale for targeting FN in myelofibrosis with broader therapeutic relevance to fibrosis-driven diseases.

title: Lipid nanoparticle shape and morphology determine the magnitude and duration of mRNA transfection
abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNP) are widely used for nucleic acid delivery, with current optimization efforts mainly focusing on refining formulation features, enabling extrahepatic targeting, and improving therapeutic efficacy. Particle shape and internal architecture are variables often overlooked in LNP design, although they critically influence particle stability, biodistribution, cellular uptake, and transfection. Here, we investigate how formulation and process parameters impact LNP shape, morphology, and internal structure, and how these structural features, in turn, influence mRNA loading, cell uptake, and expression. We demonstrate that modulation of lipid composition by increasing DSPC content drives a transition from compact spherical to vesicular non-spherical morphologies, with altered RNA loading at the single-particle level. While non-spherical LNP exhibited higher cellular uptake than spherical LNP, it was identified that this increase was relatively modest compared with the substantially higher and sustained protein expression for non-spherical structures. This suggests that increased uptake alone cannot explain the enhanced transfection performance. The trend was conserved across LNP formulations comprising clinically relevant ionizable lipids SM-102, ALC-0315 and DLin-MC3-DMA. Taken together, these findings establish LNP shape and internal morphology as functionally relevant design variables that should be considered in the design of next-generation LNP with improved mRNA delivery and expression.

title: Human neutrophils release extracellular RNA that modulates Aspergillus fumigatus gene expression across kingdoms.
abstract: Extracellular RNAs (exRNAs) are emerging as potent bidirectional interkingdom effectors of host-pathogen interactions, particularly in plant and insect systems. Here, using small RNA-sequencing and genetic manipulation, we provide evidence consistent with a function of the human neutrophil exRNA-ome in modulating gene expression across kingdoms in the fungal pathogen Aspergillus fumigatus. The neutrophil extracellular space contains a diverse repertoire of RNA, which was corroborated using a droplet-digital stem-loop RT-PCR protocol to measure differential abundance of several tRNA-derived RNAs between two extracellular fractions. A closer inspection of the extracellular miRNA pool revealed enrichment of antimicrobial Let-7 family sRNAs and immunomodulatory miR-223, among others. Secretion of these sRNAs was largely impervious to infection status, suggesting that neutrophils produce and maintain an antimicrobial exRNA environment against A. fumigatus that requires further targeting. Cross-kingdom miRNA target prediction and exRNA delivery experiments revealed that putative fungal targets are modulated independently of the fungal argonaute proteins and in a donor-dependent manner. Although heterogeneous, for donors that exhibited a silencing effect, mutated target sequences in the fungus did reverse silencing. We hypothesize that the exRNA landscape produced by neutrophils contributes to their multifaceted role in antifungal defense.

title: StoichRNA: A Scalable Framework to Map and Optimize Combinatorial RNA Systems at Single-Cell Resolution
abstract: RNA-based genetic cargos have emerged as versatile tools in both fundamental research and translational medicine, with growing applications in regenerative medicine, gene therapy, cell therapy, and vaccination. As the field advances beyond single-RNA delivery, coordinated engineering of multiple RNA species is enabling increasingly sophisticated and combinatorial biological functions. However, this shift raises a fundamental challenge: what combination and stoichiometry of RNA species should be delivered together to achieve a desired cellular function? As the number of RNA components increases, the design space expands combinatorially, making conventional optimization strategies labor-intensive and poorly scalable. Here, we introduce StoichRNA, a framework for scalable exploration of multi-RNA stoichiometry in a single experiment. Individual RNA species are delivered independently, each coupled to a distinct fluorescent marker that reports its intracellular abundance. Because uptake is stochastic, each cell acquires a unique combination and copy number of RNA components. Across a sufficiently large population, cells collectively sample a broad stoichiometric landscape, allowing single-cell readouts such as flow cytometry to quantitatively map system output as a function of intracellular RNA composition. We first establish the conceptual validity of this approach by showing that StoichRNA-derived single-cell data can recover and predict the behavior of fixed-ratio RNA formulations. We then apply this framework to representative RNA circuits, demonstrating that StoichRNA can reveal design principles and identify improved stoichiometries that would be difficult to uncover through conventional workflows. Finally, we extend StoichRNA optimization to translationally relevant settings, including control of cell-state engineering in human induced pluripotent stem cells and tuning of RNA-based logic circuits for precision medicine applications. Together, these results establish StoichRNA as a generalizable strategy for engineering combinatorial RNA systems and provide a scalable solution to a central bottleneck in RNA circuit design.

title: CAI-Vax: Computational Design of Personalized mRNA Cancer Vaccine Constructs After Antigen Selection
abstract: CAI-Vax (Cancer Antigen Individualized Vaccine Design) arranges selected antigens and generates synonymous coding sequences for personalized mRNA vaccine constructs. We evaluated 357 vaccine-candidate peptides from 31 patients across four published cohorts. At the primary cumulative MHCflurry percentile-rank threshold of [≤]2%, HLA-aware search reduced predicted junction-spanning peptide-allele binder occurrences by 3.49 per junction relative to amino-acid-pattern optimization (paired Hodges-Lehmann estimate; nominal 95% interval 2.75-4.48; Holm-adjusted P = 7.45 x 10-). All 31 primary paired differences and the estimated effects in all 16 threshold-by-normalization settings favored HLA-aware search within the MHCflurry model used for optimization. Among 25 patients with an exact solution for the additive search objective, single-start greedy search found the minimum in 5 patients and the best individual heuristic in 16. Selecting each patients best result across all tested heuristics increased this to 19. MHCflurry and NetMHCpan EL identified identical tied best-plan sets in 6 of 31 patients after rescoring six frozen plans per patient. In a retrospective internal analysis, repeat-aware synonymous encoding reduced maximum 10-mer multiplicity in every patient, with mean codon-use-preference losses of 0.0041-0.0055 across cohorts; however, it performed worse than matched random encoding for 6-mers. These findings demonstrate that HLA-guided construct optimization can reduce predicted junctional binding within the optimization model, although the preferred antigen arrangement depends on the prediction model used. Experimental studies are needed to determine the biological and manufacturing relevance of these computational differences.

title: Dysregulation of miR-103a-3p/AGFG1 axis links endocytic trafficking dysfunction to ER stress in Parkinson's disease
abstract: Background: Parkinson's disease is defined by progressive dopaminergic neurodegeneration and -synuclein pathology. Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and clathrin-mediated endocytosis dysfunction are implicated in disease pathogenesis, but the molecular mechanisms connecting these processes remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate a miR-103a-3p/AGFG1 axis as a regulator link between endocytic trafficking and ER stress in Parkinson's disease. Methods: MiR-103a-3p and AGFG1 were examined in plasma and postmortem substantia nigra from patients with Parkinson's disease and controls. Gain- and loss-of-function studies, target validation and live-cell imaging were used to define the role of the miR-103a-3p/AGFG1 axis in ER stress and endocytic trafficking. The pathway was further investigated in SNCA A53T and LRRK2 G2019S hiPSC-derived neurons. Therapeutic targeting of AGFG1 was evaluated using antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) in vitro and in a 6-hydroxydopamine mouse model. Results: MiR-103a-3p was significantly reduced in Parkinson's disease plasma and substantia nigra, whereas AGFG1 was increased in nigral tissue. MiR-103a-3p directly repressed AGFG1 and attenuated thapsigargin-induced ER stress, while miR-103a-3p inhibition or AGFG1 overexpression exacerbated stress signalling. AGFG1 knockdown reversed the effects of miR-103a-3p inhibition, establishing AGFG1 as a functional downstream effector. Mechanistically, AGFG1 associated and co-trafficked with clathrin-positive vesicles, whereas ER stress progressively disrupted AGFG1-clathrin vesicle dynamics, revealing an association between endocytic trafficking and stress signalling. In genetic Parkinson's disease models, SNCA A53T and LRRK2 G2019S neurons showed mutation-dependent differences in AGFG1 expression and stress regulation. eIF2 phosphorylation increased in both SNCA A53T and LRRK2 G2019S neurons, whereas AGFG1 and GADD34 upregulation was selective to SNCA A53T neurons. Importantly, ASO-mediated AGFG1 suppression attenuated ER stress in vitro and preserved nigral dopaminergic neurons with improved motor performance in vivo. Conclusion: Our findings identify the miR-103a-3p/AGFG1 axis as a previously unrecognised molecular link between endocytic trafficking dysfunction and ER stress in Parkinson's disease, and support AGFG1 as a mechanistically potential therapeutic target.

title: The human-specific lncRNA HD-LINC drives lipid droplet-associated neurodegeneration in Huntington's disease
abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is characterized by degeneration of striatal medium spiny neurons (MSNs), yet the human-specific regulatory mechanisms that contribute to neuronal vulnerability remain poorly understood. Here, we identify HD-LINC (LINC01139), a human-specific long intergenic noncoding RNA selectively induced in symptomatic HD patient-derived MSNs (HD-MSNs) and human HD caudate. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis in HD-MSNs revealed that HD-LINC was enriched in a symptomatic HD neuronal state associated with lipid metabolic and protein clearance regulation, while not observed in non-degenerative reprogrammed MSNs derived from pre-manifest HD individuals. Reducing HD-LINC attenuated mutant HTT aggregation, dystrophic neurites, DNA damage, and neuronal death, whereas HD-LINC overexpression exacerbated these phenotypes. Transcriptomic and lipidomic analyses further implicated HD-LINC in neuronal lipid regulation. We found that HD-MSNs exhibited aberrant accumulation of enlarged, low-mobility lipid droplets (LDs) within neurites, a previously unrecognized phenotype in patient-derived neurons. Critically, increased lipid peroxidation was observed within LD-enriched dystrophic neurites in HD-MSNs. HD-LINC knockdown cleared neuritic LD accumulation, restored soma-enriched LD distribution, and reduced lipid peroxidation. Finally, we developed antisense oligonucleotides that effectively reduced HD-LINC and reversed HD-LINC-associated phenotypes, nominating HD-LINC lowering as a potential therapeutic strategy in HD. These results identify HD-LINC as a human-specific regulator of neuronal LD spatial organization, lipid peroxidation, and neuronal degeneration in HD. They further reveal dysregulated neuritic LD accumulation driven by HD-LINC, and highlight lincRNA-mediated lipid dysregulation as a significant contributor to neuronal vulnerability to degeneration.

title: Decoy and antisense RNA oligonucleotides targeting the EGFR exon 3 splice site suppress proliferation of A172 glioblastoma cells
abstract: Short RNA oligonucleotides directed at the 3' splice site region of EGFR exon 3 reduced the proliferation of A172 glioblastoma cells, while the same oligonucleotides had no detectable effect on A549 lung adenocarcinoma cells. Glioblastoma carries EGFR amplification in roughly a third of IDH-wildtype cases, and the A172 line harbours a tandem duplication in the EGFR tyrosine kinase domain. Because exon definition in human genes depends on RNA-binding proteins that engage exonic sequence near splice sites, we used the SpliceAid database to identify candidate RNA-binding proteins at EGFR exons 2 and 3. Y-box binding protein 1 (YB-1, encoded by YBX1), reported to drive glioblastoma growth through its RNA-binding function, scored highly immediately adjacent to the exon 3 3' splice site. We designed four 2'-modified RNA oligonucleotides carrying a nuclear localisation signal: two antisense oligonucleotides against the exon 3 region (asRNA1, spanning the splice site; asRNA2, downstream of it), a decoy complementary to the asRNA2 target (dRNA2), and a decoy carrying the YB-1 consensus binding sequence (dYB-1). In A172 cells, all four reduced EGFR protein in a single Western blot experiment, and asRNA1, asRNA2 and dRNA2 reduced proliferation relative to scrambled RNA at days 1 to 3; dYB-1 produced a comparable reduction at day 3. None of these effects was seen in A549 cells. YB-1 protein level and subcellular distribution were unchanged by the oligonucleotides, arguing against an indirect route through altered YB-1 abundance. These observations are preliminary. Every experiment reported here was performed once: the proliferation data come from single plates with three wells per group, analysed by Dunnett's test against the scrambled-RNA control, and the Western blot, RT-PCR and immunocytochemistry panels are single runs presented as representative observations. Direct binding of YB-1 to the targeted EGFR sequence has not been demonstrated. We post this work as a preprint so that the design strategy and the initial observations are available while these questions remain open.

title: A bivalent Lassa virus mRNA vaccine protects guinea pigs from lethal infection with Lassa virus
abstract: Lassa virus (LASV), the causative agent of the life-threatening febrile disease, Lassa fever, remains a major public health concern in West Africa, where hundreds of thousands of infections occur annually. However, no licensed vaccine is currently available, highlighting the urgent need for effective preventive measures. We previously demonstrated that an mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccine expressing LASV glycoprotein precursor (GPC; LASgpc-mRNA-LNP) conferred protection against lethal infection with a recombinant lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus expressing LASV GPC in mice. In this study, we extended our previous work with the aim of evaluating the efficacy of an mRNA-LNP vaccine expressing LASV nucleoprotein (NP; LASnp-mRNA-LNP) and a bivalent vaccine combining LASgpc-mRNA-LNP and LASnp-mRNA-LNP. Using a lethal CBA/N mouse model of infection with ML29, an LASV live-attenuated vaccine candidate encoding LASV GPC and NP, we found that LASgpc-mRNA-LNP and LASnp-mRNA-LNP each conferred protection in the absence of detectable neutralizing antibody responses. We identified LASV GPC- and NP-derived CD4 and CD8 T-cell epitope peptides in CBA/N mice and demonstrated that vaccination induced robust antigen-specific T-cell responses. Importantly, the bivalent vaccine provided complete protection against lethal challenge with doses at which monovalent vaccines failed to protect all mice, suggesting a potential dose-sparing benefit of the bivalent formulation. Furthermore, the bivalent vaccine fully protected guinea pigs against lethal challenge with authentic LASV. Together, these findings establish LASV NP, in addition to GPC, as a protective antigen in the mRNA vaccine platform and provide a rationale for developing bivalent mRNA-LNP vaccines to improve protection against Lassa fever.

title: Structural basis for repeat-associated non-AUG translation initiation on C9orf72 mRNA
abstract: A GGGGCC (G4C2) hexanucleotide repeat expansion in the first intron of C9orf72 is the most common monogenic cause of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) and Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD). This element serves as a template for repeat-associated non-AUG (RAN) translation, which generates neurotoxic dipeptide repeat (DPR) proteins that aggregate in patient brains and contribute to neurodegeneration in model systems. To understand the mechanisms underlying RAN translation initiation, we used cryo-electron microscopy to determine the structure of an in vitro assembled human late-stage C9orf72 translation initiation complex at 3.2 A resolution and a near-native complex purified from human cell lysate at 3.5 A resolution. RAN translation on C9orf72 mRNA initiates predominantly at a near-cognate CUG codon that is located 24 nucleotides upstream of the G4C2 repeat and is flanked by a strong endogenous Kozak sequence. The structures further reveal a direct interaction between the G4C2 repeat and 18S ribosomal RNA expansion segment 9 (ES9S) on the 40S small ribosomal subunit through a kissing-loop interaction. Preventing this RNA-RNA interaction using complementary antisense oligonucleotides significantly reduces RAN translation in vitro and in patient-derived iNeurons, indicating that this structural interaction is functionally important. These findings provide mechanistic insights into RAN translation initiation and highlight a novel potential therapeutic approach to mitigate toxic DPR production in C9orf72-associated neurodegenerative disease.

title: Population-scale genome-wide prioritization of targets for allele-specific antisense oligonucleotide therapy design
abstract: Background: Allele-specific antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) are increasingly used to selectively suppress transcripts containing pathogenic gain-of-function or dominant negative (GOF/DN) variants. However, most current approaches rely on patient-specific target selection of SNVs in cis with the disease-causing variant. This individualized approach may limit broader ASO applicability and could exacerbate inequities in access. Population-level selection of ASO-targetable SNVs is an alternative approach not previously explored at scale. Methods: For a curated set of >400 disease genes with putative toxic GOF/DN mechanisms, we applied a greedy algorithm to identify ASO-targetable SNVs that maximize population coverage in the 1000 Genomes Project dataset. Population coverage was evaluated across ''superpopulation'' ancestry groups and assessed in multiple diverse replication datasets. For each prioritized SNV we attempted to design allele-specific 15-mer and 20-mer ASOs meeting standard chemistry and sequence criteria. The presence of prioritized SNVs was assessed in two local cohorts with GOF/DN disorders: infants with epilepsy diagnosed by rapid short-read genome sequencing, and children with long-read genome sequencing data generated for bespoke ASO development. Results: We identified 7,927 SNVs (median 17.5 per gene) achieving a median cumulative heterozygous population coverage of 88.9% across 408 disease genes. More than two-thirds of genes (70.6%) reached [≥]80% coverage using a median of only four prioritized SNVs. Coverage was consistently high for all ''superpopulation'' ancestry groups, with median coverage proportions of [≥]85%. Prioritized SNVs generalized to independent ancestrally diverse replication datasets, achieving median coverage of 86.4% in the Human Genome Diversity Project and 90.3% in the All of Us Research Program. Many prioritized targets were compatible with established ASO design principles, enabling generation of candidate allele-specific 15-mer and 20-mer ASOs at scale for future experimental validation. The presence of prioritized targets in the rapid short-read sequencing cohort, and the overlap between prioritized targets and manually curated long-read genome sequencing targets, supports the clinical relevance of population-informed target selection. All SNV targets and candidate allele-specific ASO sequences are available at hawk-eye.research.sickkids.ca/knockdown. Conclusions: Prioritization of common SNV targets may facilitate the development of ASO therapies with broader population coverage, helping move the field beyond single-patient applications and toward more equitable opportunities for access.

title: An OmpX mRNA-LNP vaccine induces protective humoral and cellular immunity against Klebsiella pneumoniae in a C57BL/6 mouse model
abstract: Klebsiella pneumoniae (KP) poses a significant threat to global public health, and effective preventive measures are urgently needed. The widespread antibiotic resistance of KP underscores the critical need for vaccine-based strategies. Although numerous vaccine candidates against KP have been investigated, none has yet been licensed. mRNA-LNP vaccines against KP have only recently begun to be explored, and their ability to deliver conserved outer membrane protein antigens remains largely untested. In this study, we constructed an mRNA vaccine encoding the highly conserved outer membrane protein X (OmpX) of KP-the first mRNA-LNP vaccine targeting this antigen-and evaluated its immunogenicity and protective efficacy in mice. Immunoinformatics analyses predicted concordance between the in silico and in vivo outcomes: bioinformatics tools were used to evaluate the antigenicity, immunogenicity, physicochemical parameters, and secondary and tertiary structures of OmpX, and the C-ImmSim server was used to simulate the vaccine-elicited immune responses. We then performed mouse immunization and challenge experiments to characterize the humoral and cellular immune responses induced by the OmpX vaccine. The mRNA vaccine was immunogenic in mice, eliciting high titers of OmpX-specific antibodies. OmpX-Fc mRNA-LNPs also induced robust cell-mediated immunity, with significantly elevated IFN-{gamma} and IL-4 levels indicative of combined Th1/Th2 cellular responses. Serum from OmpX-immunized mice promoted significantly greater complement-mediated KP cell lysis than serum from the alum or luciferase mRNA-LNP control groups. Notably, OmpX-Fc mRNA-LNP immunization conferred complete protection against lethal KP challenge, with 100% survival and a significant reduction in visceral bacterial burden. These data establish a promising mRNA vaccine strategy for inducing broad immune responses and promoting serotype-independent immunity against KP.

title: The deficiency of htr6 gene results in aberrant brain development and epileptiform discharges in zebrafish larvae.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The 5-Hydroxytryptamine Receptor 6 (HTR6) is a G protein-coupled receptor implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders and epilepsy. Our previous studies identified a somatic HTR6 mutation in brain surgical specimens from patients with focal cortical dysplasia type II, suggesting its potential involvement in disease pathogenesis.
OBJECTIVE: To investigate the functional role of the htr6 in zebrafish, focusing on its impact on neurodevelopment and seizure susceptibility.
METHODS: A F0 mosaic htr6 crispant zebrafish model was generated using CRISPR/Cas9 and validated by sequencing and TIDE analysis. Morphological and central nervous system (CNS) abnormalities were assessed at 5 days post-fertilization (dpf) by bright-field and Tg (HuC: eGFP) fluorescence imaging. Survival was monitored to 21 dpf. Locomotor behavior was evaluated using DanioVision, and epileptiform activity was examined by local field potential recording. Human HTR6 mRNA rescue experiments, transcriptome sequencing, and qPCR validation were also performed.
RESULTS: Deficiency of htr6 resulted in significant reductions in interocular and central nervous system areas. In addition, F0 mosaic htr6 crispant showed significantly reduced survival compared with Cas9 controls. While locomotor activity was markedly unaffected, electrophysiological recordings revealed epileptiform events in 9 of 24 F0 mosaic htr6 crispant but none in the Cas9 controls. Co-injection of human HTR6 mRNA rescued both neurodevelopmental abnormalities and epileptiform activity. Transcriptome analysis identified 402 differentially expressed genes, including the upregulation of 355 and the downregulation of 47 genes, suggesting profound neuronal impacts from htr6 deficiency. KEGG pathway enrichment analysis linked these changes to ABC transporters and metabolic pathways, demonstrating the significance of htr6 in maintaining neuronal health.
CONCLUSION: Deficiency of htr6 in zebrafish results in abnormal brain development and epileptiform activity, underscoring its critical role in neurodevelopment and neuronal excitability. These findings suggest the importance of HTR6 in neurodevelopment and epilepsy, providing a foundation for further research on therapeutic strategies targeting HTR6-related pathways in neurological disorders.

title: Individualized and Platform-Designated Gene-Editing Studies in the Registered Clinical Record: A Case-by-Case Census Against 148 Eligible Studies.
abstract: Introduction In February 2025, a single infant with carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 deficiency received a customized base-editing therapy, and individualized gene editing has since been discussed as an emerging category of care. No one has yet counted whether this category exists in the registered study record. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional census of interventional studies of human gene-editing agents registered on ClinicalTrials.gov. Records were retrieved through the ClinicalTrials.gov application programming interface, version 2, with a verbatim, intervention-scoped query and a fixed census date of 17 September 2026. Eligibility was verified from each record's own fields, and every exclusion is supported by the field value that justifies it. Two independent screening passes classified each eligible record as single-participant or n-of-1, multi-variant umbrella or platform-designated, or conventional cohort. Agreement was quantified with Cohen's kappa and a 95% confidence interval (CI). Records in the individualized and platform classes were re-verified against their complete registry entries and version histories. We also searched public US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) records for the regulatory route of each census record. Reporting follows the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) statement. Results Of 212 retrieved records, 64 were excluded, and 148 were eligible. Four eligible records were single-participant or n-of-1 designs, and three were multi-variant umbrella or platform-designated designs, giving a census of seven studies. Of the remainder, 140 were conventional cohorts, and one was an editing arm inside a non-editing platform trial. Version histories confirmed the four single-participant designs; one of them reached an enrolment of one through a revision made before enrolment began. The same histories showed that three other records had an enrolment of one or two only because of termination or under-enrolment. Only two of the 148 eligible records describe a construct designed for the individual participant. No publicly verifiable platform technology designation was located for any census record, and the census query returned no expanded-access record. Of 23 studies completed more than 12 months before the census, five had posted results (21.7%, Wilson 95% CI: 9.7%-41.9%); because this interval is wide, the figure is reported as context only. Agreement on design class was moderate (kappa, 0.540; 95% CI, 0.264-0.815). Conclusions Nineteen months after the first individualized CRISPR treatment, the registry contains seven individualized or platform-designated gene-editing studies, and only two records describe an individualized construct. The regulatory pathway used by the index case was not retrievable from the registry, and no regulatory route could be verified from public records; this is an absence of public evidence, not evidence that no route existed. These counts describe the ClinicalTrials.gov record, not the prevalence of individualized gene editing, and the design-class counts are provisional given moderate agreement.
