title: Randomized, Double-blind, Phase II Trial of Vortosiran to Evaluate Safety, Tolerability, and Pharmacodynamic Efficacy in Participants With Prior Venous Thromboembolism After Completion of Initial Anticoagulant Therapy (Cohort A) and in Cancer Patients at High Risk of Venous Thromboembolism (Cohort B)
abstract:
Blood clots remain a serious cause of illness and death. Long-term treatment and prevention of these clots with blood thinners is often limited by bleeding risk, drug interactions, and daily dosing, leading many patients to stop treatment early. Both cancer and chemotherapy further increase the risk of clot formation.

Vortosiran is an injectable therapy that lowers Factor XI (one of the body's natural clotting helpers) production in the liver, leading to a strong and long-lasting reduction in blood clotting activity with less risk of bleeding compared to current available treatments. Studies conducted so far have shown that vortosiran is safe and shows a dose-dependent Factor XI suppression (that is, a higher dose results in a higher level of suppression) that lasts for several months, supporting testing using a limited number of injections in patients who are at higher risk of blod clot formation.

This study aims to study how safe and effective vortosiran is in patients who have had blood clots in the past and in cancer patients who are at high risk of developing blood clots.
description:
Venous thromboembolism, encompassing DVT and PE, is a common condition with a durable risk of recurrence after completion of initial therapy with systemic anticoagulation. In a systematic review and meta-analysis of patients with a first unprovoked VTE who completed at least 3 months of anticoagulant therapy and then discontinued treatment, the cumulative incidence of recurrent VTE was approximately 10% in the first year, 25% at 5 years, and 36% at 10 years, with recurrent events carrying measurable case fatality (Khan et al, 2019). Decisions about extended therapy are frequently individualized because continued anticoagulation reduces VTE recurrence but also exposes patients to ongoing bleeding risk, treatment burden, and complexity of care.

Venous thromboembolism, including in patients with cancer and chemotherapy, remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality. Despite effective anticoagulants, long-term management is constrained by clinically meaningful bleeding risk, drug-drug interactions with anticoagulation therapy, and the need for continuous dosing and adherence. Furthermore, many patients discontinue therapy when they perceive recurrence risk to be moderate or when bleeding risk, treatment burden, or patient preference argues against indefinite anticoagulation. These combined factors constitute an unmet need for a convenient strategy that can reduce recurrent VTE risk with a lower risk of bleeding.

Vortosiran is a subcutaneously administered siRNA designed to selectively inhibit hepatic synthesis of FXI, resulting in robust and durable suppression of FXI activity. FXI inhibition is novel and innovative anti-thrombotic strategy inhibiting blood clot formation by the intrinsic pathway without interfering with hemostatic control through the extrinsic and commen clotting pathways. Thereby reducing blood clot formation and VTE without increasing the risk of bleeding compared to current available anti-coagulant treatments.

This Phase II trial is designed to establish dose-related FXI suppression, characterize safety with repeated dosing, and generate an initial signal on clinical outcomes in two VTE prevention settings.

This multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group Phase II trial will be conducted in two cohorts. Cohort A and Cohort B are independently enrolled and randomized. Participants are randomized (2:2:1) to low-dose vortosiran, high-dose vortosiran, or matched placebo, with dosing on Day X and Day Y and follow-up through Week 56. This trial aims to evaluate vortosiran in two complementary populations where FXI suppression could provide clinically relevant benefit and where the risk-benefit of conventional anticoagulation is often challenging.

* Cohort A (post-VTE, with participants judged to be at equipoise for extended therapy): Participants have completed 3 to 12 months of standard anticoagulation for symptomatic proximal DVT and/or PE as originally prescribed, and have had no recurrence during that initial treatment period. The cohort is restricted to patients for whom discontinuation of anticoagulation is consistent with local standard of care and where there is true equipoise about extended therapy vs only follow-up and observation.
* Cohort B (active cancer; high VTE risk): Ambulatory patients initiating a new course of systemic chemotherapy and with intermediate to high VTE risk (Khorana score ≥2), but no history of prior VTE.

title: Immunogenicity and Safety of Two Respiratory Syncytial Virus Vaccine Strategies in Lung and Allogeneic Haematopoietic Stem Cell Transplant Recipients: A Phase 2 Trial
abstract:
Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a major cause of acute respiratory infections (ARIs), which occur in seasonal outbreaks. Among the adult population, immunocompromised individuals, particularly lung transplant recipients and recipients of allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplants (HSCTs), are at the highest risk of severe ARI. RSV can also cause prolonged inflammation of the airways, leading to persistent deterioration in lung function. Thus, in lung transplant recipients, RSV is a major cause of chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD), the leading cause of lung transplant failure and mortality beyond the first post-transplant year. In recipients of ACSH, RSV infection is associated with the onset and/or worsening of bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome, which leads to increased mortality. Preventing RSV-associated lower respiratory tract disease (LRTD) and its short- and long-term consequences in these populations is therefore a key priority.

Three inactivated RSV vaccines, targeting the RSV fusion glycoprotein in its pre-fusion conformation (RSVpreF), have recently been approved for use in adults. These comprise two recombinant protein vaccines - one with an adjuvant (RSVpreF3-AS01, Arexvy®, GSK) and one without (RSVpreF, Abrysvo®, Pfizer) - and one mRNA vaccine. Although these vaccines have demonstrated their safety, immunogenicity and efficacy (reducing the risk of RSV-related IMRI by approximately 80-85 per cent) in adults aged 60 and over, the pivotal trials excluded immunocompromised patients.

To date, there is limited data on the efficacy, immunogenicity and tolerability of these vaccines in high-risk immunocompromised populations, such as recipients of bone marrow transplants and allogeneic stem cell transplants. Real-world studies suggest that RSV vaccines may reduce the risk of RSV-associated acute respiratory infection and hospitalisations in elderly immunocompromised adults. With regard to immunogenicity, the available cohort studies, conducted on small sample sizes, indicate that the vaccine response is heterogeneous and, overall, lower than that observed in immunocompetent older people. Preliminary data suggest that booster vaccination regimens may be necessary to optimise the immune response in these populations.

Given the significant morbidity associated with RSV in recipients of bone marrow transplants and allogeneic stem cell transplants, it is a priority to assess the immunogenicity and safety profile of RSV vaccines, and to determine the optimal vaccination schedule for these high-risk, immunocompromised populations.

The investigators hypothesise that the immune response to RSV vaccines in severely immunocompromised TP and ACSH recipients is weaker than in immunocompetent older adults, and that enhanced vaccination strategies may be required. In this study, two vaccination strategies will be evaluated in these populations:

* a single dose of the adjuvanted RSVpreF3-AS01 vaccine (Arexvy®),
* or a booster regimen comprising two doses of the non-adjuvanted RSVpreF vaccine (Abrysvo®), administered one month apart.

title: A Randomized Controlled Evaluation of Vitamin E Versus Silymarin on Liver Through Modulation of mRNA Profiles, NLRP3 Inflammasome Signaling, and Oxidative Stress in Non Diabetic MASLD Patients
abstract: MASLD (Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease), is a chronic liver condition marked by excessive fat buildup (steatosis) in liver cells, linked to at least one metabolic risk factor like obesity, type 2 diabetes, high blood lipids, or hypertension. Vitamin E serves as a recommended antioxidant therapy for select MASLD patients. It reduces liver inflammation markers such as ALT and AST, alongside benefits in steatosis and MASH resolution. Silymarin has clinical evidence supports its use as an adjunctive hepatoprotective agent due to antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antifibrotic effects.
description: To evaluate the efficacy of vitamin E (800 IU/day) versus silymarin (420 mg/day, divided TID) in modulating MASLD-associated mRNA expression, NLRP3 inflammasome levels, and MDA in adult patients with MASLD

title: An Exploratory Clinical Study to Evaluate the Safety, Feasibility, and Preliminary Efficacy of Intratumoral Delivery of CA9-Targeted Chimeric Antigen Receptor Macrophage Therapy in Patients With Unresectable or Metastatic Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma
abstract: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma is the most common type of kidney cancer. Although new treatments such as immune checkpoint inhibitors and targeted therapies have improved outcomes for many patients, some patients with advanced disease may still experience disease progression and require new treatment approaches. This study evaluates the safety, feasibility, and preliminary effectiveness of a novel cell therapy called CA9-targeted chimeric antigen receptor macrophage (CAR-M) therapy in patients with unresectable or metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma. CA9 is a protein that is highly expressed on many clear cell renal cell carcinoma cells and can be recognized by CAR-M cells. In this study, patients will receive a local injection of CM-BA-9, a CA9-targeted CAR-M cell product, into selected tumor lesions. The study will primarily assess treatment safety and tolerability, while also exploring whether this therapy can control tumor growth. The information collected in this study may help researchers better understand the potential role of CAR-M therapy in the treatment of advanced clear cell renal cell carcinoma.
description: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) represents the predominant histological subtype of renal cell carcinoma and is characterized by frequent alterations in the tumor microenvironment, including immune suppression and abnormal angiogenesis. Despite advances in immune checkpoint inhibitors and targeted therapies, patients with unresectable or metastatic ccRCC may develop resistance and have limited treatment options. Carbonic anhydrase IX (CA9) is a tumor-associated antigen highly expressed in most ccRCC tumors with limited expression in normal tissues, making it a potential therapeutic target. Chimeric antigen receptor macrophage (CAR-M) therapy is an emerging cellular immunotherapy strategy designed to enhance macrophage-mediated recognition and elimination of tumor cells. This exploratory clinical study is designed to evaluate the safety, feasibility, and preliminary efficacy of intratumoral delivery of CM-BA-9, a CA9-targeted CAR-M cell therapy product, in patients with unresectable or metastatic ccRCC. The study will evaluate treatment-related adverse events, dose-limiting toxicities, feasibility of product administration, and preliminary antitumor activity. The findings from this study will provide preliminary clinical evidence regarding the safety profile and potential therapeutic value of CA9-targeted CAR-M therapy and may support further investigation of cellular immunotherapy approaches for advanced ccRCC.

title: A Randomised Active-controlled Trial to Assess the Safety and Pharmacodynamics of Two Blinded Doses of Vortosiran and Open-label Apixaban in Patients With Non-valvular Atrial Fibrillation (AF)
abstract:
This is a randomised, actively controlled Phase IIb trial to evaluate the safety and pharmacodynamics (PD) of two blinded doses of subcutaneously administered vortosiran and open-label apixaban in patients with AF.

The trial consists of three groups including 50 participants each. The participants will be randomized to either the low dose group or the high dose group receiving vortosiran or to the group receiving apixaban. The treatment will be open-label for vortosiran vs apixaban. The vortosiran dose will be blinded to patients and investigators.

Both the low- and the high-dose group will receive two doses of vortosiran, the first dose at Day X and the second at Day Y. After 24 weeks, at the end of the vortosiran treatment period, the participants will start an open-label part of the trial and will be switched to standard-of-care apixaban treatment until Week 64 (End of Trial; EOT). Participants in the open-label apixaban arm will receive apixaban as standard of care during the entire trial.
description:
Atrial fibrillation (AF) is among the most prevalent cardiovascular conditions, affecting approximately 2 4% of the adult population worldwide. AF represents the most common sustained supraventricular arrhythmia and is associated with substantial morbidity, mortality, and health-care burden. Patients with AF are at an elevated risk of thromboembolic complications, particularly ischemic stroke and systemic embolism, while also facing an increased risk of bleeding associated with long-term antithrombotic therapy administered to prevent these complications. The principal aim of management in AF is to prevent stroke while minimizing haemorrhagic risk through careful risk stratification for both thromboembolic risk and bleeding risk, and informed and individualised treatment selections.

According to current guideline recommendations, oral anticoagulation is recommended for stroke prevention and may be guided by CHA2DS2 -VASc clinical risk assessment tool. Nonvitamin K antagonist oral anticoagulants (NOACs, also referred to as direct oral anticoagulants, or DOACs) are preferred over vitamin K antagonists (VKAs) in most cases due to their superior safety profile and lower incidence of intracranial bleeding. Bleeding risk can be assessed using validated tools such as HAS-BLED, and modifiable risk factors should be addressed to reduce overall treatment-related complications.

Despite a superior efficacy-safety profile of NOACs relative to VKAs, patients treated with NOACs remain at residual risk for stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular mortality. Furthermore, although NOACs are associated with reduced rates of intracranial haemorrhage compared with VKAs, they still confer a considerable risk of major bleeding and clinically relevant non-major bleeding events. Consequently, the clinical need for strategies that further optimize the balance between thromboembolic prevention and bleeding risk in patients with AF remains.

Recent advances have positioned coagulation factor XI (FXI) inhibition as a promising strategy in anti-thrombotic drug development. FXI is a crucial element of the intrinsic coagulation pathway, and genetic FXI deficiency (haemophilia C) is typically associated with only mild bleeding even in complete deficiency, suggesting the potential for improved safety compared to conventional anti-thrombotic drugs by disengaging physiologic haemostasis from pathologic, intraluminal thrombosis. FXI inhibition reliably prolongs activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) in vitro, and epidemiological studies demonstrate that inherited FXI deficiency confers protection against venous thromboembolism (VTE) and ischemic stroke. Conversely, elevated circulating activated FXI (FXIa) is linked to higher risks of ischemic stroke, VTE, and acute coronary syndrome (ACS). Contemporary research utilizing coagulometric assays has confirmed FXIa and tissue factor activation in patients with stable coronary artery disease, ACS of less than 12 hours' duration, and heart failure, reinforcing FXI's role as a pathogenic factor in these conditions.

From the patient perspective, the limitations of current DOAC-based strategies extend beyond rare catastrophic haemorrhage to include a spectrum of patient-relevant bleeding and treatment burdens that erode quality of life and adherence. Easy bruising, epistaxis, gingival bleeding, menorrhagia, and minor gastrointestinal bleeding are often labelled nuisance or non-major events in clinical trials, but patients describe these as anxiety-provoking, stigmatizing, and disruptive to daily activities. Such events, together with polypharmacy, twice-daily dosing for some agents, drug drug interactions, and the need for uninterrupted long-term therapy, frequently lead to missed doses, dose reductions, or unsupervised discontinuation of DOACs, which in turn compromises stroke protection at the population level. In parallel, important patient subgroups including those with advanced chronic kidney disease or dialysis, advanced liver disease, prior intracranial haemorrhage, or frailty have been underrepresented in pivotal DOAC trials and often withheld treatment or remain untreated because of bleeding concerns. By targeting FXI, vortosiran has the potential to dissociate pathological thrombosis from physiological haemostasis, and to deliver sustained antithrombotic protection with a lower risk bleeding than currently available therapies and an adherence profile that is better aligned with patients' priorities and lived experience.

Clinical trials targeting FXI inhibition in the context of cardiovascular disease, including AF, are ongoing or recently completed. Several Phase 2 and 3 trials are investigating FXI/FXIa inhibitors by use of different modalities such as monoclonal antibodies and small molecules across multiple high-risk groups, evaluating efficacy and bleeding outcomes against standard anticoagulants for stroke prevention in AF (SPAF). These studies collectively support the notion that FXI/FXIa may be a favourable anticoagulation target, capable of reducing thrombotic events with a lower side effect profile, especially bleeding, compared to traditional agents. However, while several trials confirm safety advantages, data on efficacy remain to be further demonstrated, necessitating continued research focus. Vortosiran is an N-acetyl galactosamine (GalNAc) conjugated small interfering ribonucleic acid (siRNA), enabling highly specific and highly durable enrichment of the siRNA in hepatocytes, offering a modality specifically inhibiting the production of FXI. Vortosiran is under development to achieve a durable antithrombotic effect by reducing the levels of FXI.

The rationale for the current trial is based on data from multiple Phase 2 and 3 studies of FXI/FXIa inhibitors that have assessed FXI clotting activity and the effect on venous thrombosis inhibition, and is currently being tested for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation patients. Based on the collective observations for these studies, that FXI clotting activity inhibition translates into a lower risk of thrombosis with a lower risk of bleeding compared to standard of care, the ongoing Phase 3 studies, and that vortosiran treatment can achieve identical or even higher degrees of FXI clotting activity inhibition, there is a rationale that vortosiran could potentially improve benefit-risk balance for stroke prevention in patients with atrial fibrillation compared to standard of care with FXa inhibitors.

title: The Supplementation With Urolithin A During Pulmonary Rehabilitation in COPD (SUPRA-COPD) Trial
abstract:
SUPRA-COPD is a multicenter triple-blind, parallel arm, placebo-controlled randomized controlled trial investigating the efficacy and safety of Urolithin A supplementation during pulmonary rehabilitation in patients with COPD.

The goal of the SUPRA-COPD study is to investigate whether Urolithin A supplementation during pulmonary rehabilitation in patients with COPD improves exercise tolerance, along with several other clinically important outcomes, above and beyond pulmonary rehabilitation participation alone.

Study participation will be approximately 14 weeks and involves in-person visits evaluating exercise tolerance before and after PR.
description:
Pulmonary rehabilitation is a central standard of care intervention for chronic disease management in patients with COPD.

Urolithin A is a natural health product found in berries, pomegranates, and nuts. Urolithin A is approved by the FDA and Health Canada, but no study to date has investigated whether taking Urolithin A improves outcomes in patients with COPD. In previous studies in people without COPD, Urolithin A has been found to stimulate the cellular process known as mitophagy, improving the function of mitochondria, as well as functional capacity. In patients with COPD, it is therefore possible that Urolithin A may lead to improved exercise capacity and muscle strength.

Urolithin A, in combination with pulmonary rehabilitation, may lead to a greater benefit in patients with COPD in terms of exercise capacity and other important health outcomes than pulmonary rehabilitation alone.

Patients with COPD participating in a standard pulmonary rehabilitation program are being recruited for this study. Study participants will be randomly assigned and provided either with Urolithin A or with a visually identical placebo, to be taken every day during the 8-week pulmonary rehabilitation program. Study outcomes will then be compared between the Urolithin A group and the placebo group.

title: A Multicenter, Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled, Phase 2a Clinical Study to Evaluate the Efficacy, Safety, and Pharmacokinetic Characteristics of Kylo-0603 Capsule in Study Participants With Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD)
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a metabolic stress-related liver injury closely associated with insulin resistance, with a global prevalence of approximately 25%. It may progress to metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), which can lead to cirrhosis, end-stage liver disease, and increased cardiovascular risk, representing a major unmet medical need. Thyroid hormone receptor beta (THRβ) is predominantly expressed in the liver; selective agonism regulates hepatic lipid metabolism, reduces fat accumulation, suppresses hepatic inflammation and fibrosis, and may delay MASH progression. Kylo-0603 is a liver-targeted, highly selective THRβ agonist modified with GalNAc to enrich hepatic exposure and reduce peripheral effects. This multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 2a study will evaluate the efficacy, safety, and pharmacokinetics of once-daily oral Kylo-0603 capsules in approximately 120 participants with MASLD and overweight or obesity. Participants will be randomized 1:1:1:1 to Kylo-0603 8 mg, 12 mg, 16 mg, or placebo for 12 weeks. The primary endpoint is the percentage change from baseline in liver fat content assessed by MRI-PDFF at Week 12.

title: A Randomized, Double-blind, Placebo-controlled Phase II Trial to Evaluate Safety, and Pharmacodynamics of Repeated Subcutaneously Administered RBD1119 in Participants With CAD
abstract:
CAD is driven by atherosclerosis in the coronary arteries and is a major cause of myocardial infarction, heart failure, arrhythmias, and premature death. Despite contemporary secondary prevention including lipid lowering, revascularization when indicated, and antiplatelet therapy, participants with established CAD, particularly those post-ACS, remain at clinically meaningful residual risk of recurrent atherothrombotic events.

Intensifying antithrombotic therapy can reduce ischemic events but typically increases bleeding, as exemplified by the addition of low dose rivaroxaban to aspirin in stable atherosclerotic disease. This persistent efficacy-safety trade-off supports development of antithrombotic approaches that reduce pathological thrombosis while preserving hemostasis.

RBD1119 is a GalNAc-conjugated siRNA that targets factor XI mRNA in hepatocytes. The GalNAc moiety binds the asialoglycoprotein receptor on hepatocyte surfaces, enabling receptor mediated endocytosis and preferential hepatic uptake. Once internalized, RBD1119 mediates cleavage of factor XI mRNA via the RNA interference pathway, reducing hepatic factor XI expression and lowering circulating factor XI levels.

This multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase II trial will evaluate the PD, safety, and PK of subcutaneously administered RBD1119 in participants with stable coronary artery disease (CAD).
description:
CAD is caused by atherosclerosis in the coronary arteries and remains a leading cause of MI, heart failure, arrhythmias, and premature death, with substantial residual risk of recurrent atherothrombotic events even after standard secondary prevention. More intensive antithrombotic therapy can lower ischemic events, but this benefit is often offset by increased bleeding, highlighting the need for treatments that better separate antithrombotic efficacy from bleeding risk. Factor XI, part of the intrinsic coagulation pathway, has emerged as a promising target because its inhibition reduces thrombin amplification and prolongs aPTT without affecting prothrombin time, suggesting potential for safer anticoagulation with less disruption of normal hemostasis.

The trial comprises screening, treatment, and long-term safety follow-up periods. Participants will be allocated to one of three different dose levels of RBD1119 or placebo: low-dose (n=40), medium-dose (n=60), high-dose (n=60) or placebo (n=40). Approximately 200 participants will be randomized.

Randomization to the RBD1119 low-dose dose group and corresponding placebo proceeds without dose-specific staggering. Randomization to the medium-dose group is initially limited to 10 participants, comprising 8 participants assigned to RBD1119 medium-dose and 2 assigned to placebo. Further randomization is paused until participants have received Dose X on Day Y and completed safety follow-up through Day 43. Randomization resumes only after IDMC review, a recommendation to continue, and Sponsor authorization. Initiation of the high-dose group requires prior IDMC review of the initial medium-dose cohort and Sponsor authorization. The same initial cohort, safety follow-up, IDMC review, and authorization process is then applied to the high-dose group. A planned IDMC review will not be delayed solely because fewer than all 10 participants in an initial dose cohort have received the second dose or completed follow-up through Day 43.

title: A Phase 1/2 Multicenter Clinical Study to Evaluate Safety, Tolerability, Biological Activity, and Efficacy of an In Vivo LNP-Delivered Prime Editor Complex (PM647a) for the Treatment of Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency (AATD)
abstract:
The purpose of this study is to evaluate the safety, tolerability, biological activity, and initial efficacy of PM647a, an investigational Prime Editing therapy, in adults and adolescents with Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency (AATD).

AATD is caused by a mutation (change) in a gene called SERPINA1 that prevents the cells in your liver from producing a functional protein (alpha-1 anti-trypsin; AAT) that helps protect your lung tissue. PM647a is designed to precisely correct the prevalent disease-causing mutation (SERPINA1 Pi\*Z (E342K)) with the goal of restoring functional AAT. This is the first study of PM647a in humans. Participants will receive a single intravenous (IV) infusion of PM647a and will be monitored closely to evaluate safety, how the body responds to treatment, changes in AAT protein levels, and whether treatment may improve signs and symptoms of AATD.
description:
This is a Phase 1/2 open label study evaluating PM647a in adults and adolescents with Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency (AATD) who are homozygous for the SERPINA1 p.E342K pathogenic variant, also known as the PiZ allele (PiZZ genotype). Enrollment and treatment will begin with Group A, which includes participants with lung manifestations only. Group B will open subsequently and will include participants with both lung and liver manifestations or liver manifestations only. Additionally, a set of 3 to 6 participants with AATD penetrant lung disease (with or without liver disease), will be enrolled to further understand the effects of PM647a on local pharmacodynamic effects through BAL (BAL cohort).

The study will evaluate the safety of PM647a, determine an appropriate dose for future studies, and assess whether treatment restores normal synthesis and secretion of functional AAT and improves clinical measures of AATD. Participants will receive a single IV infusion of PM647a and will undergo regular safety evaluations, laboratory testing, imaging, and clinical assessments for approximately 48 weeks after treatment. Participants will then be asked to enroll in a separate long-term follow-up study to continue monitoring safety and treatment effects for an additional 14 years.

title: Systemic and Topical Geroprotective Rejuvenation Assessed by START/REST Aging Clocks
abstract:
This study tests whether certain medicines and a skin treatment can slow down or partly reverse the body's aging process.

As people age, the activity of their genes changes in predictable ways. Researchers can now measure a person's "biological age" from these gene-activity patterns in skin and blood. This study uses that measurement to see whether treatment can lower a person's biological age compared with their own starting point.

Adults in the study take geroprotective ("age-protecting") agents by mouth or by injection. A separate skin serum containing small anti-aging peptides is applied to certain areas of skin, and those treated areas are compared with untreated areas on the same person.

Skin and blood samples are taken at set times to measure biological age and markers of cell aging before, during, and after treatment. The main goal is to find out whether treatment lowers measured biological age in skin and blood. The study also looks at whether the treatments are safe and well tolerated.
description:
This is a prospective, single-group interventional study with two treatment components, systemic and topical. Each participant contributes paired treated and untreated samples and serves as their own internal control, reducing inter-individual variability in clock measurements.

Systemic component: participants receive geroprotective agents administered orally or subcutaneously. Candidate agents include metformin, low-dose chloroquine, ivermectin, and a defined nutritional supplement (collagen lysate; black seed oil or its active constituent thymoquinone; urolithin; and controlled pH modulation with citric, acetic, or glycolic acid), used alone or in combination per protocol.

Topical component: an aqueous serum of small, water-soluble anti-aging peptides below the \~500-Dalton stratum corneum penetration cutoff - GHK-Cu (\~404 Da), AHK-Cu (\~418 Da), Epitalon (\~390 Da), PGP/Pro-Gly-Pro (\~269 Da), and CLV/Cys-Leu-Val (\~333 Da) - is applied at approximately 1-3 mg/mL to defined skin sites. Treated sites are compared with matched untreated contralateral, adjacent, or distant sites on the same participant.

Blood, skin biopsies, exfoliated skin cells, plucked hair follicles, and saliva are used to assess treatment effect locally and systemically.

Objectives Primary: determine whether treatment produces a statistically significant reduction in START/REST-derived transcriptomic biological age in skin, hair, saliva, and peripheral blood, relative to each participant's baseline and untreated reference tissue.

Secondary: characterize changes in molecular markers of cellular senescence, inflammaging/SASP, transcriptional fitness, and metabolic cofactors; assess concordance between systemic and local rejuvenation signals; evaluate safety and tolerability of each agent across the treatment period.

Procedures and Sampling Skin biopsies, exfoliated keratinocytes, plucked follicles, saliva, and blood are collected at scheduled baseline, on-treatment, and post-treatment timepoints for transcriptomic profiling and senescence-marker analysis.

Outcome Definition Age-reversal is defined prospectively as a statistically significant decrease in clock-derived biological age in treated tissue relative to both baseline and untreated reference tissue.

Significance The study aims to provide the first transcriptional clock-anchored human evidence that combined systemic and topical geroprotection can drive coordinated rejuvenation across tissues.

title: A Phase 1b Study of Tocilizumab Combined With Chemo-Immunotherapy in Metastatic Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Patients With Cancer-Associated Weight Loss and Elevated Inflammatory Markers. The TOCI Study
abstract: This is a Phase 1b/2, multi-site, single-arm, open-label, non-randomized study looking at whether adding tocilizumab to standard treatment for metastatic Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC) is safe, possible, and effective. The study includes people with metastatic NSCLC, that is lung cancer that has spread, who have experienced significant loss of weight or muscle mass.
description:
Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality globally, with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounting for approximately 85% of all diagnoses. For patients with metastatic NSCLC lacking actionable driver mutations (e.g., EGFR, ALK), the standard first-line therapeutic strategy involves immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) targeting the programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) or programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) axis, administered either as monotherapy or in combination with platinum-doublet chemotherapy. While these regimens have significantly improved overall survival (OS), a substantial proportion of patients fail to derive durable clinical benefit, and long-term survival rates for metastatic disease remain suboptimal, often due to host-related factors that impair the anti-tumor immune response.

A critical determinant of poor therapeutic outcomes in advanced NSCLC is cancer-associated cachexia (CAC), a multifactorial paraneoplastic syndrome characterized by systemic inflammation, negative protein-energy balance, and the involuntary loss of skeletal muscle mass (sarcopenia). Primary observational studies demonstrate that nutritional derangements closely associated with cachexia - such as significant weight loss and malnutrition - are highly prevalent in lung cancer, particularly in advanced disease, with lung cancer-specific cohorts reporting rates ranging from approximately 35% - 70% depending on disease stage and assessment method. Unlike starvation, it is driven by aberrant systemic inflammation and not fully reversible via nutritional support.

Clinically, cachexia is defined by the international consensus (Fearon criteria) as weight loss \>5% over 6 months, or weight loss \>2% in individuals with a body mass index (BMI) \< 20 kg/m2 or sarcopenia. Sarcopenia is specifically defined by a low skeletal muscle index (SMI) at the L3 vertebral level, with widely validated cutoffs of \< 52.4 cm2/m2 for men and \< 8.5 cm2/m2 for women.

This is a Phase 1b/2, multi-site, single-arm, open-label, non-randomized study looking at whether adding tocilizumab to standard treatment for metastatic Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC) is safe, possible, and effective. The study includes people with metastatic NSCLC, that is lung cancer that has spread, who have experienced significant loss of weight or muscle mass.

Primary Objective Evaluate the safety/feasibility and efficacy of adding tocilizumab to standard first-line chemo-immunotherapy in biomarker-selected patients with stage IV NSCLC, defined by weight loss ≥5% within the prior 6 months, or ≥2% if BMI \< 20 kg/m².

Co-primary endpoint 1: Safety/Feasibility Proportion of patients completing four cycles of chemo-IO + tocilizumab without grade ≥3 autoimmune or non-hematological treatment-related adverse events (TRAE). Feasibility will be defined as ≥80% completion; unacceptable toxicity as \>30% incidence of grade ≥3 serious AEs.

Co-primary endpoint 2: Progression-Free Survival Rate at 6 months Proportion of patients alive and progression-free at 6 months after starting therapy per RECIST v1.1, estimated by Kaplan-Meier and presented with a 95% CI.

Secondary Objectives Assess the effect of tocilizumab on body composition, inflammatory biomarkers, and treatment response.

Secondary Endpoints: change in weight/muscle mass (CT-based sarcopenia/Fearon index); Overall Response Rate (ORR); median Overall Survival Rate; and CRP levels from baseline to end of treatment.

Correlative Objectives Evaluate associations between treatment response (PFS rate at 6 months, ORR) and baseline inflammatory biomarkers (CRP) as well as molecular biomarkers (KRAS, STK11) identified by next-generation sequencing (NGS) of tumor tissue.

Exploratory Objectives Identify associations between treatment response (PFS rate at 6 months, ORR) and longitudinal measurements of CRP, IL-6, Cyclin D1 and Bcl-xL mRNA, as well as baseline PTPRT methylation.

Participants will go through the screening and baseline process to assess eligibility. If eligible, participants will attend study treatment visits every 21 days for about 3 months, an End of Treatment (EOT) visit about 30 days after the last dose of treatment, and follow up for up to 12 months after the EOT visit. Tocilizumab will be administered in addition to standard treatment regimens for NSCLC, at a dose of 8 mg/kg intravenous (IV) once every three weeks (once every 21 days); on day one of each treatment cycle. Tocilizumab is administered as a single IV drip infusion over 1 hour; it cannot be administered as bolus or push. Tocilizumab will be given for 4 doses, at the beginning of treatment, or until disease progression or unacceptable toxicities.

The study will be open at 4 VA hospitals, and planned enrollment is about 43 participants in total with about 11 participants from each site. This research study is expected to take about 4 years. Individual participation in the study will take about 18 months.

title: Study on the Mechanism of Central Obesity Induced by Sleep Restriction and the Therapeutic Effect of n-3 Polyunsaturated Fatty Acid: a Randomized, Double-blind, Placebo-controlled Trial (COSPA Study)
abstract:
This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial aims to investigate whether n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) supplementation attenuates abdominal visceral fat accumulation induced by experimental sleep restriction.

Forty healthy adults aged 18-50 years will be randomly assigned to receive n-3 PUFA supplementation (approximately 1.1 g/day of EPA and DHA) or a matching placebo. The intervention will last approximately 75 days, including a 19-day residential sleep protocol consisting of 3 adaptation days, 14 days of sleep restriction (4 hours per night), and 2 recovery days.

The primary outcome is the change in abdominal visceral adipose tissue area measured by CT. Additional assessments include body composition, metabolic and inflammatory markers, gut microbiota, microbial metabolites, and adipose tissue molecular profiles.
description:
Experimental sleep restriction provides a controlled model for investigating the metabolic consequences of insufficient sleep. This study will examine whether n-3 PUFA supplementation modifies visceral fat accumulation and related biological responses during sleep restriction.

Participants will undergo a standardized residential sleep protocol with continuous polysomnographic monitoring. Abdominal CT will be performed on Days 3 and 17 to assess changes in visceral and subcutaneous adipose tissue. Additional measurements will include dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, ambulatory blood pressure monitoring, cognitive assessments, biological sample collection, and exploratory molecular analyses.

The study will also explore potential mechanisms involving gut microbiota, microbial metabolism, inflammation, and adipose tissue responses.

title: Impact of Significant Surgical Reduction of Adipose Tissue on Plasma Levels and Genetic Expression of Adipokines Associated With Ischemic Heart Disease in Type I Obesity.
abstract:
Adipose tissue is with endocrine properties and secretes many cytokines. Some of these cytokines are concerned with ischemic heart disease. I hypothesized that significant surgical reduction in adipose tissue mass leads to decrease in its cell population which may pose significantly reduced production of adipokines ( Leptin and Angiotensin) associated with ischemic heart disease in obese people.

Study objectives are analysis of Leptin, Angiotensin-II, mRNA expression analysis of leptin, leptin receptor and Angiotensin-II. investigation of genetic variations in the Leptin, Leptin receptors, Angiotensin-I and Angiotensin-II receptors, confirm SNPs of selected sample. Ddetermination of the association of genetic variation in Leptin receptor, angiotensin-I and Angiotensin-II receptors with Leptin and Angiotensin-II levels and determination of effect of genetic variation on the transcriptional regulation.

Case control study having 212 patients (106 patients in each group) with type I Obese adults, both males and pre-menopausal females belonging to ASA 1 and 2 requiring stagged liposuction will be included. Exclusion of subjects with Diabetes mellitus, Metabolic syndrome, Endocrine disorders, on statin drugs, not willing to participate.

After informed consent, blood samples will be taken to quantify plasma levels of Leptin and Angiotensin II pre-operatively by ELISA.

DNA will also be extracted from blood and SNPs will be analysed. The selected SNPs will be amplified by PCR and product will be purified and analysed by agarose gel electrophoresis.

Patients will undergo liposuction and RNA will be isolated from subcutaneous adipose tissue for reverse transcription.

After 3 months, patients will be called back for second session of liposuction and plasma level of Leptin and Angiotensin II will be quantified again. Similarly, expression profile of transcription factors will also be analysed again. Paired t-test will be used to compare clinical parameters like serum adipokines levels and adipokines expression levels and p value \<0.05 will be taken as statistically significant. The results will be utilized to determine impact of surgical reduction on plasma level and expression of the adipokines in minimizing cardiovascular risk factors.
description:
INTRODUCTION:

Overweight and obesity belong to the main public healthcare problems in many developed countries. Causes of obesity are considered to be the combination of genetic, epigenetic and environmental factors. In case of morbid obesity, the human organism suffers from an excess of subcutaneous and visceral adipose tissue.1 Adipose tissue plays a principal role in overall metabolic homeostasis, and its dysfunction can lead to metabolic disorders, most notably type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.2 Mature adipocytes express all components of the renin- angiotensin system (RAS) including angiotensin Il (Ang II), and also express the type 1 (AT1) and type 2 (AT 2) angiotensin receptor subtypes.3 For cardiovascular disease, perivascular adipose tissue (PVAT) is a specific adipose tissue and now recognized to be an endocrine organ with important physiological and pathological effects on vascular homeostasis and vascular diseases.(4) PVAT dysfunction may induce several pathophysiological states such as obesity, atherosclerosis or hypertension.4-6 There are essentially two major types of adipose tissue with different functions: brown adipose tissue (BAT) containing multiple lipid droplets and densely packed mitochondria, and white adipose tissue (WAT) with large lipid droplets and relatively low expression levels of UCP-1(mitochondrial uncoupling protein-1).4 Ang II is produced from angiotensin I (Ang I as a result of the catalytic action of angiotensin-converting enzyme I (ACE-1). Ang Il plays an important role in the regulation of blood volume, blood pressure, cardiac function, and electrolyte balance.7 On the other hand, Leptin is a protein classified within the adipokine family and is currently recognized as a hormone consisting of 167 amino acids with a molecular weight of 16 kD. It is predominantly synthesized in adipocytes, and its production is contingent upon the volume of fat deposits in the body. It is known that leptin inhibits the orexigenic pathway and stimulates the anorexigenic pathway, underscoring its pivotal role in body weight regulation.8 The relationship between leptin and the RAAS is bi-directional. Leptin not only stimulates sympathetic nervous system activation and angiotensin-dependent mechanisms, but it also seems to be a major driver in the aldosterone production in obese patients.9 Moreover, leptin appears to play a role in heart protection. The increased blood volume in obese patients increases cardiac output and stimulates biomechanical stress and structural remodeling that may result in cardiac hypertrophy. A correlation between plasma leptin levels and cardiac hypertrophy has been clinically demonstrated.10 There is evidence for both angiotensin and leptin receptors in several brain regions involved in regulation of sympathetic nerve activity. Ang II may modulate the action of leptin and adiponectin in obesity. Blocking of RAS increases plasma adiponectin suggesting a role of Ang II in decreased levels of adiponectin. Supporting this, Ang I1 infusion decreased plasma adiponectin and adiponectin mRNA in adipose tissue. Ang II also interacts with adiponectin in their target cells.11 Considering the role of Ang II and Leptin in the regulation of obesity, I hypothesized that significant surgical reduction in adipose tissue mass leads to decrease in its cell population which may pose significantly reduced production of adipokines associated with ischemic heart disease in obese people.

OBJECTIVES:

Analysis of adipokine levels (Leptin, Angiotensin-II) in patients with type I obesity (Quazi Experimental).

mRNA expression analysis of leptin, leptin receptor and Angiotensin-II (Quazi Experimental).

Investigation of genetic variations in the Leptin, Leptin receptors, Angiotensin-I and Angiotensin-II receptors (Case Control).

Confirm SNPs of selected sample. Determine the association of genetic variation in Leptin receptor, Angiotensin-I and Angiotensin-II receptors with Leptin and Angiotensin-II levels.

Determine effect of genetic variation on the transcriptional regulation.

OPERATIONAL DEFINITION:

Significant Fat Reduction A removal of 1 liter or more lipoaspirate through liposuction will be considered as significant.

Tumescence Injection of fluid in the fat removal area containing Ringer Lactate each litter with 40ml 2% xylocaine and 1ml of 1:1000 Epinephrine till the area is blanched and showing fountain sign.

Polymorphism Defined a discontinuous genetic variation resulting in the occurrence of several different forms or types of individuals among the members of a single species. A discontinuous genetic variation divides the individuals of a population into two or more sharply distinct forms.

HYPOTHESIS:

Significant surgical reduction of adipose tissue reduces the level of adipokines (Leptin and Angiotensin) associated with cardiac risk in plasma and their expression in adipose tissue.

MATERIAL AND METHODS:

Study design Case control study. Setting The study will be conducted at Advanced Research Centre for Biomedical Sciences (ARCBS), KEMU and Jinnah Burn and Reconstructive Surgery Center / AIMC, Lahore.

Duration The study will be expected to complete within two years after the approval of synopsis.

Sample size Sample size of 212 patients (106 patients in each group) is estimated by using 95% confidence level and 10% absolute precision with expected percentage LEPrs7799039 as in FEN as 19.1% and healthy control as 14.1%.(12) n = Z 1-α/2 \[P1 (1- P1) +P2 (1- P2)\] d2 Z 1-α/2 = confidence level 95 % = 1.96 P1 = population proportion I = 19.1% P2 = population proportion II = 14% d2 = absolute precision 10% SNP analysis will be done in all the 212 subjects with 106 taken as cases (Obese type 1) and 106 as controls (Normal BMI).

Out of 106 cases, liposuction will be performed in selected subjects. Similarly, sequencing will be done in selected subjects. Sampling technique Non Probability Consecutive Sampling.

SAMPLE SELECTION:

Inclusion Criteria: Type I Obese adults, both males and pre-menopausal females, Patients requiring stagged liposuction, American Society of Anesthesiology (ASA) class 1 and 2 (as determined by consultant anesthesiologist) Exclusion Criteria: Patients who are with Diabetes mellitus, Metabolic syndrome, Endocrine disorders, on statin drugs, not willing to participate.

DATA COLLECTION PROCEDURE:

Informed consent will be obtained from the study subjects for donation of blood and adipose tissue samples in the proposed study, which will be conducted under a protocol approved by the Institutional Review Board of King Edward Medical University (Appendix I). The information of the study subjects will be kept confidential, and the subjects will be recruited against lab record number or archive number.

Sample Collection: Patients will undergo lipo-aspiration under tumescence by Colman's technique. Each unit of tumescent fluid will include xylocaine 40ml, Hartmann's solution 1000ml and 1ml adrenaline. A multi hole 5mm liposuction cannula attached with suction machine will be inserted through the incisions using controlled back and forth motion. All the patients will be followed fortnightly. Analysis of pre and post procedure blood and adipose tissue samples will be done. For DNA extraction, 5ml blood will be collected.

Quantification of Serum Adipokines levels by ELISA: Serum will be separated after clotting through centrifugation at 3000 rpm and stored at -70°C. ELIS A will be performed on samples by standard protocol for the quantification of adipokines (Leptin, Angiotensin I1) pre-operatively and three months post operatively DNA Extraction: 5ml blood will be collected in EDTA-coated tubes. Genomic DNA will be extracted from whole blood by using commercially available kits.

Restriction Fragment Length Polymorphism Analysis of SNPs: The selected SNPs will be amplified by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) by using the primers given in Table 1. Amplicons will be detected on 2.5% agarose gel and stained with DNA gel stain. DNA bands will be detected by gel documentation instrument under UV light. PCR product will be purified by using commercially available kit and digested with restriction enzymes. The restriction product will be analyzed by agarose gel electrophoresis.

Sequencing of SNPs: Sequencing of SNPs will be done using specific primers by Sanger Sequence using ABI 3500, Genetic Analyzer (Applied Biosystems, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) and the sequences will be analyzed using the BLAST program at National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI). Amino acid sequences will be predicted by the standard code and will be aligned using the ExPASY online tool for translation. Sequencing will be done on study subjects and compared with same number of healthy persons for comparison.

RNA Isolation and cDNA Synthesis: RNA will be isolated from subcutaneous adipose tissue by using commercially available kits. 1ug RNA will be reverse transcribed using commercially available Transcription First Strand cDNA kit and oligo (dT) primers.

Real-time PCR Analysis for Gene Expression Analysis: Quantitative real-time PCR analysis will be carried out by using SYBR Green real-time PCR Master Mix and an ARIAmix, real-time PCR system (Agilent Technologies). Cycling conditions for real-time PCR will be 3 min at 95°C, followed by 40 cycles of 30 S at 95°C, 30 S at 60°C and 30 S at 72°C. Results will be analysed using the ΔΔCt method and will be presented as fold difference in mRNA level relative to GAPDH. The expression profile of transcription factors will be analyzed.

DATA ANALYSIS PRODECURE:

Data will be entered and analyzed using statistical Package for Social Sciences (SPSS-26). Quantitative variables like age, BMI, lipid profile and adipokine levels will be presented as mean ± SD. Qualitative variables like family history of obesity, family history of heart diseases and gender will be presented frequency and percentages. Paired t-test will be used to compare clinical parameters like serum adipokines levels and adipokines expression levels. Odds ratio and 95% CI will be used for SNP analysis. Whereas p value \<0.05 will be taken as statistically significant. Pearson equation will be used to determine association of adipokines levels with clinical parameters and expression levels.

OUTCOME \& UTILIZATION:

The results will be utilized to determine impact of surgical reduction on plasma level and expression of the adipokines in minimizing cardiovascular risk factors.

title: A Randomized, Double-blind, Placebo-controlled, Single-Dose Phase 1 Study to Evaluate the Safety, Tolerability, Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamic Profile of RG002C0106 Injection in Healthy Participants
abstract:
The goal of this clinical trial is to learn if RG002C0106 is safe in healthy participants . It will also learn about how the drug is absorbed, distributed， metablized and excrited. The main questions it aims to answer are:

What medical problems do participants have when taking RG002C0106? Researchers will compare RG002C0106 to a placebo (a look-alike substance that contains no drug) to see if RG002C0106 is safe to participants.

Participants will:

Take RG00C2C0106 or a placebo once. Visit the clinic once every 2 weeks/1 month for checkups and tests.
description:
This is a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, single-dose, phase I study in healthy adult participants.

A Safety Review Committee (SRC), composed of the sponsor, the Investigator and the sponsor representatives, will be established prior to study initiation.

Escalation to the next higher dose level will only be permitted if the SRC confirms an acceptable safety and tolerability profile based on safety data and available PK/PD assessments collected.

title: Inducible tristetraprolin suppresses malignant phenotypes and directly targets glucosaminyl (N-acetyl) transferase 3 in lung cancer cells.
abstract: Tristetraprolin (TTP/ZFP36) regulates mRNA expression; however, its target genes in lung cancer remain unclear. Using a CRISPR/Cas9-engineered doxycycline-inducible TTP knock-in model in H460 cells, we investigated the function of TTP in lung cancer cells. Induced TTP expression suppressed clonogenicity, spheroid growth, proliferation, invasion, and migration. Transcriptomic analyses integrated with public lung adenocarcinoma datasets identified glucosaminyl (N-acetyl) transferase 3 (GCNT3) as a key effector of TTP in cancer progression. Mechanistic analyses indicated direct TTP binding to GCNT3, reducing its expression. GCNT3 knockdown attenuated invasion and migration, and GCNT3 re-expression in TTP-induced cells restored and further enhanced these malignant behaviors, establishing a functional relationship between TTP and GCNT3. Transient TTP expression in H1299 cells also reduced GCNT3 levels. These findings identify GCNT3 as a direct TTP target that contributes to malignant behaviors in lung cancer cells, providing insights into post-transcriptional regulation of tumor progression.
